en: The Perfection of Wisdom in Eighteen Thousand Lines, Chapters 55–70.
Chapter 55. [f.
215b] Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even while in a dream, does not long for the level of a śrāvaka, nor the level of a pratyekabuddha, nor anything within the triple world, and does not give rise to a mind that finds merit in them,
but perceives all phenomena as being like a dream;

He contemplates all phenomena as being like an echo, up to and including being like a magical creation, yet he does not realize them [as final]. Subhūti, this should be known as the mark of irreversibility of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, if even when in a dream, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva...

[He was] with a retinue of many hundreds, a retinue of many thousands, a retinue of many hundreds of thousands, a retinue of many *koṭis*, a retinue of many thousands of *koṭis*, a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of *koṭis*, and a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of *niyutas*—
consisting of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.
He sees the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded and honored, teaching the Dharma;
having heard that Dharma, thinking, "I shall understand the meaning of this Dharma," he dwells practicing in accordance with the Dharma.

One who practices with proper conduct and acts in accordance with the Dharma— Subhūti, this too should be known as a characteristic of irreversibility for an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, even while in a dream,
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva beholds a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Having risen into the air, he teaches the Dharma to the community of monks, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, possessing a fathom-wide aura, displaying miracles of supernatural power, and manifesting emanations—
emanations which perform the work of a Buddha in other world-systems. Subhūti, this too is a sign of one who is irreversible.

The characteristics of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva Mahāsattva are to be known. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, even when in the midst of a dream, does not tremble, does not become terrified, and does not fall into fear— whether during a village raid, a city siege, or a conflagration— [he is to be known as non-retrogressive].
Whether seeing wild beasts, or other species of fierce animals, or seeing the imminent threat of decapitation, or seeing other such terrifying and formidable causes of fear;
Having seen suffering, dejection, and despair; or having seen one who is hungry or thirsty;
or having seen the death of a mother, the death of a father, the death of a brother, or the death of a sister.

Or, having seen the death of a friend, a kinsman, or a blood relative, no terrifying or intense fear born of grief arises. Then, immediately upon waking from that dream, it occurs to him: "Truly, this entire triple world is like a dream;
even after I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, all phenomena of the triple world will be like a dream."

They should be taught. Subhūti, this too should be known as a mark of irreversibility for an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, how is it to be understood that when an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in that buddha-field, in every way, in all respects, and entirely—
The three lower realms will no longer exist?

If even when he has entered the midst of a dream, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having seen beings in the hells, or having seen beings in the animal realm, or having seen beings in the world of Yama, recovers such mindfulness:

Having regained mindfulness, it occurs to him: "I shall act in such a way and practice in such a way that, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in that Buddha-field there will not be the three lower realms in any way, at all times, or in any manner whatsoever.
For what reason?"

For indeed, that which is a dream and that which is the end of a dream—all this is non-dual and indivisible. Subhūti, this too should be known as a mark of irreversibility for an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, whether in a dream or when awake, [perceives...]
Or when a city fire is occurring, he reflects thus:
"Whatever forms, whatever marks, and whatever signs were seen by me while in a dream or while awake—
by which forms, by which marks, and by which signs a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is to be known as irreversible."
If those modes, those signs, and those marks are present in me,
by this truth, by this utterance of truth, may this city fire be pacified, become cool, and go out; and if it is indeed pacified, becomes cool, and goes out, [then know that these signs are present].

Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has been predicted to the state of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti, if that mass of fire, transgressing that word of truth, were to burn from house to house, [it would not do so].
It burns from street to street;
it burns some houses while it does not burn others,
and it burns some streets while it does not burn others.

Subhūti, it should be understood by that bodhisattva mahāsattva that these beings have accumulated karma conducive to the rejection of the Dharma, by which some of these beings' houses are burned while other houses are not burned; this karma of theirs ripens in this very life, arising from that very rejection of the Dharma.
Karma ripens with a remainder remaining. Subhūti, this is the cause, this is the condition, by which causes and by which conditions an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be known.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by which aspects, by which marks, and by which signs an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva [is to be known]...
It should be understood that I shall teach those aspects, those marks, and those signs. Subhūti, if some woman or man were to be possessed by a non-human being,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva should reflect in this way:
If I have been predicted for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas, then my resolute intention is pure,
just as I desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, just as I [desire] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Desiring to fully awaken, [he thinks: "Just as I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may my mental attention toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment be completely pure;
may my thought of a disciple be removed, and may my thought of a solitary buddha be removed."
One should realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening with a mind free from the thoughts of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, thinking:
"It is not that I will not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;

I shall indeed realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. This applies even to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves in those incalculable and immeasurable world-systems.
And they teach the Dharma;

for those Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, there is nothing unknown, unseen, unperceived, unrealized, or not fully awakened to. For in this way, those Blessed Buddhas know my intention.
"I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. By this truth, by this word of truth, may that non-human being—by whom this woman or man has been seized or harassed—depart.
Subhūti, if that non-human being does not depart from there,"

Subhūti, when that bodhisattva mahāsattva speaks in this way, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has not been predicted to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. If...

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva speaks in this way, if that non-human being departs, it should be known, Subhūti, that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has indeed been predicted to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those previous Tathāgatas,
Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas. By these modes, Subhūti, by these...
Endowed with these signs and marks, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as irreversible.
Furthermore, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not practiced the six perfections and is devoid of skill in means—

To one who has not practiced the four foundations of mindfulness, nor the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and who has not yet entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, Māra the Evil One will approach by means of a "truth-statement. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva should perform a truth-statement, saying:

"By that truth, by that word of truth, I have been prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas," [then Māra will come].

"By this truth, by this utterance of truth, let this non-human being depart. Thereupon, Māra the Evil One will become anxious, thinking, "How can this non-human being be made to depart? For what reason?
Because Māra the Evil One, being more powerful and more majestic, will exert himself there with great intensity.
"How might this non-human being depart from here? Thinking thus, that Māra will withdraw by means of his supernatural power (*adhiṣṭhāna*). And this thought will occur to that bodhisattva mahāsattva:
"This non-human being has departed through my own majesty. But he will not know:
"This non-human being has departed through the majesty of Māra. On account of that, he will hold other bodhisattva mahāsattvas in contempt, mock them, deride them, revile them, and disparage them.
"I have been predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
whereas these others have not yet been predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment"—
by that much alone he will increase his pride and give rise to conceit.

He will distance himself from omniscience; he will distance himself from the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha. Such a being, being unskilled in means, will give rise to overweening pride on that account, and two destinies are to be expected for him. Which two destinies?
Namely, the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. Thus, through his reliance upon [false] reality, that bodhisattva—

Mara’s deeds will arise for that bodhisattva mahāsattva. Therein, he will not serve, attend to, honor, or rely upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). He will thereby tighten those very bonds of Māra. Why is that?
Because he has not practiced the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and because he has not been sustained by skill in means (*upāyakauśala*). It is thus, Subhūti.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize the work of Māra. And how, Subhūti, will Māra the Evil One approach a bodhisattva who has not yet practiced the six perfections and has not yet entered the fixed course of rightness, by means of an empowerment through a name? Here, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, approaching in one or another guise, will speak to the bodhisattva thus:
"Noble son, you have been prophesied by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, for unexcelled perfect enlightenment.

This is your name; this is your mother’s name; this is your father’s name; this is your brother’s name; this is your sister’s name; and these are the names of your friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relatives."
He will even point out the names of his parents back to the seventh generation, saying:
"From such a country, from such a direction, you were born in such a country, or in such a city or village. If he is by nature gentle, he will speak to him thus:
"In the past as well, you were just like this—gentle. If he should become harsh, he will say this to him:
'In the past as well, you were just like this—harsh. If he should become a forest-dweller, or if he should become an alms-collector..."

If he will be a wearer of rag-robes, if he will be one who eats only after the midday meal, if he will be a sitter-at-one-session, if he will be a collector-of-alms, if he will be a dweller-in-cemeteries, if he will be an open-air-dweller,
if he will be a tree-root-dweller, if he will be a sitter-only, or if he will be a taker-of-whatever-bed-is-offered.

If he will be one who possesses only the three robes, if he will be one with few desires, if he will be contented, if he will be secluded, up to: if he will be wise, if he will be free from foot-unguent, and if he will be one who speaks little,
he will say this to him:
Even in the past, you were one who spoke little. If he is one who possesses few mantras, he will say this to him:
"Even in the past, you were one who possessed few mantras. For what reason?"
For these very qualities of ascetic purification (dhutaguṇa) exist in you; certainly, you must have possessed these same ascetic practices and refinements even in the past.
Thus, by means of this reference to his former name and clan, and by this present reference to his ascetic practices and refinements, he will give rise to conceit. Māra [will then approach] him...
The Evil One, perceiving that he is deluded, will approach him and say:

"Noble son, you have been prophesied by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding your non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Such qualities as these truly exist in you. He...
Sometimes appearing in the guise of a bhikṣuṇī, sometimes in the guise of a householder, sometimes in the guise of a mother, and sometimes in the guise of a father, he will approach and say:
"Noble son, you have been prophesied by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for unexcelled perfect enlightenment. For what reason?
Because these very qualities are found in you."

Those [qualities] which belong to the irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas—Subhūti, those modes, tokens, and signs of the irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas that have been described by me do not exist in that bodhisattva. Subhūti, it should be known by other bodhisattva mahāsattvas that this bodhisattva is indeed possessed by Māra. For what reason?

For it is thus, Subhūti: those forms, marks, and signs that belong to an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva do not exist in him. And by means of this mere designation of a name, he will hold other bodhisattva mahāsattvas in contempt, will mock them, deride them, revile them, and disparage them. This too, Subhūti...

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize it as the work of Māra through the basis of a name. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should recognize it as the work of Māra through the basis of a name. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva who has not practiced the six perfections does not know the Māra of the aggregates.
He does not know form;
he does not know feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. And Māra, the Evil One, will prophesy regarding him by means of a name:
"Up until the time he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, this shall be his name. If that Bodhisattva has already reflected upon, contemplated, and deliberated upon this name,
then for a Bodhisattva who is of an unwise nature and unskilled in means, it will occur to him as follows:

"That name which has been mentally deliberated, reflected upon, and examined by me shall be my name when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Just as Māra the Evil One will declare it, or the deities of Māra’s host, or a monk under Māra’s influence,"
In this way, it will come to pass for him:
that my arising of the thought of enlightenment and the name proclaimed for me by this monk coincide; indeed, I am that very Tathāgata by that name.

"He has been prophesied by the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. However, Subhūti, those modes, tokens, and signs of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva Mahāsattva which I have described do not exist in that Bodhisattva.
And by means of that name and that teaching of the prophecy, he will hold other bodhisattva mahāsattvas in contempt.

Because of that contempt, he will become distant from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. For him—devoid of skill in means, devoid of the perfection of wisdom, separated from spiritual friends, and gripped by evil friends—two stages are to be expected.
Namely, either the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha;

or else, after wandering and transmigrating for a long time, indeed for a very long time, having served, frequented, and attended upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), he will, by relying on this very perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi). If...

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva does not frequently obtain the opportunity to see, pay homage to, and attend upon spiritual friends during that very acquisition of a physical existence, and if he neither censures nor confesses those former productions of thought,
two destinies are to be expected for him.

Namely, the level of the śrāvaka or the level of the pratyekabuddha. Subhūti, it is just as if a monk belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas were to commit any one of the four root offenses; he would no longer be a monk, he would no longer be a śramaṇa, he would no longer be a son of the Śākya, and he would be incapable of attaining the four fruits of śramaṇaship with that very same body.
or to attain any one of the fruits of the ascetic life. In the same way, Subhūti, this production of thought is more serious:

namely, when a production of thought accompanied by conceit has arisen in a bodhisattva under the pretext of a name, and because of that mere name he would judge, despise, or look down upon other bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas—it should be understood that this production of thought is more serious.

For in this way, Subhūti, these subtle deeds of Māra will arise under the designation of names. Let alone, Subhūti, the four grave root downfalls; more grievous than the five acts of immediate retribution is this production of thought which has arisen in a bodhisattva under the designation of a name—a production of thought accompanied by conceit. By that [production of thought], he...

The production of the thought of awakening should be understood as being even more weighty. Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will approach a bodhisattva mahāsattva under the pretext of teaching the virtues of solitude; having approached, he will speak thus:
"The Tathāgata [has taught] solitude..."
"Subhūti, I do not speak of such a form of seclusion for a bodhisattva mahāsattva as this: namely, dwelling in forest retreats, jungle thickets, or remote lodgings. He asked:

"But, Blessed One, if it is not dwelling in forest retreats, jungle thickets, or remote lodgings, what then is another form of seclusion for a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Of what nature, Blessed One, is that other seclusion of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is secluded— secluded from mental engagements associated with the disciples and solitary buddhas— that bodhisattva mahāsattva is secluded in forest retreats, jungle thickets, and remote areas."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in lodgings and seats while dwelling in solitude alone. Subhūti, this is the solitude authorized by me for a bodhisattva mahāsattva; if he dwells day and night with this solitude, then that bodhisattva dwells in solitude alone.
Subhūti, that which is the solitude authorized by me for bodhisattva mahāsattvas,

and furthermore, that solitude which Māra the Evil One will teach— one should dwell in it in remote forest retreats and secluded lodgings; yet, being actually crowded even while practicing that solitude, one remains associated with the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If he is not separated from mental attentions but is not yet conjoined with the perfection of wisdom, he will not fulfill omniscience.

Thus, dwelling in this state, his mental attentions will not be completely pure, and he will hold in contempt other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who dwell in the vicinity of villages, even though they possess pure minds and mental attentions free from the thought of a śrāvaka.

Unmixed with the mind of a pratyekabuddha, unmixed with other evil thoughts, and unmixed with [worldly concerns], they have reached the fulfillment of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and thorough knowledges (*parijñā*). Nevertheless, that bodhisattva who lacks skill in means, even if he is in forest wildernesses extending for hundreds of *yojanas* that are not free from predatory beasts, wild animals, and birds—

In places not free from thieves and outcasts, and frequented by fanged beasts, venomous serpents, and rākṣasas— having entered into the midst of such places— one might conceive the intention to remain for a year, or a hundred years, or a thousand years, or a hundred thousand years, or ten million years,
or a hundred ten-million-year periods, or a thousand ten-million-year periods, or a hundred thousand ten-million-year periods.

Even for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years, or even longer than that, one might not know this solitude— the solitude by which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having set out with resolute intention, dwell; [if one does not know it], that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in a state of confusion.
Being thoroughly defiled, he relies upon, clings to, adheres to, and remains attached to that very seclusion;

yet for all that, he does not please my mind. And as for that seclusion which I have described for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas—one who is endowed with that seclusion is not even seen in that seclusion. Why is that?
For he is devoid of that very solitude. Then Māra, the Evil One, approaches him and, standing in the air above, says this:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! This is that true solitude taught by the Tathāgata; dwell in this solitude.
In this way, you will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. From that solitude...

Regarding that solitude as the most preeminent and worthy of honor, he will again descend into the vicinity of villages and despise those other monks who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle— those whose mental attention is completely pure, up to those who are gentle and possessed of wholesome qualities— thinking,
"These venerable ones dwell in a crowded manner."

Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who dwell in solitude, he will accuse them of dwelling in confusion and accuse them of dwelling in crowds, and he will hold them in contempt. But those who dwell in confusion,
he will urge them toward dwelling in solitude.
And he will conceive reverence for that [teaching]. Yet, toward that for which reverence should be conceived, he will instead conceive pride. Why is that?
Because he will think:
"I am being exhorted by non-human beings; I am being reminded by non-human beings."
“Subhūti, this is the dwelling by which I dwell. Who will rebuke those who dwell in the vicinity of villages? Who will remind those who dwell in the vicinity of villages?
In this way, that bodhisattva will hold those sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle in contempt. Subhūti, such a person is...”
A bodhisattva who is such a person should be known as a caṇḍāla, should be known as a defiler of bodhisattvas, and should be known as a counterfeit bodhisattva;

he should be known as a thief in the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Furthermore, sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle should not associate with, nor rely upon, a person of such a kind.
He should be attended upon. For what reason?

Subhūti, those persons of such a kind should be known as being full of conceit. However, for that bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not abandoned the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) and has not abandoned unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*), [he should be attended upon].
That bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring with resolute intention to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,

and wishing to act for the benefit of all sentient beings, should not serve, associate with, or attend upon such persons. Rather, he should be devoted to the application of his own welfare and should always have a mind that is apprehensive [of worldly things].

With a mind terrified of cyclic existence and unattached to the three realms, one should generate loving-kindness even toward those who are like outcaste Bodhisattvas; therein, out of compassion, one should generate pity, and one should generate sympathetic joy and equanimity. And one should resolve the mind in this way:

"I shall act in such a way that these faults of mine will, in every respect, entirely, and in all ways, no longer exist and will not arise. Even if they should arise, I shall quickly abandon them"—this is the training that should be undertaken. Subhūti, this should be understood as the personal exertion through supernormal knowledge of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Furthermore, Subhūti...

(AdSPG I 16) A bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with resolute intention, desires to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, should serve, associate with, and attend upon spiritual friends. But, Blessed One, who are to be known as the spiritual friends of bodhisattva mahāsattvas?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, should be known as the spiritual friends of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas also should be known as the spiritual friends of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas."

Subhūti, even the Śrāvakas should be known as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—those who proclaim, teach, illuminate, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and fully manifest the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). Subhūti, these also should be known as the spiritual friends of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. Furthermore, Subhūti, the six perfections themselves are the spiritual friends of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
The four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, should be known as the spiritual friends of bodhisattva mahāsattvas;

suchness, the limit of reality, and the realm of phenomena should be known as the spiritual friends of bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Furthermore, Subhūti, the six perfections should be known as the teachers of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
The six perfections are the path; the six perfections are the light. The six perfections are a torch, an illumination, intelligence, wisdom, and insight;
the six perfections are a protection.
The six perfections are the refuge; the six perfections are the ultimate resort;

the six perfections are the mother. The four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects, lead to the abandonment of all habitual tendencies and their continuations. For what reason?

For it is thus, Subhūti: even those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who appeared in the past—of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, these very factors conducive to awakening were their mothers and fathers. Those...
Subhūti, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future time—
Subhūti, for those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, these very factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣya-dharma) will be their mother and father.
And Subhūti, those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones who currently reside and dwell in the world-systems in the ten directions...
They maintain themselves and teach the Dharma;
for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, these very factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*) are their mother and father. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, it is from this [source] that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present have emerged. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening—
One who wishes to purify a buddha-field and one who wishes to bring sentient beings to maturity should gather sentient beings through the four means of attraction. What are the four?
Namely, by means of generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency between words and deeds. Subhūti, seeing this very significance, I say:

"These factors conducive to awakening are the teachers, the mother and father, the shelter, the protection, the island, the refuge, and the final resort for these bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain independence from others—
by one who wishes to abide in independence from others,
who wishes to sever the doubts of all sentient beings,
and who wishes to purify a buddha-field;
And by one who wishes to bring sentient beings to maturity, one should train in this very perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
For it is in this perfection of wisdom that those dharmas are taught in detail, in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva must train. Subhūti said:
"Of what characteristics, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of being unattached like space. Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is not a characteristic."
"What is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom? He said:
"Blessed One, might there be a way in which all phenomena exist by the same characteristic by which the perfection of wisdom exists?
The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. By whatever characteristic the perfection of wisdom exists, by that very same characteristic all dharmas exist. For what reason? Because, Subhūti, all dharmas have a nature that is secluded; all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. In this manner, Subhūti, by whatever characteristic the perfection of wisdom exists, by that very same characteristic all dharmas exist—namely, by the characteristic of emptiness and the characteristic of seclusion. Subhūti said:

If, Blessed One, all dharmas are secluded from all dharmas and all dharmas are empty of all dharmas, then how, Blessed One, is the defilement and purification of sentient beings discerned? For, Blessed One, that which is secluded is neither defiled nor purified;
emptiness is neither defiled nor purified. Is it not the case that what is secluded [is likewise]?

Emptiness awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Through seclusion, no phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended within emptiness. Through seclusion, no sentient being whatsoever is apprehended within emptiness who might awaken to enlightenment.
Blessed One, how should we understand the meaning of these words you have spoken?
The Blessed One said: "What do you think, Subhūti? For a long time have sentient beings wandered in 'I-making' and 'mine-making'?
He replied: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. For a long time sentient beings have wandered in 'I-making' and 'mine-making'. The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Are 'I-making' and 'mine-making' secluded and empty?

He replied, "They are empty, Blessed One; they are empty, Sugata. The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti? Do beings, by means of 'I-making' and 'mine-making,' transmigrate and wander through cyclic existence? He replied:
"So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. It is through the notions of 'I' and 'mine' that beings run on and wander in saṃsāra. The Blessed One said:
"In this way indeed, Subhūti, the defilement of beings is recognized: where there is neither 'I'-making nor 'mine'-making, there is no grasping."
There is no grasping; therein beings do not run about, nor do they transmigrate, and therein there is no affliction. It is in this way, Subhūti, that the purification of beings is known. He said:
"Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in this manner, he does not course in form."

He does not course in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations, nor in consciousness. He does not course in the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is that?
Because those dharmas cannot be apprehended—neither the one who would course, nor that by which he would course, nor that wherein he would course. Coursing in this way...
“Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes invincible by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
Furthermore, Blessed One, while practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be overcome by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Why is that?”
For he stands in an unassailable position, namely, the path of the bodhisattvas;

for, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is indeed unassailable when he is never separated from the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Practicing in this way, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws near to the knowledge of all aspects. The Blessed One said:
What do you think, Subhūti? Suppose all the beings in Jambudvīpa were to obtain a human body, and having obtained a human body, were to realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family, remaining for as long as their life lasts, were to honor, revere, respect, and worship them.
And one should dedicate that root of merit toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
What do you think, Subhūti, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
He said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata. The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much greater merit on that basis who would explain, teach, illuminate, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and fully manifest the perfection of wisdom to others.
And he should dwell with mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom;

suppose that all the beings as many as there are in the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system were to obtain a human body, and some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish them all in the ten paths of wholesome action.

If one were to establish [beings] in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, up to the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,

and were to dedicate those roots of merit toward unsurpassed perfect enlightenment— what do you think, Subhūti, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
He said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata. The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who would explain, teach, illuminate, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and fully proclaim this perfection of wisdom to others, [endowed] with the aspects of all-knowledge."
And if he should dwell with such mental attentions, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes worthy of the offerings of all sentient beings. For what reason?
Because no sentient being whatsoever possesses a dwelling such as that of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Except for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. For what reason?
Because those sons of good family, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, bring forth great loving-kindness and regard all sentient beings as if they were standing at the place of execution.
They bring forth great compassion;
dwelling in that state, they rejoice with sympathetic joy and experience intense gladness.
They bring forth great sympathetic joy. They do not dwell together with that sign. They [bring forth] great equanimity.
They attain it. Subhūti, this is the great light of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, namely:

the light of the perfection of generosity, the light of the perfection of ethical discipline, the light of the perfection of patience, the light of the perfection of vigor, the light of the perfection of meditative concentration, and the light of the perfection of wisdom. Even though they have not yet attained full awakening, those sons of good family become worthy recipients of offerings for all sentient beings.
And they do not turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, those who enjoy their robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
while dwelling with mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom, purify the offerings of the donors and benefactors.

And they practice for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to consume the alms of the kingdom fruitfully, who wishes to teach the path to all sentient beings,
and who wishes to produce a vast illumination— [should train in this].
One who desires to liberate beings who have fallen into the bonds of the triple world,
and who desires to generate the unsurpassed eye of wisdom for all beings,
should dwell constantly and continuously with mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom. If, Subhūti, [one so desires]...

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dwell with those mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom; he should speak only such discourse as is associated with the perfection of wisdom. Having spoken only such discourse as is associated with the perfection of wisdom, he should dwell with only those mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom. By him...

One who dwells with mental attention associated with the perfection of wisdom should not allow any opportunity for other forms of mental attention; rather, one should act in such a way that one dwells day and night with those very same mental attentions associated with the perfection of wisdom, never laying down the burden. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, some man had never before obtained a precious jewel.

Suppose that at some time he were to obtain that precious gem, and having obtained it, he would be endowed with a sublime sense of joy, rapture, and gladness. Yet, as soon as he had obtained that precious gem, it were to vanish again;
on account of that, he would be joined with great suffering and dejection. What do you think?
His mental attentions would proceed constantly and continuously associated only with jewels, thinking:

"Alas, I am separated from that delightful jewel! In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be separated from mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, thinking: "This is a jewel."
It must be so. And that jewel of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is not to be bent down; it will always abound in happiness and mental well-being. He said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, all mental engagements (*manasikāra*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); all mental engagements are empty of intrinsic nature."
"In that case, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva remain unseparated from mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects?
For a bodhisattva is not perceived when separated [from them], nor is there mental engagement, nor is there the knowledge of all aspects. The Blessed One said:

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands thus: "All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; they were not made by śrāvakas, nor made by pratyekabuddhas, nor made by the Buddha Bhagavats; this dharma-nature and the stability of these phenomena remain as they are."

The fixed nature of phenomena, suchness, non-falsity, non-alteration, the realm of phenomena, and the limit of reality—by these a bodhisattva mahāsattva is never separated from the perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
Subhūti, it is because this perfection of wisdom is by its very nature secluded.
It is empty by its own nature;
it neither increases nor decreases. He said:
"Blessed One, if the perfection of wisdom is secluded by its own nature and empty by its own nature,"
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully mastered the perfection of wisdom, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Blessed One replied:
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully realized the perfection of wisdom, neither increases nor decreases;
the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) neither increases nor decreases;
the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) neither increases nor decreases. Why is that?
For the perfection of wisdom is neither one nor two.

Subhūti, if, when this is being spoken, the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink, does not falter, is not terrified, does not tremble, and does not fall into terror, then it should be concluded that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is established in the state of non-retrogression. This bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti...
"Furthermore, Blessed One, is that which is this perfection of wisdom—emptiness, vanity, insubstantiality, and corelessness—that which courses in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He said:
“Blessed One, apart from the perfection of wisdom, is any dharma to be found that practices the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said, “Not so, Subhūti. He said:
"But, Blessed One, does the perfection of wisdom course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, does emptiness course in emptiness?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He said:
"But, Blessed One, does one course in emptiness apart from emptiness?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He said:
"But further, Blessed One, does form course in the perfection of wisdom? Do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He said:
"But further, Blessed One, do the six perfections course in the perfection of wisdom?
Up to and including, do the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He asked:

"But then, Blessed One, is that which is the emptiness, the voidness, the insubstantiality, the lack of core, the suchness, the non-falsity, the unaltered suchness of form; is it the nature of phenomena, the realm of phenomena, the fixed order of phenomena, and the limit of reality?"
“Does she course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: “Not so, Subhūti. He said:

"Furthermore, Blessed One, does that which is the emptiness, hollowness, vanity, insubstantiality, suchness, non-falsity, non-other-suchness, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) practice in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He said:
"But if, Blessed One, these dharmas do not course in the perfection of wisdom, how then does a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that dharma which courses in the perfection of wisdom?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that perfection of wisdom in which a bodhisattva should course?
He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "What do you think, Subhūti? As for that dharma which you do not perceive—can that dharma be apprehended at all?"
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Regarding that dharma which is not apprehended—would that dharma arise or cease?
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, this is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena belonging to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with such patience as this is prophesied by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, this is called the great loving-kindness consisting of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges.

Great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the analytical knowledges—by practicing these, by conducting himself thus, by striving thus, and by exerting himself thus, it is impossible that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not attain the gnosis of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the great gnosis, the gnosis of the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that? Because such a thing cannot occur.

For that bodhisattva mahāsattva has attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). There shall never be any decline in those phenomena for him until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Subhūti said:
"But, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva predicted for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment on account of the arising of all phenomena?"
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He asked:
"But then, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment on account of the non-arising of all dharmas?"
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He asked:
"Then, Blessed One, is a bodhisattva mahāsattva not predicted for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment neither from the perspective of arising nor from the perspective of non-arising?"
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. Subhūti said:
"If, moreover, Blessed One, a bodhisattva is not predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment neither from the standpoint of arising nor from the standpoint of non-arising,"
"In that case, how does the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment now come about?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that dharma which is predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?"

He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One. I do not perceive any such dharma that is predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, Blessed One, I do not perceive any dharma that awakens, nor any dharma by which one awakens. The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. For a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not apprehend any phenomena, it does not occur: 'I shall fully awaken,' or 'by this he will fully awaken,' or 'this will be fully awakened. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, none of these conceptual constructions exist. Why is that?"
For the perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, is indeed non-conceptual.
Chapter 56.
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:
“Profound, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom; it is difficult to see, difficult to understand, beyond reasoning, not accessible to logic, and beyond the sphere of [ordinary] thought.
To the extent that it is subtle, precise, and to be realized by the wise, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is so because it is based on absolute seclusion.”

"Blessed One, those beings who shall hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and who shall uphold it, recite it, master it, and practice in accordance with suchness, will not be endowed with inferior roots of merit;
nor will they allow any opportunity for other mental states or mental factors."
...until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Kauśika, so it is. Those beings who shall hear, retain, and recite this profound perfection of wisdom will not be endowed with inferior roots of merit; they will be endowed with suchness."

And they will practice it and will not allow any opportunity for other mental states or mental factors, until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. What do you think, Kauśika: if all the beings in Jambudvīpa, as many as there are, were all endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action?

[The merit of] one who possesses the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five superknowledges— compared to that of a son of good family or a daughter of good family who would take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and having taken up, borne in mind, recited, and mastered this profound perfection of wisdom, practice in accordance with suchness. (AdSPG I 28)

Kauśika, this former root of merit does not approach even a hundredth part of this [present] root of merit; it does not approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part. It does not approach a ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-ten-million-billionth part.
It does not admit of any calculation, fraction, reckoning, comparison, or likeness. Then...
A certain monk said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"The Kaubhīṣakya [heretics] have been overcome.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to him:

O Kauśika, all those who are endowed with the four dhyānas, endowed with the four immeasurables, endowed with the four formless attainments, and endowed with the five superknowledges— even they are surpassed by that son of good family or daughter of good family who,
with an undistracted mind, will take up, bear in mind, and recite this perfection of wisdom.

He will master it and practice for the sake of suchness; he will not allow any opportunity for other mental states or mental factors until he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, spoke thus to that bhikṣu:
"By a single production of the thought of awakening, O bhikṣu, all those beings of Jambudvīpa [are surpassed] by that bodhisattva mahāsattva."

They are endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action, endowed with the four dhyānas, endowed with the four immeasurables, endowed with the four formless attainments, and endowed with the five superknowledges; they have overcome all adversaries. How much more so, then, for one who will take up, retain, and master this profound perfection of wisdom?

Having taken it up, retained it, recited it, and mastered it, he will practice for the sake of suchness. By that, the world with its gods, humans, and asuras will be surpassed; he will go forth surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Not only will the bodhisattva mahāsattva go forth surpassing the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, but even those who are stream-enterers...
The bodhisattva mahāsattva will surpass all those— once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas— not only the stream-enterers up to the pratyekabuddhas,
but even those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of generosity while being devoid of skillful means and devoid of the perfection of wisdom.

The bodhisattva mahāsattva will surpass all of them as well. Not only those who practice the perfection of generosity, but even those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of ethical discipline while being devoid of skillful means and devoid of the perfection of wisdom—the bodhisattva mahāsattva will surpass them too. Not only those who practice the perfection of patience...

Furthermore, that bodhisattva mahāsattva will surpass even those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of vigor but are devoid of skill in means and devoid of the perfection of wisdom; not only those who practice the perfection of vigor,
but also those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of meditative concentration yet are devoid of skill in means.
Even those who are devoid of the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will surpass them.

Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice according to the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught cannot be overcome by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom follows the perfection of wisdom exactly as it has been taught.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva abides for the sake of not interrupting the lineage of the knowledge of all aspects. This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not distance himself from the Tathāgatas. This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in this way, does not become disenchanted.
The seat of awakening. This bodhisattva mahāsattva desires to uplift beings who are sinking.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in this way, trains in the training of a bodhisattva, not in the training of a śrāvaka, nor does he train in the training of a pratyekabuddha. Thus...
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva is training, the four great kings will think that they should approach him;
having approached, they will say:
"Quickly, O Great Being, train! Train swiftly! Here are those four bowls which [should be used] by you."

They should be embraced by one seated at the seat of awakening after having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment— those very things which were embraced by the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way within the perfection of wisdom, the four great kings of the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm will think that they should approach him, together with [their retinues].

The sons of the gods belonging to the retinue of the Great Kings will again think that they must approach him; together with the sons of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, Suyāma, the king of the gods, will also think that he must approach him;
and together with the sons of the Yāma gods, Saṃtuṣita, the king of the gods, will also think that he must approach him.

Together with the sons of the gods of Tuṣita, even the divine king Nirmāṇarati will think that he must approach him; together with the sons of the gods of Nirmāṇarati, even the divine king Vaśavartin will think that he must approach him;
together with the sons of the gods of Vaśavartin, even Brahmā Sahāmpati will think that he must approach him;
and together with the sons of the gods of the Brahmakāyika realm, even the Ābhāsvara gods will think that they must approach him.

The Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Śuddhāvāsakāyika gods will think that they should approach that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught.
That bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices this profound perfection of wisdom will be constantly attended by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing thus in this profound perfection of wisdom, whatever worldly sufferings or injuries caused by others may arise—

Those [afflictions] that would arise in the body will not arise in the body at all; they will not descend upon it. These are the qualities pertaining to the present life that will belong to that bhikṣu, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, while he courses in this profound perfection of wisdom.
At that time, whatever those illnesses arising from the humors may be, they will not occur.

Namely: eye disease, ear disease, tongue disease, toothache, body ache, and mental anguish—all these shall not arise nor descend upon his body. These are the qualities to be expected in this present life for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this profound perfection of wisdom. Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Ānanda:

"Does Śakra, the lord of the gods, teach this perfection of wisdom through his own personal inspired eloquence, and [expound] the qualities and benefits of the perfection of wisdom, or rather through the power of the Buddha? Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, knowing the reflection in the mind of the venerable Ānanda with his own mind, said to the venerable Ānanda:

"Venerable Ānanda, it should be understood that this is through the power of the Buddha, that I teach the perfection of wisdom and the qualities and benefits of the perfection of wisdom. Then the Blessed One [addressed] the venerable...
He said this to Ānanda:
"It is so, Ānanda, it is so.
This is the power of the Tathāgata, this is the sustaining grace of the Tathāgata, that Śakra, the lord of the gods..."
He teaches the perfection of wisdom and the qualities and benefits of this perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom,
applies himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom, and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, [at that time...]

At that time, all the Māras, the Evil Ones, within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system fall into doubt, wondering: "Will this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), attain the fruit of stream-entry, or will he attain the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or the state of a Pratyekabuddha?"
Or will he indeed fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?

Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the perfection of wisdom, at that time Māra, the Evil One, becomes pierced by the arrow of grief. Furthermore, Ānanda...

Māra, the Evil One, hurls down meteors at the bodhisattva mahāsattva and creates fear, thinking that perhaps the bodhisattva mahāsattva might become discouraged, or experience horripilation, or have a state of mental despondency, or even a single moment of distraction of mind from the mental engagement with omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Then the venerable Ānanda—
He said this to the Blessed One:
"Why, Blessed One, does Māra the Evil One approach all bodhisattvas mahāsattvas with the intention of causing them harm?
The Blessed One replied:
"Indeed, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One does not approach all bodhisattva mahāsattvas with the intention of causing them harm. Ānanda said:
"With what kind of persons does he approach?
The Blessed One said:

Ānanda, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas whose minds have not been resolved upon this profound perfection of wisdom while it was being taught from the past— Māra, the Evil One, approaches them with the intention of causing them harm.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught here, those bodhisattvas...
They fell into doubt, thinking, "This might be the perfection of wisdom, or this might not be the perfection of wisdom.

Ānanda, Māra the Evil One approaches them with the intention of causing them harm. Furthermore, Ānanda, another case is that a bodhisattva is deprived of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Not seeing a spiritual friend, he does not hear this profound perfection of wisdom; not hearing it, he does not understand it.

Not knowing, one does not practice for the sake of suchness. [Thinking], "How should the perfection of wisdom be cultivated?"—furthermore, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva is devoid of the perfection of wisdom and embraces what is not the true Dharma, then, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One gains an opportunity against that bodhisattva mahāsattva as well. Furthermore...
Ānanda, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoid of the perfection of wisdom speaks in praise of the non-Dharma,
it occurs to Māra the Evil One:
"This one who speaks in praise of the non-Dharma is my ally."

"Even for many who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle, he has become a companion who speaks in praise of the false dharma. He will fulfill my intention, in that those belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle will come to abide on two levels—namely, either the level of the Śrāvaka or the level of the Pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, Ānanda, what kind of Bodhisattva does Māra find an opportunity to exploit?"

When this profound perfection of wisdom is being taught, if a bodhisattva says: "Profound indeed is this perfection of wisdom! What is the use of your hearing, teaching, retaining, reciting, or mastering this profound perfection of wisdom?
I myself do not find a firm footing; how could you possibly find one?"
Ānanda, Māra the Evil One gains an opportunity even against this bodhisattva. Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva says to certain other bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
"I practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom, whereas you do not practice the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom," even against him—

Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will find an opportunity to gain entry into a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time a bodhisattva considers himself superior, at that time, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One becomes satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; such is the case for that bodhisattva as well, Ānanda.
Māra, the Evil One, finds an opportunity for attack. Furthermore, Ānanda, at whatever time the name or the clan of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is proclaimed,
by that mention of his name or clan, he [seeks to disparage] other bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are virtuous.
As long as one considers oneself to possess virtuous qualities, one exalts oneself and disparages others;
yet those qualities do not exist in him, which are the modes, marks, and signs of irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas. By means of those...
Based on non-existent modes, signs, and characteristics, he gives rise to afflictions, exalts himself, and disparages others. And he speaks thus:
"You are not seen here in the Bodhisattva Vehicle; you are not seen in the Bodhisattva lineage."

Just as I am seen here in the Bodhisattva Vehicle and the Bodhisattva lineage, he reviles and disparages those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva Vehicle. Then, this thought occurs to Māra, the Evil One:
"My abode will not be empty; the great hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama will become overcrowded."

And there is the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). In such and such ways, Māra the Evil One will empower that bodhisattva so that his words become authoritative. Because of that authoritativeness of his speech, many people will think that what he says is worth hearing and worth having faith in.
Having heard him, they will fall into conformity with what they have seen. As they fall into conformity with what they have seen, they will [act] for the sake of suchness (*tathātva*).
They will train; training for suchness and practicing for suchness, they will increase their afflictions.
Thus, with a perverted mental continuum, whatever action they undertake—whether by body, speech, or mind—[it will be unwholesome].
Or all that will lead to what is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable. In this way, those great hells will become overcrowded;

the animal realm, the world of Yama, and the domain of the hungry ghosts will become overcrowded; and the abode of Māra will become overcrowded. Seeing this purpose, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will be overjoyed.

He is delighted, filled with joy and gladness. Furthermore, Ānanda, if a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle should quarrel with a son of good family belonging to the śrāvaka vehicle, saying, "I am superior,
not you," then Māra the Evil One thinks to himself:
"Alas, this son of good family will distance himself from all-aspect omniscience; he will not be near to all-aspect omniscience. Why is that?

Because these quarrels, brawls, conflicts, and disputes are not the path to all-aspect omniscience; this is the path to hell, this is the path to the animal realm, this is the path to the world of Yama—this is not the path to all-aspect omniscience. Furthermore, Ānanda, if one who belongs to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas..."
When a person engages in quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute with another person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, Māra the Evil One thinks to himself:
"Both of these will distance themselves from the knowledge of all aspects; both of these will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?
For this is not the path, this is not the practice for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which has been undertaken by these two sons of good family;
rather, this is the path to the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, which has been undertaken by these two sons of good family. Furthermore:
Ānanda, if an unprophesied bodhisattva should harbor a malicious thought toward a prophesied bodhisattva, or should engage in quarreling, reviling, strife, or dispute with him,
he must once again don the armor for as many eons as there were those thoughts of malice produced by him.
"Evil thoughts have arisen, and they engage in quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute. If, however, their omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) has not been abandoned, what then? Ānanda said:
"Blessed One, is there an escape from these productions of thought, or must he nevertheless don his armor for that many eons?"
The Blessed One said:

"Ānanda, I have taught a Dharma that leads to liberation for persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. In this regard, Ānanda, as for this person belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas..."
If a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle should quarrel, dispute, revile, or abuse another, and having quarreled,
disputed, reviled, or abused, does not confess it, but harbors resentment and dwells persistently bound by that resentment—
Ānanda, I do not say there is any escape for such a person.
That person must certainly don the armor for that many eons,

provided that their knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) has not been relinquished. Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having quarreled, disputed, reviled, or abused [another], confesses [the fault], does not harbor a latent tendency (anuśaya), and undertakes restraint for the future;

"It is a great gain for me that I have been told: 'You must remove the suffering of all sentient beings,' yet I respond with a counter-mantra. I, who ought to be a bridge for all sentient beings, am instead doing what is unpleasant to others."

"I shall speak; I shall give a reply"—even this must not be done by me. I must be like one who is dull-witted and mute, and my resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) must not be disturbed—that intention by which these beings are to be led to final nirvāṇa after I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

"Therefore, I would fall away right here; therefore, I would become agitated right here. I must not fall away here; I must not become agitated here. Ānanda, I declare this to be the escape for this bodhisattva mahāsattva;
Māra, the Evil One, finds no opportunity against this bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore..."

Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not associate with persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas. Even if they remain present, he should not harbor malice toward anyone nor become agitated. Why is that?
Because it would not be fitting for me to harbor malice or become agitated in their presence. Why is that?
"For it is thus: having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, these must be liberated by me from all sufferings. Ānanda said:
"Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva conduct himself toward those persons who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle?
The Blessed One said:
"Just as, Ānanda, one should stand toward the Teacher, so should a bodhisattva mahāsattva stand toward a person belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle. Why is that?
This person is my companion, embarked on the same ship; just as he should train, so must I train. In whatever he should train, in that very thing must I train—namely, in the perfection of giving."

Up to the point of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). He should generate this thought: "He is the one who shows me the path to complete enlightenment. However, if he were to dwell in distraction, with mental engagements dissociated from the knowledge of all aspects, I should not train under him. But if this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells without being separated [from those qualities], [then I shall follow him]."
"I too must train in this way through mental engagements associated with the knowledge of all aspects.
Training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes one who trains equally.
(AdSPG I 39)
Chapter 57. Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the sameness of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, in which sameness a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, internal emptiness is the sameness of bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas; Subhūti, external emptiness is the sameness of bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas."

Subhūti, internal-external emptiness is the sameness of bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Up to the point where the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is the sameness of bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Form is empty of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of consciousness; up to the point where awakening is empty of awakening.

This, Subhūti, is the equality of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; established in this equality, a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains for the exhaustion of form, does he train in omniscience? When he trains for the dispassion toward form, does he train in omniscience? When he trains for the cessation of form...

One trains in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). When one trains for the non-arising of form (*rūpa*), one trains in omniscience; up to when one trains for the exhaustion of awakening (*bodhi*), one trains in omniscience. Likewise, up to when one trains for the dispassion, cessation, and non-arising of awakening, one trains in omniscience. The Blessed One said:

As for what the Elder Subhūti has said: "When one trains for the sake of the exhaustion of form, one trains in omniscience; up to: when one trains for the sake of the non-arising of form, one trains in omniscience; and so on, up to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

He trains for the sake of their exhaustion; he trains in omniscience. Likewise, to the extent that he trains for the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he trains in omniscience.

To the extent that one trains for the sake of the destruction of awakening, one trains in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Likewise, to the extent that one trains for the sake of the fading away, cessation, and non-arising of awakening, one trains in omniscience. This should be elaborated in detail.
What do you think, Subhūti? Is the suchness (*tathatā*) of form, the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness [different]?

"As far as the suchness of awakening extends, so far extends the suchness of the Tathāgata—that suchness by which a Tathāgata is designated. Does that suchness diminish, cease, or perish? Subhūti replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One; certainly not, Sugata. The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way trains in suchness; he trains in omniscience."

Suchness does not diminish, nor is it ceased, nor is it abandoned. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way trains in suchness; he trains in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way trains in the six perfections, up to and including the four foundations of mindfulness.
As long as he trains in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, he trains in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way attains the perfection of all trainings.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way cannot be [overcome] by Māras or by those belonging to the host of Māra.

[It is] so that he cannot be overcome by the deities. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way very quickly reaches the stage of non-retrogression. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way [abides] in his own ancestral domain of the Tathāgatas.
He practices. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the qualities that constitute a protector.
Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in great loving-kindness; he trains in great compassion;
he trains for the purification of the buddha-field; he trains for the maturation of sentient beings. Training in this way...
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains for the sake of turning the wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects.
Training in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains with the thought: "I shall bring all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa.
Training in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [trains] for the sake of the non-interruption of the lineage of the Tathāgatas.

He trains. Subhūti, training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains with the thought, "I shall open the door to the deathless," and he trains with the thought, "I shall reveal the unconditioned realm. Subhūti, inferior beings are not capable of training in this sublime training. It is that bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to deliver all beings from saṃsāra who [trains] in this training.
He trains. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this way is not reborn in the hells;
he is not reborn in the animal realm, nor in the world of Yama, nor in the borderlands; he is not reborn in the families of *pukkasa*s or *caṇḍāla*s.
He does not become one-eyed, nor does he become hunchbacked, nor lame, nor deficient in any limb.

He does not become deaf; he does not fall into a mire; he does not have impaired faculties; his faculties are complete, not incomplete. He does not become a killer of living beings; he does not take what is not given; he does not engage in sexual misconduct;

he does not speak falsely; he does not speak maliciously; he does not speak harshly; he does not engage in idle chatter; he is not covetous; he does not have a mind of ill will; and he does not hold wrong views.

He does not intend to live by means of wrong livelihood. He does not become a receiver of what is unreal, nor does he become a receiver of those who are immoral. Training in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not reborn among the long-lived gods. For what reason?
He possesses skill in means, by virtue of which a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with that skill in means is not reborn among the long-lived gods. What, then, is that?

It is this very skill in means taught here in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Endowed with that skill in means, he enters the meditative concentrations (dhyāna), enters the immeasurables (apramāṇa), and enters the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti).

He is not reborn by the power of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), or the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way attains the complete purity of all the powers of the buddha-dharmas;
that is to say, through the purification of the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. He said:
“Blessed One, since all phenomena are pure by nature, of which phenomenon does the bodhisattva mahāsattva attain purity?
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is, just as you say. All dharmas, Subhūti, are pure by nature.
Subhūti, regarding all dharmas that are thus pure, the non-despondency and non-dejection of the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom—[that is what this refers to]."
This, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom. All foolish ordinary people do not know and do not see this true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);

for the sake of those beings, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of giving, up to practicing the perfection of wisdom, and even practicing up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Training in this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva...

Training in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the power and fearlessness regarding all dharmas and does not fall to the level of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; thus training, he reaches the further shore of the movements and fluctuations of the minds and conduct of all sentient beings. Subhūti, it is just as, for example, those areas of the great earth where Jāmbūnada gold is found are few.

Just as gold and fine gold are produced, even so, Subhūti, those beings who train in this training—that is, the training in the perfection of wisdom—are few. Much more numerous are those beings who establish themselves on the level of a śrāvaka or on the level of a pratyekabuddha.
It is just as, Subhūti, those beings who are destined for the state of a universal monarch (cakravartin) are few.

They proceed having undertaken such karma. Therefore, those beings who proceed having undertaken karma leading to the status of a local king (*koṭṭarāja*) are far more numerous. Just so, Subhūti, those beings who ascend this path to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) are few;
far more numerous are those beings who ascend the path of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, Subhūti, those...

Bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, have set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; yet those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who practice toward suchness are fewer than those who remain fixed on the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, Subhūti, as for those sons of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle who dwell in the perfection of wisdom—
Without doubt, they enter the stage of non-retrogression; therefore, those who do not enter the stage of non-retrogression are far more numerous.
For this reason, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to attain the stage of non-retrogression—
One who wishes to be counted among those on the stage of non-retrogression should train right here in this perfection of wisdom. Furthermore,
Subhūti, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, no thought accompanied by stinginess arises,
nor does any thought accompanied by immorality arise.

A mind accompanied by agitation does not arise. A mind accompanied by laziness does not arise. A mind accompanied by distraction does not arise. A mind accompanied by ignorance does not arise. A mind accompanied by attachment does not arise. A mind accompanied by aversion does not arise. A mind accompanied by delusion does not arise.
A mind accompanied by stubbornness does not arise. A mind accompanied by form does not arise;
a mind accompanied by feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness does not arise. Up to and including, a mind accompanied by awakening does not arise. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices here in this profound perfection of wisdom, he does not...
He does not apprehend any dharma. Not apprehending anything, he does not give rise to a thought toward any dharma whatsoever.

It is in this way, Subhūti, that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains here in this profound perfection of wisdom, all six perfections are fully embraced by him, all six perfections are brought to completion by him, and all six perfections [are perfected].
They are included within it. For what reason?
