Because, Subhūti, all the perfections are included within this profound perfection of wisdom. It is just as, Subhūti, the sixty-two types of views are included within the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
In the same way, Subhūti, all the perfections are included within this profound perfection of wisdom.

Just as, Subhūti, when a person has passed away and the life-faculty has ceased, all the other faculties cease as well; even so, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva in this profound [perfection of wisdom]...

For one who courses in the perfection of wisdom, all the perfections are included within it. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to reach the further shore of all the perfections should train in this profound perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva training in this profound perfection of wisdom...
The Mahāsattva trains for the sake of preeminence among all beings. What do you think, Subhūti, are the beings in this trichiliocosm many?
He replied: "They are many, Blessed One; they are many, Sugata. Even the beings in Jambudvīpa alone, Blessed One, are many, let alone those beings in the trichiliocosm."
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, suppose all the beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system were to obtain a human body one after another in succession and were to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Of them—"

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to live for as long as his life lasts and provide for each and every one of them with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick, what do you think, Subhūti, would that bodhisattva mahāsattva produce much merit on that account?
He said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata. The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Subhūti, that son of good family or daughter of good family will produce far more merit who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this profound perfection of wisdom, and who shall practice in accordance with suchness. Why is that?
In this way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is of great benefit for bodhisattva mahāsattvas;

it is the bringer of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to be unsurpassed among all beings, who wishes to be a protector for those beings who are without a protector, and who wishes to be a refuge for those who are without a refuge—[should train in this perfection of wisdom].

By one who desires to become a refuge; by one who desires to become a final resort for those without a resort; by one who desires to become eyes for the blind; by one who desires to become a lamp for those cast into the darkness of ignorance; by one who desires to attain Buddhahood; by one who desires to enter the domain of the Buddhas;
by one who desires to sport in the playful display of a Buddha; by one who desires to roar the lion’s roar of a Buddha; [by one who desires to beat] the drum of a Buddha...

One who desires to surpass others, who desires to blow the Buddha-conch, and who desires to engage in the Buddha’s discourse, should train right here in this profound perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom, there is no such success that he does not obtain—nothing that he ought not to obtain. Subhūti...
“Blessed One, should the perfection of a śrāvaka also be attained by this person? And should the perfection of a pratyekabuddha also be attained by this person?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, the perfection of the śrāvaka must also be attained by him, and the perfection of the pratyekabuddha must also be attained by him;
yet he should not remain there, nor should he take his stand therein. Having seen them through both knowledge and vision, he must transcend them.

One must enter the determination of a bodhisattva. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in this way draws near to all-aspect omniscience and awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, training in this way...

A bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes worthy of offerings in the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti, when training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses all other those worthy of offerings—the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—and draws near to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Training in this way, he proceeds.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not abandon the perfection of wisdom, practices the perfection of wisdom,

and is never separated from the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this way within this profound perfection of wisdom should be known as one whose nature is non-retrogression regarding all-aspect omniscience.

He keeps the levels of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas at a distance and draws near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. However, if it should occur to him: "This is the perfection of wisdom; here is the perfection of wisdom; by means of this perfection of wisdom I shall bring forth the knowledge of all aspects," [then he would fall away].

If he knows it thus, he does not course in the perfection of wisdom. Yet, if he does not know that perfection of wisdom—this is the perfection of wisdom, here is the perfection of wisdom—he does not know or see even that. He does not know for whom there is the perfection of wisdom, or by what means the perfection of wisdom, or who, having set out by means of the perfection of wisdom, awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, if it occurs to him thus:
This is not the perfection of wisdom, nor is there a perfection of wisdom here;

no dharma whatsoever emerges by means of this perfection of wisdom, because of the stability of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), suchness (*tathatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Practicing in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom.
(AdSPG I 48) Chapter 58.
Then, this thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

Even while practicing here in the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom— up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—
a bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses all sentient beings. How much more so after he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

Greatly gained are the acquisitions of those beings, and well-lived is the life of those beings whose minds incline toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). How much more so for those who generate the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*)!
Those beings by whom the mind has been generated, or will be generated, for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment are truly objects of longing.
And while they were listening to this perfection of wisdom, Śakra, the lord of the gods, took māndārava flowers and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he scattered, showered, and strewed those māndārava flowers over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha. Having scattered and showered them, he remained there.
Having scattered [the flowers] in this way, he spoke these words:

"May those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who aspire to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment attain the fulfillment of the Buddha-qualities through this root of merit; may they attain the fulfillment of the qualities of omniscience; may they attain the fulfillment of these very qualities of self-existence."

May there be the fulfillment of these very same untainted dharmas. O Bhagavat, not even a single thought arises in me that a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who has set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment would turn back. O Bhagavat, not even a single thought arises in me that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having turned back, would fall into the state of a Śrāvaka or into Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment. Rather, [it is my wish that they may attain it].

Indeed, one should generate the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. To a still greater degree, one should make a vow for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Having seen these sufferings belonging to the realm of saṃsāra, desiring the welfare, desiring the benefit, desiring the happiness, and desiring the security and well-being of the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, one is endowed with these productions of the thought [of awakening].
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should investigate in this way: "How might we, having crossed over ourselves, cause beings who have not crossed over to cross?

How might we, having been liberated ourselves, liberate beings who are not yet liberated? How might we, having found comfort ourselves, comfort beings who have not found comfort? How might we, having attained final nirvāṇa ourselves, lead beings who have not attained final nirvāṇa to attain it? To what extent...

That son of good family or daughter of good family, O Blessed One, would generate merit who rejoices in those productions of the thought of awakening of bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle; who rejoices in those productions of the thought of awakening of bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who have long practiced;
and who rejoices in those productions of the thought of awakening of bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who are irreversible.

One should rejoice in those productions of the thought of awakening; one should rejoice even in those productions of the thought of awakening belonging to Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas who are bound to only one more birth.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

Kauśika, it might be possible to measure the amount of earth in the four-continent world-system by means of the tip of a hair, but it is not possible to measure the merit of those productions of the thought of awakening accompanied by rejoicing. Kauśika, it might be possible to measure the amount of earth in the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system by means of the tip of a hair, but it is not possible to measure the merit of those productions of the thought of awakening accompanied by rejoicing.

The measure of the merit of those productions of the thought of awakening would be like this, Kauśika: suppose there were the mass of water in the great oceans within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system; the measure of the drops of water that might be drawn out by the tip of a hair split a hundred times would not equal the measure of the merit of those productions of the thought of awakening accompanied by sympathetic joy.
[This is] the authoritative testimony. When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, those beings who do not rejoice in these productions of the thought [of awakening] will be under the influence of Māra;
Blessed One, those beings who do not rejoice in these productions of the thought [of awakening] will belong to the faction of Māra."
"Blessed One, those beings who do not rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening will have fallen away from the realm of Māra. Why is that?

Blessed One, those beings who, having brought forth these productions of the thought, dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening, are indeed the ones who bring about the destruction of Māra’s realm. Those productions of the thought which are directed toward unexcelled [awakening] are to be rejoiced in."
The resolutions for perfect enlightenment have been generated. Those who have not forsaken the Buddha, have not forsaken the Dharma,
and have not forsaken the Saṅgha should rejoice in these resolutions.

Having rejoiced, they should dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, in such a way that there is neither the perception of duality nor the perception of non-duality. The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Kauśika, so it is. It is just as you say. Those, Kauśika, who shall rejoice in these productions of the thought of awakening will very quickly please the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas."

Having pleased [the Buddhas], they will never cause them to be displeased. Thus, endowed with these roots of merit arising from the production of thoughts accompanied by sympathetic joy, wherever they are reborn, there they will be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped;
and they shall never see an unpleasant form, nor shall they hear unpleasant sounds.
They will not smell unpleasant odors; they will not taste unpleasant flavors; they will not touch unpleasant tangibles; they will not cognize unpleasant mental phenomena (*dharmas*).

Furthermore, they shall never be separated from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. They will pass from buddha-field to buddha-field, and there they will plant roots of merit before those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Why is that?

For it is thus, Kauśika: those sons of good family and daughters of good family have rejoiced in the roots of virtue of incalculable bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have first set out in the vehicle— those established in the second stage,
those established in the third stage, up to those established in the tenth stage, and even those bodhisattvas bound by only one more birth.

Those roots of merit of the great beings have been rejoiced in. As those roots of merit increase, they draw near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Having fully awakened to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they will lead immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvana. Therefore, by this method as well, Kauśika—

That son of good family or daughter of good family, having rejoiced in the roots of merit of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle, should dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in such a way that there is neither a mind nor anything other than a mind. [They should rejoice in] those roots of merit of those who are practicing the conduct, those who are irreversible, and those who are bound to one more birth.

Having rejoiced, they should be dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in such a way that there is neither a mind nor anything other than the mind. Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, how will a mind that is like an illusion realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?”
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that mind which is like an illusion?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. I do not, Blessed One, perceive an illusion, nor do I perceive a mind that is like an illusion. The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that mind which awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment as being either illusion or a mind like an illusion? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive that phenomenon—which will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—as being apart from illusion or a mind like an illusion?"

He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One. Blessed One, apart from illusion and apart from a mind that is like an illusion, I do not perceive any such dharma that will realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, Blessed One, not perceiving any other dharma,"
"What dharma shall I teach—whether existence or non-existence?
A dharma that is absolutely secluded does not arrive at either existence or non-existence. A dharma that is absolutely secluded will not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;
nor does a non-existent dharma realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Why is that?"

For it is thus, Blessed One, that all phenomena do not exist—those which might become afflicted or purified. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is absolutely secluded; the perfection of meditation is absolutely secluded;
the perfection of vigor is absolutely secluded; the perfection of patience is absolutely secluded; the perfection of ethical discipline is absolutely secluded.
The perfection of giving is ultimately secluded;
even up to awakening, it is ultimately secluded. And that dharma which is ultimately secluded is neither to be cultivated nor to be eliminated, nor does it belong to any dharma whatsoever.

The perfection of wisdom is the bringer [of enlightenment] because of its ultimate purity. The perfection of wisdom is utterly secluded. How is it that, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is ultimately secluded.
"In that case, how does the awakening to the secluded by means of the secluded occur?
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is so, Subhūti, it is so. For, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is absolutely secluded."

For the perfection of meditation is absolutely secluded; for the perfection of vigor is absolutely secluded; for the perfection of patience is absolutely secluded; for the perfection of ethical discipline is absolutely secluded; for the perfection of generosity is absolutely secluded; indeed, up to awakening it is absolutely secluded, and up to the knowledge of all aspects it is absolutely secluded. Just as, Subhūti, it is absolutely secluded—

The perfection of wisdom— indeed, up to the knowledge of all aspects— is likewise utterly secluded, and thus unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is fully awakened to. Subhūti, if the perfection of wisdom were not utterly secluded, and if the knowledge of all aspects were not utterly secluded, it would not be the perfection of wisdom, and it would not be the knowledge of all aspects.

Therefore, Subhūti, just as the perfection of wisdom is absolutely secluded, and just as everything up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is absolutely secluded—in this way, Subhūti, it is not by not relying on the perfection of wisdom that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*) is fully awakened to. Nor is enlightenment awakened to by means of seclusion through seclusion; yet, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is indeed fully awakened to.
And one does not attain full awakening without having approached the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in a profound meaning. The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is."

“Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in a profound meaning. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is difficult in that he courses in a profound meaning yet does not personally realize that meaning—namely, the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. He said:
As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, he does nothing that is difficult to do. How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is one who performs what is difficult?
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, that object which would be realized is not apprehended.

That perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is also not apprehended; nor is that dharma apprehended by which it would be realized, nor is that person who would realize it apprehended. Since all dharmas are unapprehendable, O Blessed One, what object will be realized? Or by which perfection of wisdom will it be realized? Which...
or a dharma that will be realized—having realized which one does not tremble, does not fear, and does not fall into terror? Blessed One, the conduct of a bodhisattva is a conduct of non-apprehension;
practicing therein, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the state of being without darkness regarding all dharmas. Blessed One, if, while this is being spoken, a bodhisattva...

The mind of the mahāsattva does not sink, does not shrink back, is not terrified, is not utterly terrified, and does not fall into terror. Practicing in this way, O Bhagavat, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive "I am practicing," nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
He does not even perceive, "I shall fully awaken. Furthermore, O Blessed One, as that bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him:
"I shall distance myself from the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; I am near to the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). O Blessed One, it is just as if open space were not to think:
"I am either far from or near to someone. For what reason?

Because, Blessed One, open space is non-existent, because it is immovable, and because, Blessed One, open space is free from conceptual construction. In the same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him:
"Either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha is far from me; unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening is near to me. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is free from conceptual construction. It is just as if, Blessed One, a person created by illusion does not think:
'The illusion is far from me.'"
"The illusionist is near to me;
as for this multitude of people who have gathered, they are far from me, whether near or far. For what reason is that?"

“Because, Blessed One, an illusory person is without conceptual construction. In the same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to him: ‘The level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha is far from me; unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening is near to me. Just as, Blessed One, it does not occur to a reflection:
‘That objective support by which this reflection has arisen is near to me.’”

"But those who have approached here, whether in a mirror or in a bowl of water, they are far from me. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, a reflection is without conceptual construction (*avikalpa*). In the very same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it does not occur to him:
'The level of the śrāvaka or the level of the pratyekabuddha is far from me.'"
"Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is near to me. For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is free from conceptual construction. Indeed, Blessed One, there is nothing dear or undear to the perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
Because its intrinsic nature is not apprehended."

Whether it be someone dear or someone not dear. Just as, Blessed One, for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, no one whatsoever exists who is either dear or not dear, even so, Blessed One, for the perfection of wisdom, no one whatsoever exists who is either dear or not dear. Just as, Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has abandoned all conceptual constructions and discriminations (*sarvakalpavikalpa*), even so, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom.
It is free from all conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts, because it is based on non-conceptuality. Just as, Blessed One, it does not occur to a Tathāgata’s emanation:
"The level of the Śrāvaka or the level of the Pratyekabuddha is far from me."
"Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is near to me. Why is that?

Blessed One, it is because there is no conceptual differentiation between a Tathāgata and a Tathāgata’s emanation. In the same way, Blessed One, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha is likewise far from me."

"Unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is close at hand for me. Lord, it is just as if a Tathāgata were to create an emanation; that emanation performs whatever task it was created for, yet that emanation is without conceptualization and free from conceptualization.
In the same way, Lord, for whatever purpose the perfection of wisdom is cultivated, it performs that very task."

And that perfection of wisdom is non-conceptual and free from conceptualization. It is just as if, Blessed One, a skilled carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice were to construct a mechanical device in the form of a woman, a man, or an elephant.
Or it may have the form of a bull. And whatever task it was made for, that task it performs. Furthermore, that machine is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*);

in the very same way, Blessed One, for whatever purpose the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is cultivated, it performs that task. And that perfection of wisdom is itself free from conceptual construction. Then the Venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Venerable Subhūti:
"But, venerable Subhūti, is it only the perfection of wisdom that is non-conceptual, or are the perfection of meditation, and so on,
up to the perfection of generosity, also non-conceptual? Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, even the perfection of meditation is non-conceptual; indeed, even the perfection of generosity is non-conceptual. He asked:
"But, venerable Subhūti, is form also non-conceptual, up to and including consciousness, which is also non-conceptual?
Is the eye also non-conceptual, up to and including the mind, which is also non-conceptual?"
Furthermore, is form also non-conceptual,
up to and including phenomena also being non-conceptual? [Is] eye-consciousness [also non-conceptual]?
Is even the mental consciousness non-conceptual?
Is even visual contact non-conceptual, up to and including mental contact?
Are even the feelings born of visual contact non-conceptual, up to and including the feelings born of mental contact?
Furthermore, are the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) also non-conceptual?
Are the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the path (*mārga*), as well as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the signless (*ānimitta*), and the wishless (*apraṇihita*), also non-conceptual?

How much more so the ten powers of a Tathāgata (*daśatathāgatabala*), the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*)?

"Is great compassion also non-conceptual? Are even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha non-conceptual? Is awakening also non-conceptual? And are both the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm also non-conceptual? Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, all dharmas are also non-conceptual. He said:
"Venerable Subhūti, if all dharmas are also non-conceptual, from where has this distinction of the fivefold saṃsāra come—namely, hell-beings, animals, the world of Yama, gods, and humans?"
From where does this manifestation arise—of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Blessed Buddhas?
Subhūti replied:
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, those beings who perform actions arisen from perversion by means of body, speech, and mind—"

For them, such sense-bases (*āyatana*) are produced. Having grasped the ripening of karma rooted in desire and arisen from conceptual construction, they bring about the destinies of hell-beings, animals, the world of Yama, gods, and humans.
Furthermore, as for what the Venerable Śāradvatīputra has said:
From what, then, are the stream-enterers distinguished; from what the once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas;
from what the bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas;
and from what the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas are distinguished?
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is through non-conceptualization that stream-enterers are distinguished;
through non-conceptualization the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including through non-conceptualization the arhats and through non-conceptualization arhatship;
through non-conceptualization the pratyekabuddhas and through non-conceptualization pratyekabodhi.

Through non-conceptualization are the Buddhas; through non-conceptualization is awakening. Moreover, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who existed in the past time—those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, were also non-conceptual and had abandoned conceptualization.
Likewise, those of the future will also be non-conceptual. And those, Śāradvatīputra, who exist now in the ten directions...
In the world-systems, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in the present time—
those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, are also free from conceptual construction and have abandoned conceptual construction.
Therefore, by this method, O Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it should be understood in this way.

All phenomena are non-conceptual, having taken as their standard the non-conceptual suchness of reality; they have taken as their standard the suchness of the limit of reality and the suchness of the realm of phenomena. In this way indeed, venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice in the non-conceptual perfection of wisdom.
Practicing in the non-conceptual perfection of wisdom, one fully awakens to all dharmas as being non-conceptual.
(58) Chapter 59.
Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom indeed courses in the essence;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva indeed courses in the essence. When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti [said to] the venerable...
He said this to Śāradvatīputra:
"Venerable Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom indeed courses in what is essence-less. For what reason?
Because, venerable Śāradvatīputra, the perfection of wisdom is essence-less, up to and including omniscience which is essence-less. And for what reason?"

For in this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend and does not perceive even the insubstantial; how much less could he apprehend the substantial? Thus, as long as he does not apprehend the insubstantiality of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), how much less could he apprehend the substantial? Then, it occurred to many sons of the gods belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*) and the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*):

Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who have generated the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and who practice here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, and who practice in this very sense, yet do not realize the limit of reality— that realization by which one would fall to the level of a śrāvaka— are worthy of homage.

or would abide on the level of a pratyekabuddha. By this very reasoning, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who do not personally realize these dharmatās are worthy of homage. Then the venerable Subhūti said this to those sons of the gods:
"O sons of the gods, this is not difficult."
Those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who do not personally realize this true nature of phenomena— which, if realized,
would cause them to abide on the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha— this, O sons of gods, is what is even more difficult for them:
that they don the armor, thinking, "We shall bring immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvāṇa."

And those beings whom they might lead to final nirvana are ultimately not to be apprehended. Yet, practicing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva has set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment with the thought, "I shall discipline all beings. He would be regarding space as something to be disciplined.
Whoever should think that there are beings to be disciplined—for what reason is that?
One should see the solitude of beings through the solitude of space;
one should see the emptiness of beings through the emptiness of space; one should see the insubstantiality of beings through the insubstantiality of space.

The emptiness of sentient beings is to be seen through the emptiness of space. By this method as well, O sons of the gods, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are doers of what is difficult, they who don the armor for the sake of sentient beings who do not exist.
Those who don the armor for the sake of sentient beings desire to dispute with space; yet that armor is [donned] by the Bodhisattva...
The Great Being has donned the armor, yet those beings for whose sake the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has donned the armor are not to be apprehended. Why is that?
Because of the solitude of beings, the solitude of the armor should be seen. If, when this is being spoken, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not become despondent...
The bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

Because of the solitude of form, there is the solitude of sentient beings. Because of the solitude of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is the solitude of sentient beings.

Because of the solitude of form, there is the solitude of the perfection of wisdom. Because of the solitude of form, there is the solitude of everything up to and including the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not sink, does not become despondent, and his mind does not fall into terror when the solitude of all dharmas is being taught,
then that bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom. Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"For what reason, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not become despondent regarding the perfection of wisdom?
He replied: "O Blessed One, because all dharmas are non-existent, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become despondent regarding the perfection of wisdom;
O Blessed One, because they are secluded, peaceful, and unarisen, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become despondent."

In the perfection of wisdom. For this reason, O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become despondent in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because, O Blessed One, he who would become despondent, that by which he would become despondent, or that in which he would become despondent—none of these phenomena are found to exist. If, O Blessed One, when this is being spoken, a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
He does not sink, he does not despair; he does not shrink back, he does not falter, he does not withdraw;
he is not terrified, he is not frightened, he does not fall into terror. He courses in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, all these dharmas do not exist—neither one who might sink nor that by which one might sink.

Or where he might sink. "Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this way is honored by the gods together with Indra, together with Brahmā, and together with Prajāpati. The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, it is not only by the gods together with Indra, together with Brahmā, and together with Prajāpati that the bodhisattva is honored."
The Mahāsattva who courses in this way in the perfection of wisdom is honored even by those sons of the gods belonging to the Abhikrāntas,

the Abhikrāntavarṇas, the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Bṛhatphalas, up to those of the Śuddhāvāsa realm, who likewise honor that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who courses in this way in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, even those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in incalculable and immeasurable world-systems [honor him].
They remain, are sustained, and endure;
they too keep in mind that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom, thinking:
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, will fulfill the perfection of generosity," and so on, up to...

He will fulfill the knowledge of all aspects. Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva whom the Buddha Bhagavāns hold in their mindful attention while he courses in the perfection of wisdom, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be regarded as one who has set out for Buddhahood. Subhūti, as many beings as there are in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, they all—
Even if there were Māras, the Evil Ones,
and each single Māra, the Evil One, were to conjure up as many Māras, the Evil Ones, as there are,
they would all be powerless to create an obstacle for that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. For two reasons...
Subhūti, endowed with two qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes invincible to the wicked Māras.
Which two?
He has contemplated the emptiness of all phenomena, and yet he has not abandoned any sentient beings.

They exist. Subhūti, endowed with these two qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes invincible to the wicked Māras. Furthermore, Subhūti, endowed with another two qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom becomes invincible to the wicked Māras. Which two?

He acts exactly as he speaks and is attended by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Subhūti, endowed with these two qualities, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom becomes invincible to the wicked Māras. Thus...

Subhūti, as those bodhisattva mahāsattvas are practicing, those sons of the gods will think they should approach them; they will attend upon them, question them, inquire further, and give them encouragement, saying:
"Noble son, you will quickly attain the awakening of a Buddha. Therefore, noble son, by this very [method]..."
Dwell in the dwelling, that is to say, in the dwelling of emptiness, the dwelling of signlessness, and the dwelling of wishlessness. Why is that?

Because, noble son, by dwelling in this dwelling, you will become a protector for beings who are without a protector, a refuge for beings who are without a refuge, a shelter for beings who are without a shelter, and a final resort for beings who have no other resort.

"You shall be the final resort for beings who have no resort; you shall be a shelter for beings who have no shelter; you shall be an island for beings who have no island; you shall become a light for beings who have become blind. For what reason?
Because, as this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling of the perfection of wisdom, even those...
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems,

teaching the Dharma and surrounded by a community of monks— they [behold] that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who courses in this Perfection of Wisdom and is endowed with these qualities, namely, the qualities of the Perfection of Wisdom.

Proclaiming their names and lineages, they teach the Dharma and utter inspired utterances (udāna). Subhūti, it is just as I, at this very moment, while proclaiming the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ratnaketu, teach the Dharma and utter inspired utterances, and likewise [proclaim] the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sikhin.

Manifesting in this manner, I teach the Dharma and utter inspired utterances. Furthermore, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, are never separated from this perfection of wisdom.

I also teach the Dharma and utter inspired exclamation while proclaiming the names of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas. Furthermore, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, who currently reside, remain, and maintain their lives in the eastern direction, teaching the Dharma—

In that regard, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice such a holy life (*brahmacarya*) and are never separated from this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, gladden them with their appearance as they teach the Dharma and utter inspired exclamation (*udāna*). Likewise, those who are in the southern direction, the western, the northern, the nadir, and the zenith—

As far as the Buddha Bhagavāns remain, stay, and maintain themselves throughout the ten directions in all their surroundings, teaching the Dharma— there, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who practice the holy life (brahmacarya) without being separated from this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
the Buddha Bhagavāns gladden them with their appearance as they teach the Dharma and utter inspired utterances (udāna).
Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, from the first production of the thought of awakening, purify the path to awakening until they attain all-aspect omniscience—
even for them, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma with an appearance of great joy and utter inspired exclamations. Why is that?
"In this way, Subhūti, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are indeed doers of what is difficult, who have set out for the sake of the non-interruption of the Buddha-lineage. He asked:
"Blessed One, of which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, proclaim the names while they teach the Dharma? Is it of those who are irreversible (*avaivartika*), or..."
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are irreversible and who course in the perfection of wisdom. There are also bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have not yet been predicted and who course in the perfection of wisdom. To them, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma with a form that inspires joy and utter inspired utterances. Subhūti asked:
"But who, Blessed One, are they?
The Blessed One said:
"Those who practice the conduct of a bodhisattva under the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Subhūti, these are those irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattvas whom the Buddhas,
the Blessed Ones, delight with their countenances as they teach the Dharma and utter inspired utterances.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there are those who, emulating the example of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ratnaketu, practice the conduct of a bodhisattva.

They practice. For them as well, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, appear in a form that inspires joy, teaching the Dharma and uttering inspired utterances (*udāna*). Furthermore, Subhūti, there are those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice in the perfection of wisdom, who have resolute faith in the non-arising nature of all phenomena, yet have not yet attained the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding non-arisen phenomena.
They are resolved that all phenomena are empty, yet they have not attained the patient acceptance of non-arising phenomena.

They are resolved that all phenomena are peaceful, yet they have not attained the patient acceptance of non-arising phenomena. They are resolved that all phenomena are hollow, vain, empty, and without essence, yet they have not [attained the patient acceptance of non-arising phenomena].

"Patience regarding phenomena has been attained. Subhūti, those Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, also teach the Dharma and utter inspired exhortations to these Bodhisattvas, those Mahāsattvas, appearing in a form that gladdens them. Furthermore, Subhūti, for those Bodhisattvas, those Mahāsattvas, the Buddhas, those Blessed Ones, appear in a form that fully proclaims their names while teaching the Dharma."

They teach the *udāna* and inspire others with *udāna*. Subhūti, for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas as well, the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha have been abandoned, and they are prophesied for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, for whichever bodhisattva...

As a mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, proclaim his name while teaching the Dharma and uttering inspired exhortations. That bodhisattva mahāsattva will stand firm in the state of non-retrogression; established therein, he will attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva...
Having heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* being spoken, the *mahāsattva* will not be perplexed, will not doubt, and will not be bewildered, thinking,

"This is exactly as it was spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Furthermore, he will hear it in detail from the presence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Akṣobhya, and from those who belong to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas.
From the presence of these sons of good family,
this son of good family who belongs to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas will also have faith in this perfection of wisdom;
and by having faith in this profound perfection of wisdom exactly as it was spoken by the Tathāgata, he will [abide] in the state of non-retrogression.

It will remain so. For in this way, Subhūti, the hearing of the perfection of wisdom is of great benefit to bodhisattva mahāsattvas; how much more so for those who will have faith in it, and having had faith, will abide in suchness, will practice for the sake of suchness, and having abided in suchness and practiced for the sake of suchness, will remain established in the knowledge of all aspects. He said:
Furthermore, Blessed One, since one who stands in suchness and practices in such a way will not apprehend any dharma at all, how will they stand in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)?
Blessed One, since a magical creation of the Tathāgata does not apprehend any dharma, who is it that will stand in suchness?
Or who, having stood in suchness, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Or who [will stand] in suchness?
"Will he, having stood [in suchness], teach the Dharma?

Even suchness itself is not apprehended; how much less so one who will stand in suchness? That he will, having stood in suchness, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or that he will, having stood in suchness, teach the Dharma—this is impossible. The Blessed One said:

As for what Subhūti has said: "The Tathāgata’s emanation does not perceive any other phenomenon whatsoever that could abide in suchness, or, having abided in suchness, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;
nor, having abided in suchness, teach the Dharma. For even suchness itself is not perceived; how much less so [the one who would abide in it]?"
"He who will abide in suchness; having abided in suchness, he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

having abided in suchness, he will teach the Dharma—this is impossible. It is so, Subhūti, it is so, just as you say. Subhūti, a Tathāgata’s emanation does not perceive any dharma other [than suchness]."

Whoever might abide in suchness, and having abided in suchness, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, or having abided in suchness, teach the Dharma— suchness itself is first of all not apprehended; how much less so one who will abide in suchness,
or who, having abided in suchness, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
It is impossible that one, while abiding in suchness, should teach the Dharma. Why is that?

Subhūti, whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this suchness of phenomena remains established—unfailing, unchanging suchness. This very nature of phenomena remains established as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the stability of phenomena.

The fixed nature of phenomena is the limit of reality. Subhūti, herein within suchness no one will abide; nor, having abided in suchness, will anyone fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; nor, having abided in suchness, will anyone teach the Dharma. For what reason is that?

For in this suchness, neither arising is perceived, nor passing away, nor the alteration of that which is established. Since for any dharma neither arising is perceived, nor passing away, nor the alteration of that which is established, no one at all will abide therein; nor, having abided therein, will anyone awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
How much less, then, could he stand therein and teach the Dharma? This is impossible. Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said this to the Blessed One:

"Profound, O Blessed One, is this Perfection of Wisdom. Difficult is it for those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, O Blessed One, who desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?"

Moreover, Blessed One, no phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended; nor is there anyone who will abide in suchness, nor anyone who awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor anyone who teaches the Dharma. And therein they do not become discouraged, nor does any state of doubt or hesitation arise in them. Then Subhūti—
The Elder addressed Śakra, the lord of the gods, as follows: "O Kauśika, when you say, 'The Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, are doers of what is difficult,
they who here in these profound dharmas have neither doubt nor hesitation,' [it is because], O Kauśika, all dharmas are empty."
"Who here could have any doubt or hesitation?
Śakra said: "Whatever the Elder Subhūti teaches, he teaches it all by taking emptiness alone as his starting point;
it does not cling anywhere. It is just as if an arrow were shot into the air—it does not cling anywhere; even so [is Subhūti's teaching]."
The Dharma teaching of the Elder Subhūti does not adhere anywhere.
(59) (AdSPG I 69) Chapter 60.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, in speaking thus and teaching thus, am I one who speaks what has been said by the Blessed One, one who speaks according to the Dharma, and do I correctly explain the conformity to the Dharma?
The Blessed One said:

"Indeed, Kauśika, by speaking and teaching in this way, you speak as one who speaks according to the Tathāgata’s word, you speak as one who speaks the Dharma, and you explain the conformity to the Dharma (anudharmatā) of the Dharma. Śakra said:

"It is wonderful, Blessed One, how far-reaching is the inspired eloquence (*pratibhāna*) of the Elder Subhūti! All that he brings forth is based solely upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*); it is brought forth based solely upon the signless (*animitta*) and the wishless (*apraṇihita*). [He brings forth] the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)."

It appears starting from just this, up to appearing starting from the path itself; it appears starting from internal emptiness itself, up to appearing starting from the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence itself; [it appears] up to appearing starting from awakening itself. The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, the Elder Kauśika, dwelling in emptiness, does not even perceive the perfection of giving; how much less so one who practices the perfection of giving? He does not even perceive the perfection of ethical discipline; how much less so one who practices the perfection of ethical discipline? Likewise [he does not perceive] the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom.

In this way, one does not even perceive [the factors themselves]. How much less so for one who courses in the perfection of wisdom? One does not even perceive the applications of mindfulness; how much less so for one who cultivates the applications of mindfulness? Up to: one does not even perceive the path; how much less so for one who cultivates the path? One does not even perceive internal emptiness; how much less so...

One who cultivates internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, does not even perceive that [emptiness]. How much less so for one who cultivates the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence? One does not even perceive the Noble Truths themselves; how much less so for one who cultivates the Noble Truths? Thus it is.

One does not even perceive the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; how much less so one who cultivates the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments? One does not even perceive the powers; how much less so one who cultivates the powers? One does not even perceive the grounds of self-confidence; how much less so one who brings forth the grounds of self-confidence? One does not even perceive the analytical knowledges...

How much less so for one who accomplishes the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); such a person does not even perceive great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). How much less so for one who dwells in great compassion; such a person does not even perceive the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*). How much less so for one who accomplishes the unique qualities of a Buddha; such a person does not even perceive awakening (*bodhi*) itself.

How much less so for one who perfectly awakens to enlightenment? One does not even perceive all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*); how much less so for one who attains all-aspect omniscience? One does not even perceive a Tathāgata; how much less so for one who becomes a Tathāgata? One does not even perceive non-arising (*anutpāda*); how much less so for one who realizes non-arising directly?

He does not even perceive the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*); how much less so for one who possesses the primary marks on his body? He does not even perceive the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*); how much less so for one who possesses the secondary characteristics on his body? For what reason? Because, Kauśika, the Elder Subhūti dwells in the seclusion of all phenomena; he dwells in non-apprehension, he dwells in emptiness.

He dwells in the signless and dwells in the wishless. Kauśika, this dwelling of the Elder Subhūti does not approach even a hundredth part of the dwelling of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom; it does not approach even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousand-billionth part, nor any number, nor any fraction, nor any calculation.
It does not even admit of being calculated, compared, or approximated. Why is that?

Because, setting aside the dwelling of a Tathāgata, the dwelling of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, and the dwellings of the śrāvakas and the pratyekabuddhas—among these dwellings, [the former is immeasurable].
This very dwelling of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is declared to be the foremost;
it is declared to be the eldest, the best, the excellent, the most excellent, the sublime; it is declared to be the unsurpassed and the peerless.
Therefore, O Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to attain preeminence among all sentient beings [should practice this].
One should dwell by means of this dwelling; that is to say, by means of the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses here in the perfection of wisdom, [he transcends] the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

He transcends [the stage of an ordinary being]. He enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva. Having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, he fulfills the qualities of a Buddha. Having fulfilled the qualities of a Buddha, he attains the knowledge of all modes. Upon attaining the knowledge of all modes, there occurs for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the abandonment of all afflictions along with their residual impressions and habitual tendencies.

Then, in that very assembly, the gods of the Thirty-three, taking Māndārava flowers, scattered them over the Blessed One, showered them upon him, and strewn them all around him. And more than six hundred monks rose from their seats,
draped their robes over one shoulder, and placed their right knees upon the ground.

Having extended their joined palms toward where the Blessed One was, they gazed upon the Blessed One with unblinking eyes and paid him homage. Then, through the power of the Buddha, as those monks extended their joined palms, they became filled with *māndārava* flowers. With those *māndārava* flowers, they...
They scattered, showered, and strewed [flowers] over the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. While scattering, showering, and strewing them, they spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, by this root of merit and by this supreme dwelling, may we dwell in that which is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition of those monks, manifested a smile at that moment. It is indeed the natural law of the Buddha-Blessed Ones that whenever they manifest a smile, rays of light of many colors and various hues immediately issue forth from the portals of their mouths—
namely, blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, crystal-colored, and silver-colored.

Having pervaded the triple-thousand great-thousand world system with their radiance, they returned once more, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and vanished into the crown of the Blessed One’s head. Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat,
draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and [turned] toward where the Blessed One was.
Having extended his joined palms in reverence toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
"What, O Blessed One, is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting a smile?
For Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition. When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda:

Ānanda, these one hundred and sixty monks shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment during the aeon known as Tārakopama. They shall appear in the world as Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Avakīrṇakusuma. Furthermore, Ānanda, regarding those Tathāgatas, Arhats...

The community of monks of the perfectly enlightened ones will be equal; their Buddha-field will be equal; and their lifespan will be equal, namely, one thousand years. From wherever they shall go forth, having gone forth, they shall renounce the world.

Having gone forth, they will realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. In each of those places, a rain of five-colored flowers will fall. Therefore, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to dwell in the supreme dwelling, and who wishes to dwell in the dwelling of a Tathāgata, should practice the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom. For any son of good family or daughter of good family, Ānanda, who shall practice this profound perfection of wisdom, that son of good family or daughter of good family, Ānanda, must reach the ultimate conclusion.

"I have passed away from among humans and been reborn here, or else I have passed away from the Tuṣita host of gods and been reborn here. It is precisely among humans that this profound perfection of wisdom will have been heard in detail; or perhaps it was while in the Tuṣita host of gods that this profound perfection of wisdom [was heard]."

It shall be heard in detail. Ānanda, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who will practice this profound perfection of wisdom should be regarded as having been looked upon by the Tathāgata. For any son of good family or daughter of good family, Ānanda, who hears this profound perfection of wisdom and, having heard it, takes it up...
They will uphold it, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection;

and they will instruct and admonish those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle in this profound perfection of wisdom. Therefore, Ānanda, that person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle has, in my presence, received this [perfection of wisdom] directly from those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas.

"Ānanda, it should be known that by that son of good family or daughter of good family, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* will have been heard, taken up, retained, recited, and mastered; and therein, roots of merit will have been planted before the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. [He should know:
'I have not planted roots of merit in the presence of the Śrāvakas.'"

This profound perfection of wisdom has not been heard from the presence of the śrāvakas. For any son of good family or daughter of good family, Ānanda, who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, and master this profound perfection of wisdom—
He will follow it according to its meaning, its Dharma, and its phrasing;
Ānanda, that son of good family or daughter of good family should reach the conclusion:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is present before me. For whoever, Ānanda, is a son of good family...

Or, Ānanda, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being spoken, does not reject it and does not oppose it, and having heard it, gains serene confidence,
that son of good family or daughter of good family should be known as one who has performed services for previous Victors and has planted roots of merit.

They are sustained by spiritual friends. Furthermore, Ānanda, whatever root of merit has been planted by a son of good family or a daughter of good family in the presence of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, that shall not come to naught—whether in the state of a Śrāvaka or in the state of a Pratyekabuddha. Moreover, Ānanda, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva must be one who has attained thorough penetration.
While practicing the perfection of generosity, while practicing the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
and so on up to practicing the knowledge of all aspects— Ānanda, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of generosity has indeed thoroughly penetrated it.
Practicing in the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom,
and so on up to practicing in the knowledge of all aspects,
one will not abide in the state of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this to you.

Regarding this profound perfection of wisdom: Ānanda, if you were to take up, master, and then once again lose or once again abandon all those teachings of the Dharma that I have taught— setting aside the perfection of wisdom— [you would still not have lost me].

"Ānanda, you have not offended me to that extent. But if, Ānanda, having taken up this perfection of wisdom, you were to lose even a single word, then, Ānanda, you would have offended me. But if, Ānanda, having taken up this profound perfection of wisdom, you do not lose it again and do not abandon it again, then, Ānanda, [you have not offended me]."

I shall not offend you. Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this profound *prajñāpāramitā* to you, so that you may take it up and preserve it; you should recite it, master it, attend to it well, grasp it thoroughly, master it completely, and maintain it well with those who have attained excellence.
It should be well-expounded through its syllables, words, and phonemes, and it should be properly mastered. For whoever, Ānanda—
whether a son of good family or a daughter of good family— shall take up, bear in mind, recite, and master this profound perfection of wisdom,
by them the awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, future, and present, has been upheld.
It will come to pass, Ānanda, that whichever son of good family or daughter of good family shall take up this profound perfection of wisdom,

by them the awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, will be upheld. Whoever, Ānanda, should wish to honor, revere, respect, and worship me in my very presence— [they should honor this perfection of wisdom].
With flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags—
by these means this perfection of wisdom should be taken up, maintained, recited, and mastered. Having taken it up,
maintained it, recited it, and mastered it, this perfection of wisdom should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped.

By honoring, revering, respecting, and worshiping the *Prajñāpāramitā* with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags, I too shall be honored by them, and the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present shall be honored. For whoever, Ānanda...

When this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being spoken, he will generate respect, affection, and serene faith toward it; by that, he will have generated affection, serene faith, and respect toward the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present. If, Ānanda, you hold me dear, pleasing, and do not abandon me, [then you should likewise hold this in high regard].

Therefore, Ānanda, let this perfection of wisdom be dear to you, pleasing to you, and never abandoned by you. Not even a single word from this profound perfection of wisdom should be lost to you. Although I might speak at great length, Ānanda, concerning the entrustment of the perfection of wisdom, in brief, Ānanda, just as I am your teacher, so is this perfection of wisdom.
Such is this Perfection of Wisdom for you as your Teacher;
therefore, Ānanda, by an immeasurable entrustment, I entrust this Perfection of Wisdom to you.
Therefore, Ānanda, I announce it before the world with its gods, humans, and asuras: that which has not been abandoned by him...

The Buddha has not been forsaken, the Dharma has not been forsaken, the Saṅgha has not been forsaken, and the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present have not been forsaken. May this perfection of wisdom also not be forsaken by me, for it is the enlightenment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present. This is our instruction. For whoever, Ānanda...

Whether it be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who shall take up this profound perfection of wisdom, and shall bear it in mind, recite it, master it, believe in it, and attend to it with wise reflection; and who shall explain, teach, and set forth this profound perfection of wisdom in detail for others through many modes of exposition.

Ānanda, that son of good family or daughter of good family who shall set it forth, explain it, analyze it, clarify it, and reveal it will indeed very swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
They will be close to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is that?
For, Ānanda, the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is born from the perfection of wisdom.

Moreover, Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who existed in the past—the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, was likewise born solely from the perfection of wisdom. And those who...

Ānanda, in the future time there will be Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas; for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, too, supreme perfect enlightenment is born precisely from the perfection of wisdom. And as for those, Ānanda, who are now in the eastern direction, in the southern, western, northern, downward, and upward directions—

To the extent that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who dwell, abide, and maintain themselves, and who teach the Dharma, throughout the world-systems in all ten directions— the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of those Blessed Buddhas is likewise born from the perfection of wisdom alone. Therefore, Ānanda, one who desires to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the six perfections. Why is that?

Because, Ānanda, this perfection of wisdom is indeed the mother of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. For whatever bodhisattva mahāsattvas, Ānanda, shall train in the six perfections, they will all go forth [to liberation].
in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust and hand over these six perfections to you even more extensively. Why is that?
Because, Ānanda, this is the treasury of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened Buddhas.

For this treasury of Dharma is indeed inexhaustible, namely, the treasury of the six perfections. Moreover, Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who dwell, abide, and maintain themselves, teaching the Dharma, in the world systems of the eastern direction, the southern, the western, the northern, below, above, and indeed throughout all the ten directions— [all these rely upon this treasury].
And they teach it. Those Buddhas, O Ānanda, those Blessed Ones also teach the Dharma here from this very treasury of the six perfections.

And those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones who appeared in the past, O Ānanda, they too, having trained in these very six perfections, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and taught the Dharma.

...are teaching. Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future time, they too, having trained in these very six perfections, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and will teach the Dharma. [f. 235a] And those [teachings] of the Buddhas of the infinite past, future, and present—
All the disciples of the Blessed Ones, having trained in this very perfection of wisdom here, have attained final nirvana, are attaining final nirvana,

and will attain final nirvana. If you, Ānanda, were to teach the Dharma concerning the level of the disciples to persons belonging to the vehicle of the disciples, and by that teaching of the Dharma, [those in] the triple-thousand great-thousand world system...

Even if all those beings were to realize arhatship, you would still not have performed the duty of a disciple toward me as my disciple. But if you, Ānanda, were to teach or explain even a single word concerning the perfection of wisdom to a bodhisattva mahāsattva, [you would have fulfilled that duty].

In this way, would I be gratified by you as a disciple, and would the duty of a disciple have been performed by that disciple? And by that former teaching of the Dharma, those in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system...

If all the beings in the world-system were to successively and finally realize arhatship, and if there were the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, and the basis of meritorious action consisting of cultivation belonging to those arhats— what do you think, Ānanda, would that be much?
He said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata. The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Ānanda, a person belonging to the vehicle of the disciples (śrāvakayānika) would generate far more merit if they were to teach the Dharma connected with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even if only for a single day."

Let alone one day, Ānanda; if, Ānanda, it were even half a day; let alone half a day, Ānanda; if, Ānanda, it were even until the morning meal, or if it were for the interval of a finger-snap, or even for the interval of a finger-snap.

If it were even for a single moment, a lava, or a muhūrta, Ānanda, this person belonging to the vehicle of the disciples who teaches the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom to a bodhisattva mahāsattva would produce far more merit than [the merit of] all those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the vehicles of the disciples and solitary buddhas.

and it surpasses that root of merit. Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva should teach the Dharma connected with the perfection of wisdom to persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle— even for a single day, or half a day, or before a meal,
or for the duration of a nāḍikā, or a moment (kṣaṇa), or a lava, or a muhūrta—
Ānanda, this bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses the roots of merit of all sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is that?
Because he himself desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and he [establishs] others in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

He encourages, gladdens, inspires, settles, and establishes them. Thus, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the six perfections, in the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on up to the knowledge of the aspects of the path, increasing in roots of goodness—Ānanda, it is impossible and out of the question that he should fall away from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this is not possible.
Furthermore, while this Perfection of Wisdom was being spoken, the Blessed One, right there before the fourfold assembly of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas,
performed such a miraculous feat of supernatural power that,
by means of that performed feat, they all beheld the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, surrounded by a community of monks.
He was teaching the Dharma, preceded by the community of monks, surrounded by an assembly like the ocean, which was as unshakeable as the sea;
[an assembly consisting] entirely of Arhats whose taints were exhausted, who were free from defilements, had attained mastery, whose minds were well-liberated, whose wisdom was well-liberated,
who were noble steeds, great elephants, who had accomplished their task, performed what was to be done, laid down the burden, and attained their own goal.

[The assembly was] together with Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, whose fetters of existence were completely exhausted, whose minds were well-liberated through perfect knowledge, who had attained the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states, and whose intellects were like the ocean. Then the Blessed One withdrew that miraculous manifestation; and when that miraculous manifestation had been withdrawn, those four assemblies did not [perceive it].
They see again that Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha,
as well as his disciples or those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle;
yet they no longer see that buddha-field of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
The community of monks, headed by the Buddha, no longer came within the range of their vision. Why was that?
Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha had withdrawn that miraculous manifestation. Consequently, they were able to see once again. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, do you see that buddha-field of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and that Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and that community of monks and that community of bodhisattvas?"
He said: "O Blessed One, even that buddha-field does not come into the range of vision; neither does that Tathāgata, nor that community of monks, nor that community of bodhisattvas.

The Blessed One said: "In this very way, Ānanda, all phenomena do not come into the range of vision. One phenomenon does not come into the range of another phenomenon. One phenomenon does not see another phenomenon. One phenomenon does not know another phenomenon. It is just as with Akṣobhya."

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, those disciples, those persons belonging to the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, and that Buddha-field do not come within the range of the eye. For in this way, Ānanda, all phenomena do not come within the range of the eye. One phenomenon does not come within the range of another phenomenon; one phenomenon does not [perceive] a phenomenon.
He sees. A phenomenon does not know another phenomenon. For all phenomena, Ānanda, are without cognition, without vision, and incapable of action. Why is that?
Because, Ānanda, all phenomena are inactive and ungraspable due to the inactivity of space;
for, Ānanda, all phenomena are inconceivable, being like an illusory person.

"Ānanda, all phenomena are indeed without an experiencer because they are devoid of mind; this is because their characteristic is that of a mere appearance and because they lack any core substance. Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom and does not become attached to any phenomenon whatsoever. Training in this manner, Ānanda..."

The bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill all the perfections should train in the perfection of wisdom. This training is declared to be the foremost;
it is declared to be the eldest, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, the most refined; it is declared to be unsurpassed and beyond compare.
For the benefit of the entire world and for the happiness of the entire world; it acts as a protector for the protectorless, authorized by the Buddhas and praised by the Buddhas.

Abiding therein, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas might lift up this great trichiliocosm world-system with their right hand and set it down again, yet it would not occur to those beings [to think]: "We have been moved."
Or this trichiliocosm great world-system has been lifted up, or it has been set down. Why is that?

Ānanda, this is that perfection of wisdom, having trained in which the unattached knowledge and vision of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, has arisen regarding the phenomena of the past, future, and present. Ānanda, of all trainings whatsoever—this is the training of them all.

This training in the perfection of wisdom is declared to be the foremost; it is declared to be the eldest, the most excellent, the best, the most sublime, the most refined; it is declared to be unsurpassed and beyond compare. Ānanda, one might as well think that the measure or the limit of space should be grasped, as one who would think to grasp the measure or the limit of the perfection of wisdom.
One might think it should be grasped. Why is that?

Because, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is immeasurable. I have not, Ānanda, declared a measure for the perfection of wisdom; for, Ānanda, while the sets of names, phrases, and syllables are bound by measure, the perfection of wisdom is not bound by measure. Ānanda said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom not bound by measure?
The Blessed One said: "Because of its inexhaustibility, Ānanda."

The perfection of wisdom is not bound by measure, Ānanda; because it is secluded, the perfection of wisdom is not bound by measure. Moreover, Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who appeared in the past were also manifested from this very perfection of wisdom.

And the perfection of wisdom has not come to an end. Ānanda, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future time, they too shall manifest from this very perfection of wisdom; yet the perfection of wisdom will not be exhausted. And those Tathāgatas, Arhats [who exist] now in the worlds of the ten directions, Ānanda...
The perfectly enlightened Buddhas remain, endure, and maintain themselves, and they teach the Dharma;
yet those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are manifested from this very perfection of wisdom, and the perfection of wisdom is not exhausted. For what reason?
Ānanda, one who would think that the perfection of wisdom can be exhausted would think that space can be exhausted.

Furthermore, the perfection of wisdom has not been exhausted, is not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted.
