Likewise, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity have not been exhausted, are not being exhausted, and will not be exhausted. For there is no arising of these dharmas.
"For those for whom there is no arising, how could their cessation be perceived?
Then the Blessed One, having extended his tongue-faculty so that it covered the entire circle of his face up to its limits, addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Therefore, Ānanda, you should explain, teach, proclaim, establish, set forth, and reveal this Perfection of Wisdom in detail to the four assemblies."

You should make it clear and reveal it in detail. For here, Ānanda, in this profound perfection of wisdom, all dharmas are taught in detail; herein those persons belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas must train. Training as they have been instructed, they will each abide in their respective stages. Furthermore, Ānanda, this profound perfection of wisdom is [the source] of all syllables.

Ānanda, this profound perfection of wisdom is the gateway to all dhāraṇīs; it is in this gateway of dhāraṇīs that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train. For those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who maintain these dhāraṇīs, all eloquence and analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) become manifest. Ānanda, this perfection of wisdom belongs to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present.
I have declared that the treasury of the true Dharma is inexhaustible. Therefore, Ānanda, I announce to you, I make it known to you:
whoever shall take up, preserve, recite, and master this profound perfection of wisdom, they shall uphold the awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present.
This, Ānanda, is that perfection of wisdom which has been described by me as a dhāraṇī. By upholding these dhāraṇīs of the perfection of wisdom,
you will uphold all dharmas.
Chapter 61. Then this thought occurred to the venerable Subhūti:

"Profound indeed is this awakening of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Awakened Ones. What if I were to question the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One? Then the venerable Subhūti—
He said this to the Blessed One:
"Indeed, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible. The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, because space is inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible. He said:
"How, O Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom to be brought forth?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is to be brought forth because form is inexhaustible; it is to be brought forth because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible."

Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth. Subhūti, because the perfection of giving is inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth. Up to and including, Subhūti, because the knowledge of all aspects is inexhaustible, the perfection of wisdom should be brought forth.
Furthermore, Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of form and space, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.

It should be brought forth. Subhūti, by means of the inexhaustibility of space, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom through the inexhaustibility of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The perfection of wisdom should be brought forth through the inexhaustibility of space as the perfection of giving.
The perfection of wisdom should be brought forth through the inexhaustibility of space as the perfection of ethical discipline. The perfection of patience...
The perfection of wisdom is to be brought forth through the inexhaustibility of space. The perfection of vigor is to be brought forth through the inexhaustibility of space;

the perfection of meditation is to be brought forth through the inexhaustibility of space; and so on, up to the perfection of wisdom being brought forth through the inexhaustibility of space in all-aspect-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, Subhūti:

The bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by way of the inexhaustibility of the space of ignorance. Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by way of the inexhaustibility of the space of formative forces. Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom by way of the inexhaustibility of the space of consciousness.

It should be brought forth. Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of space in name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of space in the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of space in contact (*sparśa*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should bring forth the perfection of wisdom].
It should be brought forth. Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of the space-like nature of feeling (*vedanā*), a bodhisattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of the space-like nature of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, by way of the inexhaustibility of the space-like nature of grasping (*upādāna*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom through the inexhaustibility of the space of existence.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom through the inexhaustibility of the space of birth.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva [should bring forth the perfection of wisdom] through the inexhaustibility of the space of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva must bring the perfection of wisdom to accomplishment. In this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva must bring the perfection of wisdom to accomplishment.
This, Subhūti, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s contemplation of dependent origination and his avoidance of extremes. This is the unique quality of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

The Dharma belongs to one seated at the seat of awakening who thus contemplates dependent origination. Contemplating dependent origination in this way, he attains the knowledge of omniscience. Subhūti, whoever practices the perfection of wisdom by means of this accomplishment of the inexhaustible space-like [nature] and contemplates dependent origination, he does not [abide] on the level of a śrāvaka, nor...

He will abide on the level of a pratyekabuddha, or he will abide in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, whatever persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle turn back, they all turn back because they have not relied upon these mental engagements with the perfection of wisdom; and they do not know how [to proceed].

A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should contemplate dependent origination through the realization of the inexhaustibility of space. Subhūti, whatever persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle turn back, they all turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment because they have not relied upon this skill in means. Whatever persons...

Subhūti, all those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who do not turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment do so by relying on this perfection of wisdom; they do not turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. And thus, by means of skill in means, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this perfection of wisdom [should practice] the perfection of wisdom through the realization of the inexhaustibility of space.

They are to be observed and brought forth. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while observing dependent origination, does not see any phenomenon arising without a cause, nor does he perceive any phenomenon as permanent, nor as ceasing. He does not perceive any phenomenon as a self, nor as a sentient being.

One does not perceive it as a living being, nor as a creature, nor as a human, nor as a man, nor as a nourisher, nor as a person, nor as an agent, nor as one who causes to act, nor as one who instigates, nor as one who causes to instigate, nor as an experiencer, nor as one who causes to experience, nor as a knower, nor as a seer; one does not perceive it as permanent, nor as impermanent, nor as pleasure, nor as suffering, nor as self, nor as non-self.

Neither as peaceful nor as unpeaceful. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should contemplate dependent origination. Subhūti, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, [he contemplates it in this manner].

At that time, he does not perceive form as either permanent or impermanent, as pleasant or painful, as self or non-self, or as peaceful or unpeaceful; and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which he does not perceive as either permanent or impermanent,
or as pleasant or painful.
Whether it be a self or a non-self,

whether it be peaceful or not peaceful. Subhūti, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, at that time, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom.
He does not perceive even that phenomenon by which he might perceive the perfection of wisdom. In this way, he does not perceive the perfection of meditation;

he does not perceive the perfection of vigor; he does not perceive the perfection of patience; he does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline; he does not perceive the perfection of generosity; and so on, up to and including awakening, which he does not perceive.

He does not perceive even that dharma by which he might perceive awakening, nor does he perceive that dharma by which he might effect the abandonment of all latencies and their continuations. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom, through the yoga of the non-apprehension of all dharmas. In that...

Subhūti, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, not apprehending any phenomena, courses in the perfection of wisdom, at that time Māra the Evil One becomes pierced by the arrow of grief. Subhūti, it is just as if a man, upon the death of his mother and father, were pierced by the arrow of grief; he would be possessed by the most supreme arrow of grief.

"In the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend any dharma, Māra the Evil One becomes pierced by the thorn of grief; he is possessed by the most extreme thorn of grief. Subhūti asked:

"Lord, is it only this single Māra the Evil One who becomes possessed by the most extreme thorn of grief, or rather all the Māras the Evil Ones in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system?"
Are they all pierced by the supreme thorn of sorrow?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, even those who are the Māras, the evil ones, in this trichiliocosm, they are all [pierced] by the supreme...

They are possessed by the arrow of grief and find no delight in their respective seats. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is not separated from the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the world with its gods, humans, and asuras finds no entry point and finds no foothold against a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in this manner. Wherein...

Having grasped it, one would turn back. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should dwell in the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom.
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of giving reaches fulfillment through cultivation. In this same way...

The perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom reach fulfillment through cultivation. For a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom, all the perfections reach fulfillment through cultivation. Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, how does the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom reach the fulfillment of its cultivation?

Likewise, how do the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom reach the fulfillment of their cultivation?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, he gives that gift while dedicating it toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) reaches the fulfillment of its cultivation. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) reach the fulfillment of its cultivation?

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while guarding ethical discipline and dedicating it toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), guards that ethical discipline. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline reaches fulfillment. And how, Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the perfection of patience reach fulfillment?
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while accomplishing patience, dedicates that patience toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and cultivates it.

In this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s cultivation of the perfection of patience reaches fulfillment. And how, Subhūti, does the bodhisattva mahāsattva [cultivate] the perfection of vigor?
How does it reach fulfillment through cultivation?

Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, exerting vigor, exerts that vigor while dedicating it toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). It is in this way, Subhūti, that the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva [is fulfilled].
It reaches the fulfillment of cultivation. And how, Subhūti, does the perfection of meditation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva reach the fulfillment of cultivation?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while entering into the meditative concentrations, dedicates them toward omniscience.

He enters into those meditative absorptions. In this way, Subhūti, the perfection of meditation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva reaches fulfillment through cultivation. And how, Subhūti, does the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva reach fulfillment through cultivation?

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while cultivating wisdom, cultivates that wisdom by dedicating it toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). It is in this way, Subhūti, that the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva reaches fulfillment. Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, embrace the perfection of ethical discipline?
The Blessed One replied:

"In this case, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, dedicating it toward omniscience, he maintains a friendly bodily action, a friendly vocal action, and a friendly mental action toward all sentient beings."
Mental action becomes present. At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva fully embraces the perfection of ethical discipline. He asked:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while established in the perfection of generosity, fully embrace the perfection of patience?"
The Blessed One said: "In this case, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, if those who receive it revile him,
or abuse him, or treat him with unbearable or harsh words, he does not [give rise to anger] toward them."
He causes the mind to become resentful. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, embraces the perfection of patience. [Subhūti] asked:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, embrace the perfection of vigor?"
The Blessed One said: "In this case, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is giving a gift, if those who receive it revile him,
or abuse him, or address him with unbearable or harsh words— while he is being thus reviled..."

Whether being reviled, or being addressed with unbearable or harsh words, his mind is directed only toward giving; his mind is directed only toward renunciation. He thinks: "I must indeed give this gift; it is not the case that I should not give this gift."
He generates both physical and mental vigor. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, fully embraces the perfection of vigor.
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, fully embrace the perfection of meditative concentration?
The Blessed One said:

In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, he does not dedicate it to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha; rather, his mind functions only toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while established in the perfection of generosity, fully embraces the perfection of meditative concentration. Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while giving gifts with skillful means, embrace the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
“In this case, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift and relinquishes a gift, he possesses the perception of an illusion.”

She is always present for giving, yet through that giving she perceives neither benefit nor harm to any sentient being. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of generosity, embraces the perfection of wisdom through skillful means. ((6))
(AdSPG I 93) Chapter 62.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"How does the Blessed One, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline, embrace the perfection of generosity?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline [practices] whatever is bodily or vocal..."

Or, there is a mental wandering; by means of that wandering, he does not grasp at the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. Established therein in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), he does not deprive living beings of life, he does not take what is not given, he does not engage in sexual misconduct, he does not speak falsehoods, and he does not speak malicious speech. Nor...

He speaks harsh words; he does not engage in frivolous chatter, he is not covetous, he does not have a mind of ill-will, and he does not hold wrong views. Established therein in the perfection of ethical discipline, whatever gift he gives—food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink—[he gives it].

He gave vehicles to those who desired vehicles, clothing to those who desired clothing, flowers to those who desired flowers, garlands to those who desired garlands, perfumes to those who desired perfumes, ointments to those who desired ointments, bedding and seating to those who desired bedding and seating, shelter to those who desired shelter, the means of livelihood to those who desired the means of livelihood, and utensils to those who desired utensils.

He gives various human requisites, and having shared that gift in common with all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. And he dedicates it in such a way that the dedication does not lead to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. It is indeed in this manner that [he dedicates].
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, embraces the perfection of generosity.
[Subhūti] asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, embrace the perfection of patience?"
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, if all sentient beings were to come and repeatedly cut off the limbs and members of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is established in the perfection of ethical discipline, not even a single thought of malice would arise in that bodhisattva mahāsattva."
He is neither agitated nor disturbed; rather, he thinks to himself:

"I have gained a great gain, in that all beings indeed come here and, having repeatedly cut off my limbs and members, depart. And by this sacrifice of my body, I shall attain the divine, adamantine body of a Tathāgata."
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embraces the perfection of patience. He asked:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embrace the perfection of vigor?"
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not relax his vigor in body or mind: 'I must ferry all sentient beings across [saṃsāra] and establish them in the deathless realm. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva..."
The Mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, embraces the perfection of vigor. He asked:
"Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline, embrace the perfection of meditative concentration?
The Blessed One replied:

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and the fourth, up to and including the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*), he does not take recourse in the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. Rather, it occurs to him only this: "In this very samādhi-pāramitā by me..."

"Having established [myself], all sentient beings must be liberated from saṃsāra. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while established in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), fully embraces the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
He asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while established in the perfection of ethical discipline, fully embrace the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of ethical discipline does not perceive any phenomenon as conditioned, nor does he perceive any as unconditioned. He does not perceive a conditioned existence, nor does he perceive an unconditioned non-existence. He does not perceive a sign as conditioned, nor does he perceive the signless as unconditioned. Nor does he [perceive] anything of anyone...
He perceives neither the existence nor the non-existence of phenomena (*dharma*). Apart from this, he does not deviate from the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.

And by means of that perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), he does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), embraces the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, take hold of the perfection of generosity?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, beginning from the first production of the thought of awakening, gives gifts..."

Even if all sentient beings were to revile and abuse him, or cut off his limbs and members, while that bodhisattva mahāsattva remains established in the perfection of patience seated at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he thinks:
"I must indeed give to these sentient beings; I must not withhold my gift. Toward those sentient beings...

He gives food to those who seek food; he gives drink to those who seek drink; and so on, up to giving various human requisites. Having shared these roots of virtue in common with all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). As he thus dedicates them, there are three cognitions (*buddhi*).

It does not proceed. Who transforms? Or what is transformed? Or where is it transformed? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, fully embraces the perfection of generosity. [Subhūti] asked:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, fully embrace the perfection of ethical discipline?"

The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening until he sits upon the seat of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not deprive any sentient being of life; he does not take what is not given; and he does not engage in sexual misconduct."
He does not speak falsely; he does not speak maliciously; he does not speak harshly; he does not engage in frivolous chatter.
He is not covetous; he is not malevolent in mind; he does not hold wrong views.
Furthermore, his mind does not incline toward the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha. And those roots of merit...

Having made them common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. And he dedicates them in such a way that the threefold conceptualization does not arise: who is dedicating, what is being dedicated, or where is it being dedicated? It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [dedicates].
Abiding in the perfection of patience, he embraces the perfection of ethical discipline. He asked:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of patience, embrace the perfection of vigor?
The Blessed One replied:
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of patience generates such vigor:

"Having gone a hundred yojanas, or having gone up to a thousand yojanas, or having gone up to a hundred thousand yojanas, or having gone to another world-system, or even having gone to hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems, there— at the very least— "

"I shall establish even a single being in taking refuge, or in the precepts, or in patience, or in the fruit of stream-entry, up to arhatship, or in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or even in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment"— with this thought, one should arouse vigor; and those roots of merit [should be shared] with all sentient beings.

Having made them common to all together, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, embraces the perfection of vigor.
[Subhūti] asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, embrace the perfection of meditative concentration?"
The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, [dwells] quite secluded from sensual desires,
secluded from evil and unwholesome states, with applied thought and sustained thought, having the rapture and happiness born of seclusion— the first [dhyāna]."

He enters and dwells in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). He enters and dwells in them up to the fourth meditative concentration, and even enters and dwells in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). He dedicates the arisen and the unarisen mental states and mental factors associated with the wholesome toward the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). And he dedicates them in such a way that they become like the meditative concentrations themselves.

And at that time, he does not perceive the factors of meditative concentration. Indeed, Subhūti, it is not in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, takes hold of the perfection of meditative concentration.
[Subhūti] asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, take hold of the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of patience, dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena—
either in their aspect of solitude, or in their aspect of peace, or in their aspect of inexhaustibility."

And he does not directly realize that true nature (*dharmatā*) until he is seated at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Having sat there, he attains the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). And having risen, he turns the wheel of Dharma. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva...

The *mahāsattva*, established in the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), grasps the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). And he grasps it in such a way that he neither relinquishes it nor grasps it. He said:
"Lord, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), grasp the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*)?
The Blessed One replied:
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of vigor does not lay down the burden, either in body or in mind, thinking:

"I must certainly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; it is not the case that I shall not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. For the sake of sentient beings, he [travels] a yojana, or even up to a hundred yojanas, or a thousand yojanas.

Or a hundred thousand yojanas; or having gone to a world-system, or up to ten million world-systems, or a hundred million world-systems, or a hundred thousand million world-systems, while established in the perfection of vigor, he establishes even a single sentient being in enlightenment. If he does not find there a person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, [he establishes] one belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle.

He establishes a person in the state of a śrāvaka; he establishes a person belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha in the state of a pratyekabuddha; at the very least, he establishes even a single sentient being in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Having given that gift of Dharma, he satisfies sentient beings with material gifts. And that root of virtue...

He does not dedicate it toward the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha; rather, having made it common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, fully embraces the perfection of generosity. He said:
“Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, embrace the perfection of ethical discipline?
The Blessed One replied:
“In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening until sitting at the seat of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva...”

He himself abstains from taking life, and he encourages others to refrain from taking life. He speaks in praise of refraining from taking life, and he is one who commends and approves of those others who likewise abstain from taking life. This continues up to his own abstention from wrong view.

He refrains from it himself and encourages others to refrain from wrong view. He speaks in praise of refraining from wrong view, and he also commends those others who have refrained from wrong view, approving of them.
By means of that perfection of ethical discipline, he does not remain in the realm of desire, nor in the realm of form, nor...
He establishes himself in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). He does not establish himself on the level of a *śrāvaka* nor on the level of a *pratyekabuddha*.

Rather, having made those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*). And he dedicates them in such a way that the threefold conceptualization regarding them does not arise for him: [namely,] who...?

What does he dedicate? Or what is it that he dedicates? Or where does he dedicate? In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, fully embraces the perfection of ethical discipline. [Subhūti] asked:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, fully embrace the perfection of patience?"
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening until the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is seated at the seat of awakening,
if a human or a non-human being were to cause a distraction of his mind, or were to cut off his limbs and members,"
Having cut it off and taken it away, one might depart; yet for the bodhisattva mahāsattva established in this perfection of vigor, it does not occur to him:
"Someone is cutting me, or piercing me, or taking [my limb] away. Rather, it occurs to him:
"Well-gained are my gains, for whose sake I maintain this body. It is they who have come to me, [taking] my limbs and members."
Having cut them off again and again, they take them away and depart. Or else, by that means, the intrinsic nature of phenomena has been well-attended to by him.

And he does not dedicate those roots of merit to the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha; rather, having made them common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, fully embraces the perfection of patience. [Subhūti] asked:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, fully embrace the perfection of meditative concentration?"

The Blessed One said: "In this case, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, quite secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion."

He dwells; indeed, he dwells having attained the fourth dhyāna. With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, he dwells having pervaded the entire world; likewise, with a mind accompanied by compassion, with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy, and with a mind accompanied by equanimity, he dwells having pervaded the entire world.

Up to the point where he attains and dwells in the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he does not grasp the karmic maturation of those dhyānas, the immeasurables, or the formless absorptions. Rather, he takes birth wherever the welfare of all sentient beings must be accomplished. There, he brings those sentient beings to maturity in the six perfections, beginning with the perfection of generosity.
In the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom,

he travels from buddhafield to buddhafield, attending upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in order to plant roots of merit. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva stands firm in the perfection of vigor.
He embraces the perfection of meditative concentration. He asks:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor, embrace the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of vigor does not perceive the perfection of generosity as a substance, nor as an entity, nor as a sign. He does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline as a substance,
nor as an entity, nor as a sign.
One does not perceive the perfection of patience as a substantial entity, nor as a real thing, nor as a sign;
one does not perceive the perfection of vigor as a substantial entity,
nor as a real thing, nor as a sign.

He does not perceive the perfection of meditation as a substantial entity, nor as a real existence, nor as a sign. In this same way, up to the applications of mindfulness and up to the knowledge of all aspects, he does not perceive them as substantial entities, nor as real existences, nor as signs.
Perceiving all phenomena as lacking substantiality, perceiving them as lacking real existence, and perceiving them as signless, he...

No one makes a home in any phenomenon (*dharma*). He acts exactly as he speaks. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), fully embraces the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). [Subhūti] asked:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), fully embrace the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*)?"

The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, secluded indeed from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion."

Up until he attains and dwells in the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Established therein in the perfection of meditation with an undistracted mind, he bestows upon those beings both material gifts and the gift of the Dharma. He himself also gives material gifts...
He himself gives the gift of Dharma and also encourages others with both the gift of material things and the gift of Dharma.

He speaks in praise of the gift of material things and the gift of Dharma, and he commends and approves of those other beings who give both the gift of material things and the gift of Dharma. Furthermore, he does not dedicate those roots of merit toward the level of a Śrāvaka.

Or he dedicates it to the level of a pratyekabuddha; otherwise, having made it common to all sentient beings, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, fully embraces the perfection of generosity. He said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, embrace the perfection of ethical discipline?
The Blessed One replied:

"In this regard, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of meditative concentration, no thought accompanied by passion arises, nor one accompanied by hatred, nor one accompanied by delusion."
A mind accompanied by harmfulness does not arise.

Is it not so? Rather, he dwells with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and he does not dedicate those roots of merit to the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha, but [dedicates them] otherwise.
Having made it common to all sentient beings together with them, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, fully embraces the perfection of ethical discipline. [Subhūti] asked:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, fully embrace the perfection of patience?"
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, contemplates form as being like a mass of foam; feeling as being like a bubble; perception as being like a mirage; mental formations as being like a plantain tree; and consciousness as being like an illusion."

He examines consciousness. As he thus examines it, the perception of worthlessness arises toward the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*). As he thus examines them, it occurs to him: "While the limbs and members are being severed, who is it here that severs? Or what is it here that is severed? To whom does this body belong? To whom do these feelings belong? To whom does this perception belong?"
"To whom do the formative forces belong, or to whom does consciousness belong?
As he contemplates in this way, it occurs to him: "Who here is being reviled or abused, such that when one is reviled or abused, malice arises?
In this manner, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditative concentration, fully embraces the perfection of patience. He said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditation, take up the perfection of vigor?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of meditation, remains utterly secluded from sensual desires."

Secluded from evil and unwholesome states, he dwells having attained the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion. He dwells having attained the [dhyānas] up to the fourth dhyāna. Having grasped the signs of the dhyānas and their constituent factors, he experiences various kinds of miraculous powers (*ṛddhividhi*). This should be elaborated in detail as far as [the standard descriptions].
With the divine ear-element, he hears both kinds of sounds, those of gods and those of humans;

with his own mind, he knows as it really is the minds of other beings and other persons. He knows as it really is an unsurpassed mind as "an unsurpassed mind," and so forth. He recollects his manifold past abodes.

This should be explained in detail. Up to: with his divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, he perceives beings according to their karma. Having established himself in these five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), he travels from buddha-field to buddha-field, attending upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and planting roots of merit.

Maturing sentient beings and purifying the buddha-field, he does not dedicate those roots of merit to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha; rather, having made them common to all sentient beings, he dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
Abiding in the perfection of meditation, he takes hold of the perfection of vigor. He asked:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditation, take hold of the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of meditative concentration does not apprehend form; he does not apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

He does not apprehend the perfection of generosity, nor the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom. He does not apprehend the applications of mindfulness, nor the right efforts.

One does not apprehend them. One does not apprehend the bases of psychic power; one does not apprehend the faculties; one does not apprehend the powers. One does not apprehend the factors of enlightenment. One does not apprehend the noble eightfold path.
As long as one does not apprehend omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), one does not apprehend the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) and does not apprehend the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*).
Not apprehending them, one does not form [mental constructs] (*na abhisaṃskaroti*). Not forming them, one neither produces nor ceases them. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this very nature of things remains established.
The stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā) is simply the established realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); it neither arises nor ceases.
Such a person remains with an undistracted mind, never separated from mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), fully grasps the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). He said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of wisdom, take up the perfection of generosity?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom [perceives] that all phenomena are empty."
He observes thus. He asks:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, observe all phenomena as empty?
The Blessed One replied:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, while practicing internal emptiness, does not apprehend internal emptiness as "internal emptiness. He does not apprehend external emptiness as "external emptiness. He does not apprehend internal-and-external emptiness as "internal-and-external emptiness. [He does not apprehend] the emptiness of emptiness...

One does not apprehend "emptiness of emptiness" as "emptiness of emptiness. One does not apprehend "great emptiness" as "great emptiness. One does not apprehend "emptiness of the ultimate" as "emptiness of the ultimate. One does not apprehend "emptiness of the conditioned" as "emptiness of the conditioned.
One does not apprehend "emptiness of the unconditioned" as "emptiness of the unconditioned. [One does not apprehend] "emptiness of the absolute" as "emptiness of the absolute."

One does not apprehend it. One does not apprehend the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end as "the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end. One does not apprehend the emptiness of dispersion as "the emptiness of dispersion. One does not apprehend the emptiness of intrinsic nature as "the emptiness of intrinsic nature," nor does one apprehend the emptiness of all phenomena as "the emptiness of all phenomena."
He does not apprehend the emptiness of specific characteristics as being "the emptiness of specific characteristics.

Abiding in these fourteen kinds of emptiness, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend form as either empty or non-empty. He does not apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Whether as "empty" or as "not empty," one does not apprehend the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) as either empty or not empty. Up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma), one does not apprehend them as either empty or not empty. Even up to awakening (bodhi) itself, one does not apprehend it as either empty or not empty. One does not apprehend the conditioned realm (saṃskṛtadhātu) as empty...
Whether as "empty" or as "not empty," he does not apprehend the unconditioned realm (asaṃskṛtadhātu) as either empty or not empty.

While practicing here in this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), whatever gift that bodhisattva mahāsattva gives— whether food or drink, up to any other various human requisites— he does not [perceive] that gift as empty.
He does not perceive [them]; nor does he perceive that which gives, or that to whom one gives, as being empty.
For him, there is no opportunity for a mind of stinginess or a mind of grasping. Why is that?
Because none of these conceptual constructions arise for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom.

From the first production of the thought of awakening until sitting at the seat of enlightenment— just as no thought of stinginess or grasping arises in a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening— so too [is it for him].

In the same way, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, neither a mind of stinginess nor a mind of grasping arises. This very perfection of wisdom is the teacher of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
It is thus, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of wisdom, fully embraces the perfection of giving. Subhūti said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of wisdom, take up the perfection of ethical discipline?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of wisdom..."

He allows no opportunity for the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is that? Because he does not perceive the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive that mind which he might dedicate toward the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha, starting from his first production of the thought of awakening.
He teaches the Dharma for the abandonment of taking life until he reaches the seat of awakening. He himself abstains from taking life, encourages others to undertake the abstinence from taking life,
speaks in praise of the abstinence from taking life, and commends those others who likewise abstain from taking life.

He is one who gives his approval. He himself abstains from wrong view, and he encourages others to abstain from wrong view; he speaks in praise of abstaining from wrong view and approves of those others who have abstained from wrong view. Furthermore, by means of that ethical discipline, he does not grasp at any phenomenon.
Not to mention anything else—whether the state of a śrāvaka, the state of a pratyekabuddha, or the state of a buddha.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fully embraces the perfection of ethical discipline. [Subhūti] asked:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, fully embrace the perfection of patience?"
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of wisdom, a conformable patience arises. It occurs to him: 'In this, no dharma whatsoever arises or ceases; nothing is born.'"
or decays, or dies;
or is reviled, or is censured;
or is cut, or is split; or is slain—beginning from that first production of the thought...

Until reaching the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), if in the meantime all sentient beings were to come and revile him, abuse him, or strike him with clods of earth, sticks, fists, or weapons, or even cut or pierce him, he would think: "Aha! Such is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena."

And yet, in this world, no phenomenon whatsoever is reviled or censured, nor is it cut, split, killed, or bound. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of wisdom, fully embraces the perfection of patience. He said:
“Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of wisdom, take hold of the perfection of vigor?
The Blessed One said:
“In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of wisdom, [is established] in the four bases of psychic power.”

Abiding thus, endowed with skill in means, he generates physical and mental vigor; having gone even to a single world-system, or to a hundred world-systems, or to a thousand world-systems, or even to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems,
he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings and establishes them in the perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline.

or in the perfection of patience, or in the perfection of vigor, or in the perfection of meditation, or in the perfection of wisdom. He establishes them in the factors conducive to enlightenment; he establishes them in the fruit of stream-entry, in the fruit of once-returning, in the fruit of non-returning, in arhatship, in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and up to unsurpassed [enlightenment].

He establishes them in perfect enlightenment. And he establishes them in such a way that he does not establish them in the conditioned realm, nor does he establish them in the unconditioned realm. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, takes up the perfection of vigor. He said:
"How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of wisdom, take up the perfection of meditation?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the perfection of wisdom—setting aside the Tathāgata-samādhi—"

Whatever meditative concentrations there may be—whether the concentrations of śrāvakas, the concentrations of pratyekabuddhas, or the concentrations of bodhisattvas—he enters into them all. Abiding in those concentrations, he enters into and emerges from the eight liberations in both forward and reverse order. What are the eight?
In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, possessing form, sees forms;
this is the first liberation. Perceiving internal form, he sees external forms;
this is the second liberation. And he becomes intent upon the beautiful.

This is the third liberation. Through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] "space is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space;
this is the fourth liberation. Through the complete surmounting of the sphere of infinite space, [thinking] "consciousness is infinite," he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
This is the fifth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness;
this is the sixth liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, he attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is the seventh liberation. By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he attains and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.

This is the eighth liberation. He enters into and emerges from these eight liberations in both direct and reverse order. And he enters into and emerges from the nine successive attainments in both direct and reverse order. What are the nine?
Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states...

Accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), and born of seclusion (*vivekaja*), he dwells having attained the first *dhyāna*, which is characterized by joy and bliss (*prītisukha*).

He dwells having attained each stage up to the fourth *dhyāna*. Finally, through the complete transcendence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), he dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*). Herein, he enters these nine successive attainments (*anupūrvasamāpatti*) in both forward and reverse order.

He enters into them and emerges from them. Having analyzed these eight liberations and these nine successive attainments, he enters this lion’s yawn samādhi. And what, Subhūti, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s [lion’s yawn samādhi]?
What is the lion’s yawn samādhi?

Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

He dwells thus. Having emerged from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of cessation. Having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having emerged from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the first dhyāna. Having brought this Lion’s Yawn Samādhi to fruition, he [enters] the Viṣkandaka Samādhi.
He enters [into it]. And what, Subhūti, is the leap-over concentration (*viṣkandaka-samādhi*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

Emerging from the first dhyāna, he dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of cessation. Emerging from the attainment of cessation, he dwells having attained the second dhyāna. Emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the attainment of cessation.
He enters [the attainment]. Having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he dwells having attained and entered the third dhyāna.

Having emerged from the third dhyāna, he enters the attainment of cessation. Having emerged from the attainment of cessation, he dwells having attained and entered the fourth dhyāna. Having emerged from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the attainment of cessation.

Emerging from the attainment of cessation, he enters the sphere of infinite space. Emerging from the sphere of infinite space, he enters the attainment of cessation. Emerging from the attainment of cessation, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness. Emerging from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the attainment of cessation. Emerging from the attainment of cessation... (AdSPG I 110)
He enters the sphere of nothingness. Emerging from the sphere of nothingness, he enters the attainment of cessation.

Emerging from the attainment of cessation, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of cessation. Emerging from the attainment of cessation, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

He enters [the attainment]. Emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he abides in a non-concentrated mind. From the non-concentrated mind, he enters the attainment of cessation. Emerging from the attainment of cessation, he abides in a non-concentrated mind. From the non-concentrated mind, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Emerging from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he abides in an unconcentrated mind. From the unconcentrated mind, he enters the sphere of nothingness. Emerging from the sphere of nothingness, he abides in an unconcentrated mind.
From the unconcentrated mind, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness. Emerging from the sphere of infinite consciousness...

He abides in an unconcentrated mind. From the unconcentrated mind, he enters the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Emerging from the sphere of infinite space, he abides in an unconcentrated mind. From the unconcentrated mind, he enters the fourth dhyāna.
Emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he abides in an unconcentrated mind. From the unconcentrated mind...

He enters the third dhyāna. Emerging from the third dhyāna, he abides in a non-concentrated state of mind. From that non-concentrated state of mind, he enters the second dhyāna. Emerging from the second dhyāna, he abides in a non-concentrated state of mind. From that non-concentrated state of mind, he enters the first dhyāna. Emerging from the first dhyāna...
He abides in a non-concentrated mind. Having stood in this leap-over concentration (*avaskandaka-samādhi*), he attains the sameness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*).
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, established in the perfection of wisdom, takes hold of the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). ((6))
(AdSPG I 111) Chapter 63.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, for how long has this bodhisattva mahāsattva been set forth, who is endowed with such skill in means?

The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with such skill in means has been set forth for incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons. Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, how many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, has this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attended upon, who is endowed with such skill in means?
The Blessed One said:
“That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is endowed with such skill in means should be known as one who has attended upon Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges. He asked:
"Blessed One, what root of merit has been planted by that bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with such skill in means?
The Blessed One replied,
"Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, there is no perfection of giving whatsoever that has not been practiced by that bodhisattva."
There is no perfection of ethical discipline,

perfection of patience, perfection of vigor, perfection of meditative concentration, or perfection of wisdom that has not been fulfilled by that bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with this skill in means. Subhūti said:
"It is wonderful, Blessed One, that these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are endowed with such skill in means. The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. It is wonderful that these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are endowed with such skill in means. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, the disk of the sun and the moon [were to illuminate] the four..."
It illuminates the continents and traverses and revolves around the four continents;
even so, Subhūti, does the perfection of wisdom perform its function among the five perfections.

It follows and conforms to the five perfections. Because they are not separated from the perfection of wisdom, the five perfections receive the designation "perfection"; because they are separated from the perfection of wisdom, they do not receive the designation "perfection. Subhūti, it is just as, for example, a wheel-turning monarch who is separated from the seven treasures does not receive the designation "wheel-turning monarch."

In the same way, Subhūti, because they are devoid of the perfection of wisdom, the other five perfections do not receive the designation "perfection. Just as, Subhūti, a woman without a husband is easily overcome, even so, Subhūti, because they are devoid of the perfection of wisdom, the five perfections are easily overcome by Māra or by the deities belonging to Māra’s host. Just as, Subhūti, a man engaged in battle...
Just as one who is equipped with all his armor is invincible when engaged in battle by rival kings, adversaries, or enemies,
even so, Subhūti, the five perfections, because they are not separated from the perfection of wisdom, become invincible to Māra or to the deities belonging to Māra’s host.
or by conceited persons,
or even by those who are like outcaste bodhisattvas. Subhūti, it is just as if minor kings were subject to a universal monarch (cakravartin),
going to attend upon him every morning and evening.

In the same way, Subhūti, the five perfections, when embraced by the perfection of wisdom, proceed toward that which is all-aspect-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Just as, Subhūti, whatever small rivers there may be, they all flow toward the river Gaṅgā.
Just as those [rivers] flow together with the river Gaṅgā toward the great ocean,

even so, Subhūti, the five perfections, when embraced by the perfection of wisdom, proceed toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). It is just as, for example, Subhūti, a man’s right hand performs all his tasks.
In the same way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is to be regarded. Just as the left hand, so too are the five perfections to be regarded.
It is just as if, Subhūti, whatever water there is in the small streams and whatever water there is in the great rivers, once it has entered the great ocean, it all becomes of one taste.

In the same way, Subhūti, when the five perfections are embraced by the perfection of wisdom and have entered into the knowledge of all aspects, they receive the designation "perfections. It is just as if, Subhūti, the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch’s fourfold army goes before it.
And it remains. Wherever the wheel-turning monarch stays for the sake of food, there he satisfies the military forces of the wheel-turning monarch;
yet that precious wheel does not move from its place.
In the same way, Subhūti, among these five perfections, the perfection of wisdom is the guide;
by means of it they follow toward the knowledge of all aspects,
and therein they shall abide.
Abiding there, they do not deviate from that place;
just as, Subhūti, the wheel-treasure, the minister-treasure, the householder-treasure, the woman-treasure, the jewel-treasure, and the elephant-treasure of a universal monarch [do not deviate].
And just as the horse-treasure goes at the head of the fourfold army,
even so, Subhūti, among these five perfections, the perfection of wisdom goes at the head;
having gone to the front, it stands where all-aspect omniscience is.
And it does not occur to the perfection of wisdom:

"May the perfection of generosity follow after me; likewise, may the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditative concentration follow after me. Nor does it occur to the perfection of generosity:

"I should follow after the perfection of wisdom. Likewise, it does not occur to the perfection of ethical discipline, nor to the perfection of patience, nor to the perfection of vigor, nor to the perfection of meditative concentration.
Thus it occurs to him:
"I should follow after the perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
Because this is their very nature: they are incapable of anything, empty of intrinsic nature, void, and like a mirage. Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
If, Blessed One, all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature,

then how, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, [attain] unsurpassed...?
"How does one fully awaken to perfect enlightenment?
The Blessed One said:
"In this case, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the six perfections as follows:"
"Alas, this world-system has a perverted mind; it is not possible to liberate it from cyclic existence without skillful means.
For the sake of those beings, I shall practice the perfection of generosity; I shall practice the perfection of ethical discipline;
I shall practice the perfection of patience; I shall practice the perfection of vigor; I shall practice the perfection of meditative concentration."
"I shall practice the perfection of wisdom. For the sake of those beings, he relinquishes internal and external things;
as he thus relinquishes them, it occurs to him: "Nothing at all has been relinquished by me."
For what reason?

Because this very thing is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while investigating, fulfills the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*). For the sake of those very beings, he allows no opportunity for immorality (*dauḥśīlya*). For what reason?

For it occurs to him thus: "It would not be fitting for me, having set out for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, to take life, or even to hold wrong views, or to long for sense objects, or for the state of a god or the state of a Brahmā."

"Or would I seek the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while investigating, practices the perfection of ethical discipline. For the sake of those very beings, even when constantly reviled and abused with harsh and rough words, he does not give rise to a disturbed mind."

Nor does he give rise to a corrupt mind when being struck by blows from clods of earth, sticks, weapons, or stones; nor when his physical limbs are being pierced, nor when his major and minor members and parts are being cut off. Why is that?
Because he thoroughly examines all those things as being like an echo. Form is like a mass of foam, and so on, up to...
He examines consciousness as being like an illusion. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while examining thus, practices the perfection of patience;

for the sake of those very beings, he does not give rise to a mind of indolence. He pursues all wholesome qualities until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. That...
For what reason?
Because it occurs to him thus:
"One who is indolent is not able to act for the benefit of sentient beings, nor is he able to awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while thus examining, practices the perfection of vigor.

For the sake of those very beings, he does not become distracted in mind until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while thus examining...
He practices the perfection of meditation. For the sake of those very same sentient beings, he never becomes devoid of wisdom. Why is that?
Because it is not possible to bring sentient beings to maturity in any other way than by entering the perfection of wisdom;
therefore, [I must avoid] even a single instance associated with faulty wisdom.
"One should not give rise to such a thought. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom for the very sake of sentient beings. Subhūti said:

"Blessed One, if there is no differentiation among the perfections, why is this perfection of wisdom declared to be the foremost of the five perfections? Why is it declared to be the eldest, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, the most refined, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the unequaled?"
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is.
There is no distinction whatsoever among the perfections, Subhūti. If, however, the perfection of wisdom did not exist, these five perfections would not receive the designation 'perfections'."

Furthermore, it is by relying on the perfection of wisdom that these five perfections receive the designation "perfection. Subhūti, it is just as various kinds of physical forms, when they approach Sumeru, the king of mountains, become of one color;

even so, Subhūti, it is by relying on the perfection of wisdom that these five perfections receive the designation "perfection," and having entered into omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), they become of one color. That is to say:

No distinction whatsoever is perceived such that "this is the perfection of generosity," "this is the perfection of ethical discipline," "this is the perfection of patience," "this is the perfection of vigor," "this is the perfection of meditative concentration," or "this is the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because these have no intrinsic nature.
For this reason, no distinction is perceived. He said:

"Blessed One, if no distinction or differentiation of any dharma is perceived in the attainment of the goal, why is this perfection of wisdom called the foremost among these five perfections? Why is it called the eldest?"

It is called the best; it is called the excellent, the preeminent, the sublime. It is called the unsurpassed, the peerless, the unequaled. The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. In the attainment of the ultimate meaning, no distinction or differentiation of any dharma is perceived;
nevertheless, by relying upon worldly convention and designation, the perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline are known."

The perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are known by way of liberating sentient beings from cyclic existence. Yet all those sentient beings are neither born nor do they die; they neither pass away nor are they reborn.
Because sentient beings do not exist, it should be understood that all phenomena do not exist. Subhūti, it is by this method that [the non-existence] of these five perfections is to be understood.
The perfection of wisdom is called the foremost; it is called the eldest, the most excellent, the best, the preeminent, the most sublime, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the unequaled.
Subhūti, it is just as, among all women, she who is the mother of a universal monarch is called the foremost of all women.
It is called "unequaled. In the same way, Subhūti, among these five perfections, the perfection of wisdom is called the foremost, up to being called "unequaled. He asked:
"What is the intention, Blessed One, in saying that the perfection of wisdom is the foremost, up to being called 'unequaled'?"
The Blessed One said:
"For this perfection of wisdom, having grasped all wholesome dharmas, will abide in that which is the knowledge of all aspects by way of non-abiding. He asked:
"But, Blessed One, does the perfection of wisdom grasp or release any dharma whatsoever?"
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. The perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor releases any dharma. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, all those dharmas are ungrasped and unreleased. Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, which phenomena does the perfection of wisdom neither grasp nor release?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor releases form. Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor releases feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
"Subhūti, as long as the perfection of wisdom neither grasps nor releases up to awakening. Subhūti asked:
"Lord, how is form not grasped?
How are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness [not grasped]?"
It is unappropriated.
How, up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), is it unappropriated?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, through non-attention to form, form becomes ungrasped;
through non-attention to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, consciousness becomes ungrasped;
and so on, up to: through non-attention to the knowledge of all aspects, awakening becomes ungrasped. In this way indeed, Subhūti, form becomes ungrasped, up to awakening becoming ungrasped.

If, Blessed One, form is not to be brought to mind, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not to be brought to mind, up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) which is not to be brought to mind—
then, Blessed One, how do the roots of virtue increase for one who does not bring form to mind, up to and including one who does not bring omniscience to mind?
If the roots of virtue do not increase, how will the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) be fulfilled?
"If the six perfections are not being fulfilled, how will omniscience (sarvākārajñatā) be attained?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, when one does not attend to form, and does not attend to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness,"
As long as he does not direct his attention toward awakening (*bodhi*), the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) of that bodhisattva mahāsattva will continue to increase;
with those increasing roots of merit, he will fulfill the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*); having fulfilled the six perfections, he will attain all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is that?

Because without directing his attention toward form (*rūpa*), without directing his attention toward feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*), and without directing his attention toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*), he will manifest full awakening. He said:

"What is the reason here, Blessed One, that one will attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) by not attending to form, by not attending to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and by not attending to awakening?
The Blessed One said:
Through non-mental engagement (*amanasikāra*), one is not adhered;

one is not adhered in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), one is not adhered in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and one is not adhered in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Through non-mental engagement, one is not adhered anywhere at all. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) [does not adhere].
"One should adhere to no phenomena whatsoever.
He asked: "Blessed One, practicing thus, in what will the bodhisattva mahāsattva abide within the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied:

"Subhūti, practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will not abide in form; he will not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He will not abide even in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti asked:
'For what reason, Blessed One, will he not abide even in that knowledge of all aspects?'"
The Blessed One said:
"By way of non-attachment, one will not abide anywhere. For what reason?
Because one does not perceive any dharma wherein one might become attached or abide. It is indeed thus."
Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom through non-attachment and by way of non-abiding.
Furthermore, if it should occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva:
"He who courses thus and cultivates thus, he courses in the perfection of wisdom," [he courses in the perfection of wisdom].

He cultivates the perfection of wisdom. If he perceives, "I course in the perfection of wisdom" or "I cultivate the perfection of wisdom," he distances himself from the perfection of wisdom. He becomes remote from the perfection of wisdom and remote from the perfection of meditative concentration.

He becomes distant from the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity; indeed, he becomes distant from everything up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Why is that?

Because the perfection of wisdom does not adhere to any phenomenon whatsoever, nor is there any adherence within the perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in which one could adhere. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva...
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives even the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva falls away from the perfection of wisdom.
He who falls away from the perfection of wisdom falls away from all dharmas. Furthermore, if it occurs to him thus:
"The perfection of wisdom [is] the five perfections..."
He grasps [them] up to the point that he grasps the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);

such a bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Indeed, it is not possible for one who is devoid of the perfection of wisdom to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*). If, however, it should occur to him thus:
