One who has fallen away from this perfection of wisdom will not be prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; for one who has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom is not prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. However, if it should occur to him thus:

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva, remaining here in the perfection of wisdom, brings forth the perfection of giving, up to and including bringing forth great compassion—that bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because for one who has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom, it is not possible to bring forth the perfection of giving, nor is it possible to bring forth [anything] up to and including great compassion. Furthermore, if it should occur to him thus:

All dharmas have been embraced by the Tathāgata; having himself fully awakened to them, he has proclaimed, taught, and revealed them. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who [denies this] has fallen away from the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Because no dharma whatsoever has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
And why is that?

For it is thus, Subhūti: the Tathāgata does not designate any dharma whatsoever. How much less, then, could he fully awaken to any dharma? Such a thing is impossible. Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how is it that these faults do not arise for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, perceives thus: 'All dharmas are non-existent, ungraspable, and impossible to fully awaken to,' [then he does not tremble].
(AdSPG I 121)

One who courses in this manner courses in the perfection of wisdom. However, if one should nevertheless adhere to a dharma that is not grasped, that bodhisattva mahāsattva is devoid of the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
For the perfection of wisdom is not to be described in terms of adherence. He said:

Furthermore, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom not separated from the perfection of wisdom? Is it up to the point that the perfection of generosity is not separated from the perfection of generosity, and so on, up to the point that the knowledge of all aspects is not separated from the knowledge of all aspects? If the perfection of wisdom is not separated from the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to the point that the perfection of generosity is not separated from the perfection of generosity, and so on, up to the point that the knowledge of all aspects is not separated from the knowledge of all aspects, then how is the perfection of wisdom [to be understood]?
It is brought forth. How, up to and including, is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) brought forth?
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not become attached [thinking], 'This is form,' or 'Form belongs to him. Likewise [he does not become attached] to feeling, perception, and mental formations."

One does not become attached to consciousness, thinking "this is consciousness" or "this is his consciousness," up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), where one does not become attached to it, thinking "this is omniscience" or "this is his omniscience."

One does not adhere to form as either permanent or impermanent. One does not adhere to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent. This extends up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which one does not adhere to as either permanent or impermanent.
One does not adhere to form as either pleasant or painful. [One does not adhere to] feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as pleasant...
Nor does one adhere to it as suffering. Up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), one does not adhere to it as either happiness or suffering.
One does not adhere to form (*rūpa*) as self or as non-self;
one does not adhere to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) as self or as non-self. This continues up to and including omniscience.
One does not adhere to it as self or as non-self. One does not adhere to form as peaceful or as unpeaceful.

One does not adhere to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as peaceful or as unpeaceful. Up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), one does not adhere to it as peaceful or as unpeaceful. One does not adhere to form as empty or as non-empty.

One does not adhere to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either empty or non-empty. Up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), one does not adhere to it as either empty or non-empty. One does not adhere to form as either with signs (*nimitta*) or signless;
one does not adhere to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either with signs or signless. Up to and including...

One does not adhere to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) as having signs (*nimitta*) or as being signless (*animitta*). One does not adhere to form (*rūpa*) as being with aspiration (*praṇihita*) or as being without aspiration (*apraṇihita*).

One does not adhere to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*) as being with aspiration or as being without aspiration. This continues up to: one does not adhere to omniscience as being with aspiration or as being without aspiration.
One does not adhere to form as either secluded or non-secluded;

one does not adhere to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either secluded or non-secluded. This extends up to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), which one does not adhere to as either secluded or non-secluded.
Why is that?

For a dharma that lacks intrinsic nature cannot be said to be permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, peaceful or unpeaceful, empty or non-empty, with signs or signless, with aspiration or aspirationless, or secluded or unsecluded.
Thus it is possible to bring about [realization]; however, it is not possible to bring about the realization that "intrinsic nature is empty of intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of ethical discipline...

Practicing the perfection of generosity, one will abide in the knowledge of all aspects. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, wherever a universal monarch goes with his fourfold army, there the fourfold army also goes. In the very same way, Subhūti, wherever the perfection of wisdom goes, [the other perfections follow].

In accordance with that, these five perfections follow along. They will abide in that which is all-aspect-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, it is just as if a charioteer, having mounted a chariot drawn by four horses, travels along a level road. In the same way, among these five perfections, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is the charioteer; it proceeds along the level road toward all-aspect-knowledge.
By means of that, one goes. He asked:
"Blessed One, what is the path of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, and what is the non-path?
The Blessed One said:
The path of the śrāvakas is not the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas; the path of the pratyekabuddhas is not the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas;
the path of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas. This is the path of bodhisattva mahāsattvas; this is not the path. He said:

"Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom has appeared for the sake of the great task of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, insofar as it thus instructs: 'This is the path; this is not the path. The Blessed One said:

'So it is, Subhūti, so it is. The perfection of wisdom has appeared for the sake of the great task of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, in that it demonstrates what is the path and what is not the path. The perfection of wisdom [performs] an immeasurable task.'"

The perfection of wisdom has appeared for the sake of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Through its incalculable activity, the perfection of wisdom has appeared for the sake of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom describes that activity, yet it does not grasp at form; it does not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
It does not stand for the sake of grasping the state of a śrāvaka or the state of a pratyekabuddha. Indeed,
this perfection of wisdom is the guide for the bodhisattva mahāsattva toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and away from the level of a śrāvaka.

It does not lead away from the level of a Pratyekabuddha, yet it leads toward all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Thus, this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is neither the producer nor the destroyer of any dharma, taking the stability of dharmas (*dharmasthititā*) as its standard. He asked:
"Blessed One, if this perfection of wisdom is neither the producer nor the destroyer of any dharma,"
Therefore, Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom give gifts;
how should he guard his morality; how should he cultivate patience; how should he exert vigor;
how should he enter the meditative concentrations; and how should he cultivate wisdom?
The Blessed One said:

"Taking omniscience as the objective support, one should give gifts; taking omniscience as the objective support, one should maintain ethical discipline; taking omniscience as the objective support, one should cultivate patience; taking omniscience as the objective support..."

Vigor should be initiated, taking omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) as the objective support; the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) should be attained, taking omniscience as the objective support; and wisdom (*prajñā*) should be cultivated, taking omniscience as the objective support. Having made those roots of virtue common to all sentient beings, they should be dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Thus it is for the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
As those roots of merit are dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, the cultivation of the six perfections reaches fulfillment,
until the cultivation of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of all aspects reaches fulfillment. And whichever bodhisattva mahāsattva is not separated from the six perfections, he—

He is not devoid of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should train in the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). By practicing the six perfections, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will fulfill all roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) and attain the knowledge of all aspects. For that reason, then...
"Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should apply himself to the six perfections. Subhūti asked:
"Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva apply himself to the six perfections?"
The Blessed One said:

"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should investigate in this way: form is neither conjoined nor disjoined; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither conjoined nor disjoined, up to and including the knowledge of all aspects."

They are neither conjoined nor disjoined. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should apply himself to the six perfections. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should apply himself with the thought: "I shall not abide in form," and he should apply himself with the thought: "I shall not abide in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations, nor in consciousness."
One should apply oneself with the thought: "I shall abide in omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). For what reason? Because form (*rūpa*) does not abide anywhere;
neither feeling (*vedanā*), nor perception (*saṃjñā*), nor mental formations (*saṃskāra*), nor consciousness (*vijñāna*) abides anywhere; and so on, until: omniscience does not abide anywhere.
In this way, by means of the yoga of non-abiding, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a man should desire to eat mango fruits or jackfruit;
he must plant a mango tree or a jackfruit tree. Having planted it, he must from time to time give it water and tend to it.

As its trunk gradually grows, it will encounter the necessary conditions, and there will be an abundance of mango fruits or jackfruit. He will then eat those mango fruits or jackfruit. In the same way, Subhūti, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment...

Having trained in the six perfections, one should favor sentient beings with generosity; they should be favored with ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and sentient beings should be liberated from cyclic existence. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain independence from others, who wishes to purify a buddha-field, who wishes to sit at the seat of awakening, and who wishes to turn the wheel of Dharma—
"One should train in the six perfections. He asked:
"Blessed One, do you say that one should train in the perfection of wisdom by means of the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, I say that one should train in the perfection of wisdom by means of the perfection of wisdom. I say that one who wishes to attain the cultivation of mastery over all dharmas should train in the perfection of wisdom. For what reason?"

For this is the perfection of wisdom, by which the stage of mastery over all phenomena is attained. For this perfection of wisdom is the gateway to all phenomena; just as, for example, the great ocean named "Lord" is the mouth of all rivers, even so is the perfection of wisdom the gateway to all phenomena—whether by those belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or those belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.

or by persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, one should train in this very perfection of wisdom. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of generosity, in the perfection of ethical discipline, in the perfection of patience, in the perfection of vigor, in the perfection of meditative concentration, and in the perfection of wisdom.

One must train; indeed, one must train even unto the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, a master archer, having taken up a bow appropriate to his skill, becomes unassailable by adversaries or enemies.
In the very same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) becomes unassailable.

Nor by Māra, or by the deities belonging to Māra’s host. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should train in the perfection of wisdom.
And while he courses in this perfection of wisdom, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, future, and present, hold him in their mindful regard. He said:
How, Blessed One, do the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, attend to that bodhisattva mahāsattva as he practices the perfection of generosity?

How do they attend to him as he practices the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom?
"How do they attend to one who courses in internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of own-being?
How do they attend to one who courses in the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:
In this regard, Subhūti, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, future, and present, hold in their mindful attention a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is practicing the perfection of generosity;

they hold in their mindful attention one who is practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, they hold him in their mindful attention in such a way that he does not [perceive them as separate].

They do not apprehend giving, nor morality, nor patience, nor vigor, nor meditation, nor wisdom. They bring to mind the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who thus does not apprehend anything. They bring to mind the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who thus courses in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, they bring him to mind in this manner:

Just as they do not perceive omniscience at all, so too they attend to the bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not perceive it. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Buddha Bhagavāns do not attend to the bodhisattva mahāsattva by way of form; they do not attend to them by way of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
"As long as they do not bring to mind omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). He asked:
'Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in many places, or should he not train in any place at all?'"
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in many places; yet he should not train in anything at all. Why is that?
Because those dharmas are not apprehended."
In this, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train. He said:

"Furthermore, Blessed One, regarding these dharmas which have been taught by the Tathāgata both in brief and in detail, therein a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment [should train in] these..."

The six perfections should be mastered both in brief and in detail; having mastered them and made them well-familiar through speech, they should be contemplated by the mind in such a way that the mental states and mental factors do not arise. The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Training in these six perfections, both in brief and in detail, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will come to know the summary and the detailed exposition of all dharmas. Subhūti asked:
"How, Blessed One, will a bodhisattva mahāsattva know the summary and the detailed exposition of all dharmas?"
The Blessed One said:

"One who knows the suchness (*tathatā*) of form, or feeling, or perception, or mental formations, or consciousness; up to one who knows the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—such a person will know the summary and the detailed exposition of all phenomena. He asked:
"But how, Blessed One, is there suchness of form?
The Blessed One said:

"That suchness in which neither arising is perceived, nor passing away is perceived, nor the alteration of what is present is perceived—this is the suchness of form, wherein a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train]."
"One should train [in this way]. He asked:
"Lord, what is the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:

That suchness in which neither arising is perceived nor passing away is perceived, and in which no alteration of what stands is perceived—this is the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects. It is in this that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train. Knowing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva [understands] all phenomena...
He will understand it both in brief and in detail. He asked:
"Blessed One, what is that limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
The Blessed One said:
The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the absence of a limit.
Training in this limit, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will come to know the concise and detailed exposition of all phenomena.
Knowing the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva will come to know the concise and detailed exposition of all phenomena. He said:
"What, Blessed One, is this dharmadhātu?
The Blessed One said: "The dharmadhātu is no-dhātu."

For that realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), neither annihilation nor delimitation is perceived. Practicing in this way and knowing the realm of phenomena, the bodhisattva mahāsattva will understand the concise and detailed exposition of all phenomena. He asked:
"Blessed One, how should the concise and detailed exposition of all phenomena be understood?"
The Blessed One said:
"Just as all phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined. He asked:
"Blessed One, what are those all phenomena that are neither conjoined nor disjoined?"

The Blessed One said: Form is neither conjoined nor disjoined; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither conjoined nor disjoined; and so on, up to the conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm, which are neither conjoined nor disjoined. Why is that?
For there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of this which could either be joined or disjoined;
and that which lacks intrinsic nature is non-existence (abhāva), and that which is non-existent is neither joined nor disjoined with non-existence. Thus it is with all phenomena (sarvadharma).

These are to be known. Furthermore, Subhūti, this is the summary for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas. For here, Subhūti, in this summary of the perfections, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is a beginner should train; and even when established in the tenth stage, he should train in this very summary. Moreover, training here in this summary, the bodhisattva mahāsattva [understands] the concise and detailed exposition of all dharmas.
"He will know. He asked:
"Blessed One, is this the entry for a bodhisattva mahāsattva of sharp faculties?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, this is the entrance for a bodhisattva mahāsattva of dull faculties; it is also the entrance for a bodhisattva mahāsattva of middling faculties,
and even for a bodhisattva of uncollected faculties.
This is the entrance for a mahāsattva. It is not an entrance for anyone who does not desire to train as a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
it is not an entrance for one who is indolent, nor for one of inferior vigor, nor for one whose mindfulness is lost, nor for one of distracted mind.
This is the entrance for one who has initiated vigor, who is not indolent, and whose mindfulness is established.
This is the entrance for one who desires to train in the stage of non-retrogression and who desires to attain all-aspect omniscience.
If he trains in the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, and having so trained, [trains] in the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline,
the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom—

He will attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, whatever deeds of Māra may arise for that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva while he is coursing in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they shall be abandoned as soon as they arise. Therefore, a Bodhisattva who desires to embrace skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*)—

A mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom. At whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, cultivates the perfection of wisdom, and applies himself to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom—
at that time, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside, remain, and maintain themselves in incalculable world-systems [bear witness].
They teach the true Dharma. They bring their attention to that bodhisattva mahāsattva as he courses in the perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
Because from these very six perfections have the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, future, and present emerged.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should aspire thus:

"I too shall attain those dharmas which have been attained by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, present, and future; which they are attaining; and which they will attain. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva [should aspire].

A mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should apply himself to yoga. Practicing in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must not be separated from mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, if a bodhisattva...

A mahāsattva practicing in this manner will cultivate the perfection of wisdom even for as little as the snap of a finger toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). That bodhisattva mahāsattva, moreover, will generate far more merit than one who would satisfy with gifts all the beings in a triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, or [establish them] in ethical discipline.

One should establish them in meditative concentration; one should establish them in wisdom; one should establish them in liberation; one should establish them in the knowledge and vision of liberation; one should establish them in the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including establishment in arhatship; and one should establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
This person would generate far more merit than that who would practice this profound *prajñāpāramitā* for even as long as the snap of a finger. Why is that?

Because from this [perfection] have issued forth the [perfections of] giving, morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; and likewise the fruit of stream-entry, up to arhatship and pratyekabuddha-enlightenment. Also, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside in the world-systems in the ten directions...
They abide, they remain steadfast, they maintain themselves, and they teach the Dharma; they too have emerged from this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who belong to the past, the future, and the present—they too are manifested from this very perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Subhūti, whether for a moment, or a day, or a hundred days, or a year, or a hundred years...

Or for an eon, or for a hundred eons, or even for as many as hundreds of incalculable eons, he will cultivate this perfection of wisdom through mental attentions directed toward the object of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). He will generate far more merit than one who would satisfy all the sentient beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with gifts.
One should establish them in ethical discipline, in concentration, in wisdom, in liberation, and in the knowledge and vision of liberation;
one should establish them in the fruit of stream-entry up to arhatship, and one should establish them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment. For what reason?

For it is from this that those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have emerged— those by whom this basis of meritorious action consisting of giving was designated, up to and including the designation of arhatship and the designation of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva mahāsattva who shall abide in the perfection of wisdom as thus taught, that bodhisattva indeed...

That mahāsattva is to be expected as irreversible. That bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with such skill in means is to be expected as one who has been attended upon by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one who has planted roots of merit. That bodhisattva...
That bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one embraced by spiritual friends;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one who has practiced the six perfections.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one who has cultivated the fourteen kinds of emptiness; that bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one who has cultivated up to the four analytical knowledges; that bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one endowed with the six superknowledges;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one who has become a youth.
That bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to have his intentions fulfilled;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be never separated from seeing the Buddhas;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be never separated from roots of virtue; that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be never separated from Buddha-fields.
That bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one possessing unassailable eloquence;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one who has attained the dhāraṇīs;
and the perfect accomplishment of form is to be expected for that bodhisattva mahāsattva.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one perfected in grammar; that bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one who intentionally seeks rebirth; that bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one skilled in the entry into syllables.
That bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be skilled in entering the non-syllabic; that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be skilled in the dwelling of bodhisattvas;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be skilled in discourse; and that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be skilled in non-discourse.
That bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one skilled in many designations, skilled in two designations, and skilled in numerous designations;
that bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one skilled in the designation of "female," skilled in the designation of "male," and skilled in the designation of "neuter";
that bodhisattva mahāsattva is to be expected as one skilled in the past, future, and present.

He is skilled in form, skilled in feeling, skilled in perception, skilled in mental formations, and skilled in consciousness; he is skilled in everything up to nirvāṇa; he is skilled in the characteristics of the dharma-realm, skilled in the characteristics of the conditioned, skilled in existence, skilled in non-existence, skilled in intrinsic nature, and skilled in extrinsic nature;
he is skilled in the associated, skilled in the dissociated, skilled in both the associated and the dissociated, and skilled in that which is neither associated nor dissociated.

Skilled in suchness, skilled in non-falsity, skilled in non-otherness, skilled in the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), skilled in the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), skilled in causes and conditions, skilled in the absence of conditions, skilled in the aggregates (*skandha*), skilled in the elements (*dhātu*),

skilled in the sense bases (*āyatana*), skilled in the truths (*satya*), skilled in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), skilled in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and skilled in the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

Skilled in the formless attainments, skilled in the six perfections, skilled in the four foundations of mindfulness, up to being skilled in the knowledge of all aspects; skilled in the conditioned realm, skilled in the unconditioned realm, skilled in the realms, and skilled in the non-realms; skilled in the mental attention to form, up to being skilled in the mental attention to consciousness, and so forth.

He is skilled in the mental attention to the knowledge of all aspects; he is skilled in [the realization that] form is empty of form, up to being skilled in [the realization that] consciousness is empty of consciousness; he is skilled in [the realization that] awakening is empty of awakening. He is skilled in the path of tranquility, skilled in the path of non-tranquility, skilled in arising and cessation, skilled in stability and transformation, and skilled in passion, hatred, and delusion.

Skilled in non-attachment, skilled in non-hatred, skilled in non-delusion; skilled in views, skilled in non-views, skilled in wrong views, skilled in non-wrong views, up to being skilled in all views; skilled in names, skilled in name-and-form, skilled in objective supports, skilled in predominant factors, skilled in aspects, skilled in characteristics; skilled in suffering, skilled in its origin, and skilled in its cessation.
He is skilled in the path; skilled in hell; skilled in the animal realm; skilled in the world of Yama; skilled in humans;

skilled in the path of humans; skilled in gods; skilled in the path of gods; skilled in the fruit of stream-entry; skilled in the path to the fruit of stream-entry; skilled in the once-returner; skilled in the path to the fruit of the once-returner; skilled in the non-returner; skilled in the path to the fruit of the non-returner; and skilled in arhatship.
He is skilled in the path of arhatship; skilled in solitary awakening; skilled in the path of solitary awakening; skilled in the knowledge of the aspects of the path;
skilled in the path of the knowledge of the aspects of the path;
skilled in the knowledge of all aspects; skilled in the path of the knowledge of all aspects; skilled in the faculties; and skilled in the perfection of the faculties.

He is skilled in swift wisdom, skilled in sharp wisdom, skilled in rapid wisdom, skilled in penetrative wisdom, skilled in vast wisdom, skilled in incomparable wisdom; he is skilled in the past time, skilled in the future time, skilled in the present time;
he is skilled in skillful means, skilled in the inclinations of sentient beings, skilled in intentions, and skilled in resolute intentions.

That bodhisattva mahāsattva should be expected to be skilled in meaning, skilled in phrasing, and skilled in the establishment of the three vehicles. Subhūti, these benefits are to be expected for that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom, who brings forth the perfection of wisdom, and who cultivates the perfection of wisdom. He said:
“Blessed One, how should one course in the perfection of wisdom? How should the perfection of wisdom be brought forth? How should the perfection of wisdom be cultivated?
The Blessed One replied:
“One should course in the perfection of wisdom by way of the tranquility of form, the insubstantiality of form, the emptiness of form, and the corelessness of form.”

One should practice the perfection of wisdom by means of the tranquility of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; by the insubstantiality of consciousness, the emptiness of consciousness, and the corelessness of consciousness. Furthermore, Subhūti, as to what you have asked:
"How should the perfection of wisdom be brought forth? [the answer is as follows:]...

The perfection of wisdom should be brought forth by means of the accomplishment of the emptiness of space. Furthermore, as to what you asked, "How should the perfection of wisdom be cultivated?"—the perfection of wisdom should be cultivated through the cultivation of non-cultivation. He said:
"Blessed One, for how long must a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom before it is said that they have practiced the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied:

"From the first production of the thought of awakening until sitting at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), one must practice the perfection of wisdom. In this way it should be brought forth and cultivated. He asked:
"But, Blessed One, must one be devoid of the continuity of the mind?
The Blessed One said:
"One should practice the perfection of wisdom without giving any opportunity for other mental engagements."

Without relinquishing the mental attention to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), one should course in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), bring forth the perfection of wisdom, and cultivate the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, one should course, cultivate, and bring forth [the perfection of wisdom] in such a way that the mind and mental factors do not arise. He said:
"But, Blessed One, is omniscience attained by one who courses in the perfection of wisdom, who brings forth the perfection of wisdom, and who cultivates the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said: "No, indeed. He asked: "Then what [is it]?"
"By not cultivating?
The Blessed One said: "No. He asked:
"Is it by one who cultivates and by one who does not cultivate?
The Blessed One said: "No. He asked:
"In that case, is it neither by one who cultivates nor by one who does not cultivate?
The Blessed One said: "No. He asked:
"How now, Blessed One, is omniscience attained?
The Blessed One said: "As is suchness. He asked:
"What is suchness?
The Blessed One replied:
"It is like the limit of reality. He asked:
"What is the limit of reality?
The Blessed One said:
"It is just as the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu). He asked:
"What is the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)?
The Blessed One said:
"It is just as the realm of self (ātmadhātu), the realm of sentient beings (sattvadhātu), the realm of living beings (jīvadhātu), and the realm of persons (pudgaladhātu). He asked:
“Blessed One, what is the element of self, the element of sentient beings, the element of life, and the element of the person?
The Blessed One said:
“What do you think, Subhūti, is a self, or a sentient being, or a life-principle, or a person apprehended?”
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, since one does not apprehend a self, or a sentient being, or a living soul, or a person, how could we designate a self-element, a sentient-being-element, a living-soul-element, or a person-element?"

Thus, by not designating the perfection of wisdom, and thus by not designating all dharmas, one will attain the knowledge of all aspects. He asked: "But, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom non-designatable? Is the perfection of meditation non-designatable?

Is the perfection of vigor non-designatable? Is the perfection of patience non-designatable? Is the perfection of ethical discipline non-designatable? Is the perfection of generosity non-designatable?"

The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is ineffable; indeed, all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether the dharmas of śrāvakas or the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas—are ineffable. Subhūti asked:
“If, Blessed One, all phenomena are ineffable, then from where, Blessed One, do the hells come to be designated?”

Is the animal realm or the world of Yama perceived? Are gods or humans perceived? Is one who has entered the stream, or a once-returner, or a non-returner, or an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha, or a bodhisattva, or a perfectly awakened buddha perceived?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti, is the designation 'sentient being' apprehended?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
Not perceiving any beings, Subhūti, how shall I designate hell? Or the animal realm, or the world of Yama,
or gods, or humans, or a stream-enterer, or a once-returner, or a non-returner, or an arhat,
or a pratyekabuddha, or a perfectly awakened one— how shall I designate these?
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in dharmas that are non-designatable. Subhūti said:

"But, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom not train in form, nor in feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness; and so on, up to not training in the knowledge of all aspects?"
"One should train. The Blessed One said:

One should train in form by way of neither adding nor subtracting. One should train in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness by way of neither adding nor subtracting. Up to: one should train in the knowledge of all aspects by way of neither adding nor subtracting. He asked:

“Blessed One, how should one train in form by way of neither adding nor subtracting? How should one train in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness by way of neither adding nor subtracting?
The Blessed One replied:
“One should train by way of non-arising and non-ceasing. He asked:
“Blessed One, how should one train in everything up to the knowledge of all aspects by way of neither adding nor subtracting?
The Blessed One replied:
“One should train by way of non-arising and non-cessation. He asked:
"How, Blessed One, should one train in non-arising and non-cessation?
The Blessed One said:
"In the state of non-conditioning."
[It is] neither in the cultivation of conditioned phenomena nor in their elimination. He asked:
"Blessed One, how should one train in non-conditioning?
The Blessed One said:
Seeing all phenomena as empty of their own specific characteristics, one should train in non-conditioning. He asked:
"Blessed One, how are all phenomena to be seen as empty of their own specific characteristics?"

The Blessed One said: Form is to be viewed as empty of form. Feeling is to be viewed as empty of feeling. Perception is to be viewed as empty of perception. Mental formations are to be viewed as empty of mental formations. Consciousness is to be viewed as empty of consciousness.

The eye is to be seen as empty of the eye. Likewise, the mind is to be seen as empty of the mind. Internal emptiness is to be seen as empty of internal emptiness, up to and including self-characteristic emptiness, which is to be seen as empty of self-characteristic emptiness. The meditative absorptions (dhyānas) are to be seen as empty of the meditative absorptions, up to and including the attainment of cessation, which is to be seen as empty of the attainment of cessation.

The foundations of mindfulness are to be seen as empty; the foundations of mindfulness are to be seen as empty of the foundations of mindfulness, up to and including awakening, which is to be seen as empty of awakening. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in all phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics. He said:

“If, Blessed One, form is to be seen as empty of form, and so on up to awakening being empty of awakening, then how, Blessed One, does the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom come to be? The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom for a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti asked:
“For what reason, Blessed One, is the practice of the perfection of wisdom a ‘non-practice’?
The Blessed One replied:

For in this way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended, and the bodhisattva is also not apprehended. The practice is also not apprehended. That which practices, that by which one practices, or that wherein one practices—that too is not apprehended.
This, Subhūti, is the non-practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, the practice of the perfection of wisdom, wherein all these conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are not apprehended. He said:
“If, Blessed One, the practice is the practice of the perfection of wisdom, how then should a beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:

“In this regard, Subhūti, a beginner bodhisattva mahāsattva, starting from the very first production of the thought of awakening, should train in the non-apprehension of all dharmas. While giving a gift, he...”
Giving should be practiced by way of non-apprehension;
while guarding morality, morality should be guarded by way of non-apprehension; while accomplishing patience, patience should be accomplished by way of non-apprehension. [So too] vigor...

One who exerts effort should exert vigor by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. One who enters meditative concentration should enter concentration by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. One cultivating wisdom should cultivate wisdom by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
Up to and including one cultivating the knowledge of all aspects, one should cultivate the knowledge of all aspects by means of the yoga of non-apprehension. He said:
"To what extent, Blessed One, is there non-apprehension? To what extent is there apprehension?
The Blessed One said: "To the extent that there is duality, to that extent there is apprehension. Non-duality is non-apprehension. He asked:
"What, Blessed One, is duality?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, everything from the eye and forms up to the mind and mental phenomena, and everything from awakening up to the Buddhas—this is duality. He asked:
"But, Blessed One, is non-apprehension apprehensible, or is non-apprehension non-apprehensible?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, non-apprehension is not apprehensible; nor is non-apprehension non-apprehensible. However, moreover—"

Subhūti, the equality of apprehension and non-apprehension is non-apprehension. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the equality of apprehension. Training in this manner, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes one who is without apprehension regarding the perfection of wisdom. He said:
If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not adhere to either apprehension or non-apprehension,
how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom fulfill one stage after another, and having fulfilled stage after stage, how should he attain the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not fulfill one stage after another while remaining in apprehension. For it is not possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while remaining in apprehension, [to practice] in the perfection of wisdom."
[He practices] in order to fulfill the stage from stage while coursing [in the path]. For what reason?

Because the perfection of wisdom is non-apprehension, awakening is non-apprehension, and even he who courses in the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should course] in the perfection of wisdom.
[It] should be practiced. He said:

"If, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is not apprehended, awakening is also not apprehended, and even he who practices for the sake of awakening is not apprehended—then how now should a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practice] in the perfection of wisdom?"

"While practicing, one must exercise discernment regarding all phenomena: 'This is form, this is feeling, this is perception, these are mental formations, this is consciousness,' up to 'this is awakening.
The Blessed One said:

For indeed, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not perform an analytical investigation of phenomena in such a way that, by so doing, he might apprehend form, or apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including the apprehension of awakening. Subhūti said:

If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend form, and does not apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness— up to and including awakening—

how then does he fulfill the perfection of generosity, and having fulfilled the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva? [How does he enter] the fixed course of a bodhisattva?

Having entered [the path], he purifies the buddha-field. Having purified the buddha-field, he brings sentient beings to maturity. Having brought sentient beings to maturity, he attains all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Having attained all-aspect omniscience, he turns the wheel of Dharma. Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he performs the work of a Buddha. Having performed the work of a Buddha, [he establishes] sentient beings...
"...does he liberate them from saṃsāra?
The Blessed One said: "No, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of form. Nor for the sake of feeling..."

He does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of perception, nor for the sake of mental formations, nor for the sake of consciousness, up to and including for the sake of awakening. He asked:
"For whose sake, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said: "A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of anything. For what reason?"
For thus all dharmas are uncreated and unconditioned; that perfection of wisdom is also uncreated and unconditioned;

awakening too is uncreated and unconditioned; and even the bodhisattva is uncreated and unconditioned. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom.
[They are established] through the yoga of being uncreated and unconditioned. He asked:

"Blessed One, if all dharmas are uncreated and unconditioned, then how does the establishment of these three vehicles occur—whether it be the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the Great Vehicle?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, no establishment whatsoever is perceived for dharmas that are uncreated and unconditioned. An establishment is perceived for dharmas that are conditioned and volitionally produced.
Why is that?"

For thus it is that the foolish, unlearned worldling, having become attached to the five aggregates—from form up to consciousness—and having become attached even to the knowledge of all aspects, conceives of form and perceives form; he conceives of consciousness and perceives consciousness; and so on, up to conceiving of awakening and perceiving awakening. It occurs to him as follows:
"I shall fully awaken to enlightenment; I shall liberate sentient beings from cyclic existence"—thus does he falsely conceptualize. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, that form, up to and including enlightenment, which has not been apprehended by the five eyes of the Buddhas—that very thing those deluded men, who are blind and sightless, attempt to sever from sentient beings in order to liberate them from cyclic existence. Subhūti said:
If, Blessed One, no sentient beings were perceived by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, through his five eyes as those who would be liberated from saṃsāra,

how is it that now, having awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, the Blessed One has classified sentient beings into three groups: those fixed in rightness, those unfixed, and those fixed in falsehood?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, since I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, no sentient being has been apprehended by me—neither one fixed in rightness, nor one unfixed, nor one fixed in falsehood. However, Subhūti, as for these sentient beings who perceive substantiality in what is insubstantial, I turn them away from that grasping at the unreal."
This is according to worldly convention, and not according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). He asked:
"Has the Blessed One not awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) while abiding in the ultimate truth?
The Blessed One replied:
"No," he said. "Is it by remaining in perversion that unexcelled, perfect enlightenment has been fully realized?
The Blessed One replied:
"No," he said.
"If, Blessed One, supreme perfect enlightenment was not awakened to by remaining in the ultimate truth,
nor by remaining in perversion, then surely the Tathāgata has not awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment at all."
It would be so. The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
yet it does not abide anywhere, whether in the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm. Subhūti, it is just as if..."
A Tathāgata’s emanation does not abide anywhere, whether in the conditioned realm or the unconditioned realm. That Tathāgata’s emanation goes and comes,
stands and sits.

He should practice the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom;
he should dwell having attained the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and he should cultivate the five superknowledges, the four applications of mindfulness, and so on, up to the noble eightfold path.

the concentration on emptiness, the signless concentration, the wishless concentration; from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of specific characteristics; the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, and great compassion.

[He teaches] the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha for the sake of turning the wheel of Dharma. And suppose that emanation, having himself emanated immeasurable beings, were to give them prophecies regarding the three categories—what do you think, Subhūti? Would any being at all have been prophesied by that emanation?
He replied: "No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

In the same way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata has known and reckoned all phenomena to be like an emanation; having known them to be fashioned by ignorance, not a single sentient being has been apprehended, nor has anyone been disciplined. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom. It is just as if, Subhūti, there were an emanation of the Tathāgata. Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, if all phenomena are like magical emanations, what is the distinction between a Tathāgata and a magical emanation? What is the difference, and what is the intended meaning?
The Blessed One replied:
Subhūti, no distinction whatsoever and no difference whatsoever is perceived between the Tathāgata and an emanation. For, Subhūti, the Tathāgata and an emanation are without distinction.
This is because whatever action the Tathāgata performs, that same action the emanation performs. Subhūti asked:
"But, Blessed One, does the emanation perform action only when the Tathāgata exists?"
The Blessed One said: "He does so, Subhūti. He asked: "But then, Blessed One, how can an emanation perform an action when the Tathāgata is absent?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śāntamati, not perceiving a bodhisattva, were to manifest an emanation-body of a Tathāgata and then pass into parinirvāṇa; and by that emanation, the work of a Buddha were performed for a full kalpa thereafter."
And that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having been prophesied, was subsequently perceived as having entered final nirvāṇa;

yet for a magical creation, there is neither arising nor final nirvāṇa. In this very way, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom, namely, by being convinced that all phenomena are like a magical creation.

He asked: "If there is no distinction between a magical creation (*nirmita*) and a Tathāgata, how will there be purification of the gift (*dakṣiṇā-pariśuddhi*)? Blessed One, what of these beings who seek merit and seek nirvāṇa?"

They establish an offering for a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, and that offering is never exhausted until all of them have attained final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder. In the same way, an offering established for an emanation is never exhausted until all of them have attained final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, by whatever nature of phenomena (dharmatā) the Tathāgata is a worthy recipient of offerings for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, by that very same nature of phenomena a magical creation (nirmita) is also a worthy recipient of offerings for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Let it be, Subhūti."

The offering established by a Tathāgata is such. Let alone the offering established by one emanated by a Tathāgata. Subhūti, whatever sons of good family or daughters of good family shall attend upon the Tathāgata with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, they shall all, having reached the limit of that root of merit, make an end of suffering. Let alone the mind imbued with loving-kindness.

Subhūti, whatever sons of good family or daughters of good family shall scatter flowers into the sky while keeping the Tathāgata in mind, they will all, without reaching the limit of that root of merit, bring an end to suffering. Subhūti, let alone the mental attention associated with loving-kindness; let alone scattering flowers into the sky.

"Subhūti, whatever sons of good family or daughters of good family shall pay homage to the Buddha, they will all, in due course, bring an end to suffering. Indeed, Subhūti, the offering established by the Tathāgata is of such great purpose and such great benefit.
Therefore, Subhūti, it should be understood through this method."
There is no difference whatsoever between the Tathāgata and his emanation,
having taken the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as the standard.
In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom.

Having entered into the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, that true nature of phenomena must not be disturbed. One must not think, "This is the perfection of wisdom; this is the true nature of the perfection of wisdom," and thus disturb it. One must not think, "This is the perfection of meditation; this is the true nature of the perfection of meditation," and thus disturb it. This applies up to: "This is the perfection of generosity; this is the true nature of the perfection of generosity," and one must not disturb it. In this same way, it applies to all phenomena.
[It] must be done. He said:

"If, Blessed One, the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is not to be disturbed, then why, Blessed One, has this form, up to this consciousness, been disturbed by the Tathāgata? In this way, internal and external phenomena have been taught."
"Thus have been taught the phenomena that are wholesome, unwholesome, with outflows, without outflows, mundane, supramundane, common, uncommon, conditioned, and unconditioned.
Might it not be the case, then, that the Blessed One has disturbed the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena?
The Blessed One said:

"Indeed not so, Subhūti. Those dharmas have been taught by me through names and signs, and an indication of dharmas has been made, so that others might enter [the path]. Yet, the true nature (dharmatā) of dharmas is not thereby disturbed. Subhūti said: "If, Blessed One, names and signs have been taught for the sake of enabling others to enter [the path],"
"How then, Blessed One, are dharmas that are nameless and signless expressed by means of names and signs? The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, this expression is neither a name nor a sign, nor is it an attachment.
Rather, Subhūti, I speak only of suffering; I do not speak with attachment to a name or a sign. For indeed, Subhūti, neither a Tathāgata nor a disciple of a Tathāgata [abides] in a name or a sign."
He becomes attached. Subhūti, if a name were to become attached to a name, a sign would become attached to a sign,
and emptiness would become attached to emptiness.

One would be attached to the signless in the signless; one would be attached to the wishless in the wishless. One would be attached to suchness in suchness; one would be attached to the limit of reality in the limit of reality.
If the realm of phenomena were to adhere to the realm of phenomena,

or if the unconditioned were to adhere to the unconditioned; if a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata were to adhere to names and signs— yet all these phenomena are merely names, and they do not even abide in mere names.
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in mere name and mere sign, should practice the perfection of wisdom, and therein he should not become attached. He said:
"If, Blessed One, all that is conditioned is merely name and sign,"
For what purpose, then, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva now generate the mind set on awakening,
and having generated the mind set on awakening, undergoes various kinds of conditioned hardships while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva?

He practices. While practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, he bestows various kinds of gifts; he guards ethical discipline and accomplishes patience; he exerts vigor and enters into meditative concentration;
he cultivates wisdom and courses in emptiness; he courses in the dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless attainments; and [he courses] in the applications of mindfulness.
And he dwells with the right efforts, and he dwells with [the bases of psychic power], up to dwelling with the gateways to liberation— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
and he dwells with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, until he fulfills great loving-kindness and great compassion. The Blessed One said:

As for what Subhūti has said: "If all that is conditioned is merely name and sign, then for whose sake does the bodhisattva mahāsattva now practice the conduct of a bodhisattva? Because... [AdSPG I 147]
In that case, Subhūti, all that is conditioned is merely name and sign;
and that name is empty of name, and the sign is empty of sign. Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of a bodhisattva—

He attains the knowledge of all aspects. Having attained the knowledge of all aspects, he turns the wheel of Dharma. Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he leads sentient beings to final nirvana by means of the three vehicles. Furthermore, neither the arising nor the passing away of that name and sign is perceived, nor is any alteration of what is established perceived. He said:
“O Blessed One, you say ‘the knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of all aspects. The Blessed One said:
“I say ‘the knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of all aspects. [Subhūti] said:
“Furthermore, O Blessed One, as for this ‘knowledge of all aspects’ which has been taught by the Tathāgata...”

The knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) has also been taught by the Tathāgata, and the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) has also been taught by the Tathāgata. O Blessed One, what is the distinction, what is the difference between these three types of omniscience?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) belongs to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) belongs to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas; and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) belongs to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened ones.

For what reason, Blessed One, is it omniscience for the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas? For what reason is it the knowledge of the aspects of the path for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas? And for what reason is it the knowledge of all aspects for the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the perfectly enlightened ones?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, 'all' refers only to this much: namely, all internal and external phenomena. These are known even by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, yet not all paths and not in every aspect. As for what Subhūti has said thus:"
For what reason is it that the knowledge of the aspects of the path belongs to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas?
Subhūti, all paths must be generated by the bodhisattva, the mahāsattva;
all paths must be known.

Those which are the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and those which are the paths of the bodhisattvas—all those paths must be fulfilled, and by means of those paths the tasks to be performed on the path must be accomplished; yet, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) must not be realized. He said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva must fulfill the path of a Buddha, should he not likewise realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)? The Blessed One replied:
“Subhūti, without having purified the buddha-field and without having brought sentient beings to maturity, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). He asked:
“But, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while remaining on the path, realize the limit of reality?
The Blessed One replied:
"No," he said.
"By standing on that wrong path?
The Blessed One said:
"No," he said.
"Is it by standing on both the path and the non-path?
The Blessed One said:
"No," he said. "Is it by standing neither on the path nor on what is not the path?
The Blessed One said:
"No," he replied.
"In that case, Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti: while you were standing on the path, was your mind liberated from the outflows through non-clinging?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"While you were standing on a non-path?"
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"Is it for one who stands on the path or on what is not the path?
He said: "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"Is the mind of one who stands neither on the path nor on what is not the path liberated from the outflows through non-clinging?
He replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One. Blessed One, my mind is not liberated from the outflows through non-clinging while standing anywhere;
and yet, Blessed One, my mind is liberated just as it is when standing nowhere at all. The Blessed One said:

In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) by abiding anywhere. Furthermore, Subhūti, as for what is called "the knowledge of all aspects" (sarvākārajñatā), it is called "the knowledge of all aspects" by virtue of a single aspect; that is to say, by the aspect of peace (śāntākāra). Moreover, Subhūti, by whatever aspects, whatever marks, and whatever signs [it is characterized]...
All these phenomena are indicated; all those aspects (*ākāra*), signs (*liṅga*), and marks (*nimitta*) have been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, it is called "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*). He said:

Furthermore, Blessed One, regarding omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*): is there, Blessed One, any distinction among these three types of all-knowledge with respect to the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*)— such that for one it is an abandonment with remainder, and for another it is an abandonment without remainder?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, there is no diversity in the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*). However, the Tathāgata has the abandonment of all latencies and their continuations (*sarva-vāsanā-anusandhi*), whereas the Śrāvaka and the Pratyekabuddha do not have the abandonment of all latencies, continuations, and afflictions.
Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, is this unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) attained by these [others] as well? Or, Blessed One, is any diversity perceived within the unconditioned?"
The Blessed One said: "No. He asked: "If no diversity of the unconditioned is perceived,"

“From where, Blessed One, do you teach thus: ‘For this one there is the abandonment of all latent tendencies and their connections; for that one there is no abandonment of all latent tendencies and their connections’? The Blessed One said:
“Subhūti, there is no affliction of residual impressions (*vāsanānusandhi*) for them. Nevertheless, those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have abandoned passion, hatred, and delusion;
yet certain bodily transformations still arise, which they withdraw for the sake of not causing harm to foolish ordinary people (*bālapṛthagjana*).
Such [transformations] do not occur for the śrāvakas in that way, nor does it exist for the Tathāgata. Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
If, Blessed One, the path is non-existence and nirvāṇa is non-existence,

then from where, Blessed One, is it designated: "this is a stream-enterer," "this is a once-returner," "this is a non-returner," "this is an arhat," "this is a pratyekabuddha," or "this is a bodhisattva mahāsattva"?
"What is it that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha [is]?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, all these are characterized by the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). Whether it be one who is a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), or one who is a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin)..."
“...the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and the tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened one. He asked:

“But, Blessed One, does the unconditioned manifest itself as ‘this is a stream-enterer,’ up to ‘this is an arhat,’ ‘this is a pratyekabuddha,’ ‘this is a bodhisattva mahāsattva,’ or ‘this is a tathāgata’?”
"Is he an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha?
The Blessed One said:
"Indeed not, Subhūti, does one manifest the unconditioned; rather, it is spoken by taking words as the authority. But in the ultimate sense, it cannot be manifested. For what reason? Because—"
Therein, there is no designation by way of the path of speech. He asked:
"Blessed One, how is the ultimate limit designated?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, it is by taking worldly convention as the standard that for those by whom the beginning is cut off, a 'final limit' is designated. Furthermore, for those by whom the prior limit is severed, a 'final limit' is designated. He said:
"Blessed One, since all phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), how could a prior limit ever be known?"
"But how, then, is a final limit known?
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. For all phenomena, Subhūti, which are empty of their own specific characteristics, no prior limit is known."

How much less could a "later limit" be designated? Such a thing is impossible. However, Subhūti, for those beings who do not know that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), it has been taught to them:
"This is the prior limit; this is the later limit.
But this is not so with respect to all phenomena, which are empty of their own specific characteristics.

A prior limit or a subsequent limit is not apprehended. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom regarding all phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics. While coursing in all phenomena that are empty of their own specific characteristics, one does not become attached to anything, whether internal or external.
Whether in conditioned or unconditioned phenomena, or in the dharmas of the śrāvakas or the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas. When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One:
"O Blessed One, it is said: 'perfection of wisdom, perfection of wisdom.'"
"In what sense is it called 'perfection of wisdom' (prajñāpāramitā)?
The Blessed One replied:
"Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom has reached the supreme perfection of all dharmas."
For that reason, it is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Furthermore, Subhūti, by means of this perfection of wisdom,
all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, and tathāgatas, arhats,
perfectly enlightened ones, have gone to the further shore, are going, and will go.
For that reason, it is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore, Subhūti, in the ultimate sense,
that reality which is undifferentiated among all phenomena— here, through this perfection of wisdom and by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
no further shore (*pāra*) among all phenomena is apprehended.

For that reason, it is called the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Furthermore, Subhūti, within this perfection of wisdom, suchness (*tathatā*) is included, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is included, and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is included;

for that reason, it is called the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is neither conjoined nor disjoined with any dharma, and it is neither visible nor invisible, nor subject to resistance (*sapratigha*).
or non-obstructive. Why is that?

Because this perfection of wisdom is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and has but a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics. Furthermore, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom [is the guide] of all dharmas.
Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is a giver of all eloquence and all illuminations;
it is unceasing and cannot be taken away by Māras, or by the deities belonging to the host of Māra, or by persons belonging to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas,
nor indeed can this perfection of wisdom be taken away from a Bodhisattva by any others, such as those of other sects or evil friends.
of the Mahāsattva. For what reason?
Because all those [factors] are not apprehended here in this perfection of wisdom, by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
It is in this way, Subhūti, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should course here in this perfection of wisdom. Furthermore...

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing here in this profound perfection of wisdom should practice for the sake of impermanence, practice for the sake of suffering, and practice for the sake of non-self. [He should practice] for the sake of the knowledge of suffering, for the sake of the knowledge of origination, for the sake of the knowledge of cessation, and for the sake of the knowledge of the path. For the sake of the knowledge of exhaustion, for the sake of the knowledge of non-arising, and for the sake of the knowledge of phenomena.
For the sake of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*); for the sake of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*);

for the sake of ultimate knowledge (*paramārtha-jñāna*). One should practice for the sake of knowledge as it truly is (*yathāvaj-jñāna*). In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice for the sake of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, if in this profound perfection of wisdom neither benefit (*artha*) nor harm (*anartha*) is perceived, how should a bodhisattva..."
"In what manner should a mahāsattva practice for the sake of the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing for the sake of the profound meaning of the perfection of wisdom should practice in this way."

"One should not act with the thought, 'Passion is my benefit' or 'Passion is my harm'; one should not act with the thought, 'Hatred is my benefit' or 'Hatred is my harm'; one should not act with the thought, 'Delusion is my benefit' or 'Delusion is my harm'; one should not act with the thought, 'False view is my benefit' or 'False view is my harm,' and so on, up to all modes of views."
One should not practice with the thought, "This is beneficial" or "This is harmful. Why is that?

Because the suchness (*tathatā*) of passion, hatred, and delusion, up to the suchness of all various types of views, does not bring benefit to anyone, nor does it bring harm. One should not practice with the thought, "Form is beneficial to me," nor should one practice with the thought, "Form is harmful to me."
One should not practice with the thought, "Consciousness is my benefit," nor should one practice with the thought, "Consciousness is not my benefit. This continues up to:
one should not practice with the thought, "Awakening is my benefit," nor should one practice with the thought, "Awakening is not my benefit. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, it was after the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, had fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect awakening that [he realized this].
Not a single dharma is apprehended that could bring about either benefit or harm.

Moreover, Subhūti, whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) remain ever established. That [nature] brings about neither benefit nor harm for anyone. It is indeed thus, Subhūti.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, having abandoned both benefit and harm, should practice the perfection of wisdom. He asked:
"For what reason, Blessed One, does the perfection of wisdom neither produce benefit nor produce harm?
The Blessed One replied:

For it is thus, Subhūti: the unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛtadharmatā*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which is what the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) must accomplish—by this reason, the perfection of wisdom does not bring about the welfare of anyone, nor does it bring about harm. He said:
"But, Blessed One, is not the unconditioned the goal (*artha*) of all the Noble Ones, of the Buddhas, and of the disciples of the Buddhas?"
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, is the unconditioned reality (asaṃskṛta-artha) not present for all the noble ones—the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas—neither by way of being beneficial nor by way of being non-beneficial? Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the suchness (tathatā) of space is neither by way of being beneficial nor by way of being non-beneficial to anyone."
or present;
even so, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not present as either a benefit or a non-benefit to any dharma. He said:
"But, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in the unconditioned perfection of wisdom, attain the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. A bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained here in this profound, unconditioned perfection of wisdom, attains the knowledge of all aspects."
But not by way of duality. He asked:
"But, Blessed One, does a non-dual dharma attain a non-dual dharma?
The Blessed One said:
"No," he said.
"In that case, does one dharma attain two dharmas?
The Blessed One replied:
"No," he said. "In that case, does one who possesses dualistic dharmas attain the non-dual dharma?
The Blessed One replied:
"No," he said.
"In that case, does a non-dual phenomenon attain a dual phenomenon?
The Blessed One said:
"No," he said.
"Then how is it obtained now?
The Blessed One replied:
When neither a dualistic phenomenon nor a non-dualistic phenomenon is perceived, for what reason is that?
For attainment is indeed non-perception; it is not attained by means of non-perception, nor is it attained by means of perception. (63) (AdSPG I 155)
Chapter 64. Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound; O Blessed One, the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, are performers of what is difficult."

Those who establish themselves in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment do not perceive any being whatsoever, nor even the designation "being," yet they establish themselves in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment for the sake of beings. It is just as if, for example:

“Blessed One, it would be as if some man wished to plant a pillar in space where there is no support; even so, Blessed One, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas wish to attain all-aspect omniscience for the sake of sentient beings. The Blessed One said:
“So it is, Subhūti, so it is.”

Bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, are doers of what is difficult, in that they establish themselves for the sake of beings in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
