And having fully awakened to that omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), they liberate beings from the grasping at a self. Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, some man should wish to plant a pillar; and that man—
He would not know the root of that pillar, nor the branches, nor the trunk, nor the leaves, nor the flowers, nor the fruit; yet,
having planted the trunk of that pillar, he would protect it from time to time and provide it with water, so that its trunk would gradually become endowed with branches and endowed with leaves.

It would be endowed with flowers and it would be endowed with fruit; one would enjoy the leaves of that tree, and one would enjoy its flowers and its fruit. In the same way, Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who [act] for the sake of all sentient beings...

Having set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they practice the six perfections in succession and eventually attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). They become the source of sustenance through leaves, flowers, and fruits for all sentient beings.
In this regard, Subhūti, the "leaf" is that by means of which sentient beings, having relied upon the bodhisattva mahāsattva, [are delivered] from the three miserable states.

[They] are completely liberated. "Flower" refers to that by which, having relied upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, they are reborn in great kṣatriya families, great brahmin families, and great householder families; they are reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings' realm, and so on, up to being reborn among the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. "Fruit" refers to that...
The bodhisattva mahāsattva, having attained omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), establishes those beings in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*),
establishes them in the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmīphala*), establishes them in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmīphala*), establishes them in arhatship (*arhattva*),
and establishes them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment (*pratyekabodhi*). It is by relying upon that very bodhisattva mahāsattva that they attain omniscience.

Having attained the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they too become those upon whom all sentient beings depend for their livelihood through leaves, flowers, and fruits. There, those who establish offerings (*dakṣiṇā*) all gradually attain final nirvāṇa by means of the three vehicles—
namely, by the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayāna*), the vehicle of the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddhayāna*), or the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) unto unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

They awaken to full enlightenment, yet they do not designate a "being" therein, nor do they designate the concept of a "being"; rather, they liberate those beings from their grasping at a self as beings. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom; for herein no being whatsoever, nor even the designation of a "being," is apprehended, for whose sake one would attain all-aspect omniscience. Subhūti said:
Blessed One, it should be understood that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is indeed the Tathāgata. Why is that?

Because, Blessed One, it is by depending upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that all hells are cut off, all animal births are cut off, all realms of Yama are cut off, all unfortunate states and calamities are cut off, and all forms of poverty are cut off.
All inferior destinies are cut off; the entire realm of desire is cut off; the entire realm of form is cut off;
the entire realm of formlessness is cut off. The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is."

The Tathāgata himself should be understood as the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, if the bodhisattva mahāsattva did not exist, then the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of the past, future, and present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would not be known;
nor would there be the appearance of Pratyekabuddhas in the world, nor the appearance of Arhats in the world.
There would be no appearance in the world of non-returners, once-returners, or stream-enterers.
Furthermore, all the hells would not be extinguished, nor would all the animal realms, nor all the worlds of Yama;
the entire realm of desire would not be extinguished, the entire realm of form would not be extinguished, and the entire formless realm would not be extinguished.

They will cut it off. Furthermore, Subhūti, as for what you said—that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be understood as being the Tathāgata himself—it is so, Subhūti, it is so. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should indeed be understood as the Tathāgata himself. For what reason?
Subhūti, by means of which suchness a Tathāgata is designated,
by means of which suchness a Pratyekabuddha is designated, and by means of which suchness all Noble Ones are designated— by that same suchness...

That suchness by which form is designated, up to that suchness by which consciousness is designated, and up to that suchness by which the conditioned realm is designated and the unconditioned realm is designated—all that is precisely suchness; therefore, it is called "suchness. Abiding in that suchness, the bodhisattva mahāsattva [attains] the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

He will attain [it]. Therefore, he is called a Tathāgata. Subhūti, by this method, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as being truly a Tathāgata, having made suchness his standard. Subhūti, in this way indeed should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom that is suchness. Subhūti, in the perfection of wisdom that is suchness...

The bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained, trains in the suchness of all phenomena. Having trained in the suchness of all phenomena, he will fulfill the suchness of all phenomena. Having fulfilled the suchness of all phenomena, he will attain mastery over the suchness of all phenomena.

Having attained mastery over the suchness of all phenomena, he will become skilled in the faculties of all sentient beings; being skilled in the faculties, he will attain skill in the perfection of the faculties. Having attained this, he will know that sentient beings are the owners of their own karma;
knowing that sentient beings are the owners of their own karma, he will fulfill his knowledge of aspiration.

Having fulfilled the knowledge resulting from resolution (*praṇidhijñāna*), he will purify the knowledge of the three times. Having purified the knowledge of the three times, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, he will work for the benefit of sentient beings;

working for the benefit of sentient beings, he will purify a buddha-field. Having purified a buddha-field, he will attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); having attained the knowledge of all aspects, he will turn the wheel of Dharma. Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he will establish sentient beings in the three vehicles.
He will establish [beings];

having established beings in the three vehicles, he will lead them to final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, seeing all the qualities and benefits, [should practice] for himself for the sake of unsurpassed [enlightenment].
"One should generate the mind for full and perfect enlightenment, and one should cause others to generate the mind for unsurpassed, full and perfect enlightenment. Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who practice here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, are worthy of homage by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras."
The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice here in this profound perfection of wisdom as it has been taught are worthy of homage by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti said:

"Blessed One, how much merit will a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first produced the thought of awakening generate, he who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, suppose all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system were to establish themselves on the level of a śrāvaka, or were to establish themselves on the level of a pratyekabuddha."
"Would those beings now generate much merit?
He replied: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata. It would be immeasurable, Blessed One; immeasurable, Sugata. The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, Subhūti, as for the merit of all the beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system who belong to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas..."

And whatever merit belongs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first produced the thought of awakening— compared to this mass of merit of that bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening, [the merit] of all beings in this trichiliocosm who belong to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas...
Or rather, that merit does not approach even a hundredth part; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor does it bear comparison in any way whatsoever. Why is that?
For persons belonging to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born from the Bodhisattva, but the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not, in turn, give birth to them.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Let alone all the beings in a triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system who belong to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas;
suppose that all those beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were endowed with the qualities of a śrāvaka.

If they were endowed with the qualities of a pratyekabuddha, whatever merit they possessed would not approach even a hundredth part of the merit of a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening (*prathamacittotpādika*). It would not approach even a ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part; it does not even bear comparison. Why is that?

For the qualities of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are born from the bodhisattvas; the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are not born from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Thus, if all the beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to be established on the stage of śuklavidarśanā, their merit would [be surpassed] by the merit of a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening.

It does not approach even a hundredth part, nor does it admit of any comparison whatsoever. Furthermore, if all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system were to be established on the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*),
their merit would not approach even a hundredth part of the merit of a bodhisattva who has first generated the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpādika*).

It does not even approach it by any comparison; it cannot bear it. This is so even if they were established on the stage of the eighth person, established on the stage of vision, established on the stage of refinement, established on the stage of freedom from passion, established on the stage of one who has done what was to be done, or established on the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

Whatever merit those [beings] might possess does not approach even a hundredth part of the merit of a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening; it does not approach even a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part. Indeed, it does not even bear comparison. Why is that?

For the qualities of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are born from the Bodhisattva, but Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are not born from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, if all the beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to enter the fixed course of the Bodhisattva,
their merit would not approach even a hundredth part of the merit of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

It does not even bear comparison. Furthermore, if all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were to become those who have set out for enlightenment, their merit would not approach even a hundredth part of the merit of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
it would not approach even a hundred-thousand-billionth part.
It does not even admit of comparison. He asked:
"Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first produced the thought of awakening bring to mind the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first produced the thought of awakening should bring to mind all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). He asked: "Blessed One, what is the essence of all-aspect omniscience? What is its objective support (*ālambana*)? What is its dominant influence (*ādhipateya*)? What is its aspect (*ākāra*)? What is its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? The Blessed One replied:

"Subhūti, omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is a non-entity (*abhāva*); it is without characteristics, without signs, effortless, unarisen, and non-manifest. Furthermore, as for what Subhūti said: 'What is the objective support (*ālambana*) of omniscience?'"
"What is the sovereign power of the knowledge of all aspects, what is its form, and what is its characteristic?
"Subhūti, the non-existence of the knowledge of all aspects is its objective support; mindfulness is its sovereign power."
Quiescence is its aspect;

the absence of characteristics is its characteristic. Subhūti, this is the objective support for the knowledge of all aspects, this is its dominant influence, this is its characteristic, and this is its aspect. He asked:
"Is it then that the knowledge of all aspects itself is non-existence?"
Or rather, is form also non-existence?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also non-existence?
In this way, internal and external phenomena are non-existent.

The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment,
the noble eightfold path, the concentration of emptiness, the concentration of signlessness, the concentration of wishlessness, and the eight liberations.

Are the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the first superknowledge, the second, the third, the fourth, the fifth, and the sixth superknowledge; and even the conditioned realm, the unconditioned realm, and non-existence themselves?

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, form is also non-existence; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also non-existence. Even the conditioned realm is non-existence, and the unconditioned realm is also non-existence. For what reason? Because, Subhūti, the intrinsic nature of omniscience does not exist. Furthermore, Subhūti, that which has no intrinsic nature is indeed non-existence. Subhūti asked:
"For what reason, Blessed One, does the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) not exist?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, there is no composite intrinsic nature. That which has no composite intrinsic nature is a non-entity (*abhāva*). By this...

Subhūti, in one sense, all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature. Moreover, Subhūti, all phenomena have emptiness as their intrinsic nature; all phenomena have the signless as their intrinsic nature; all phenomena have the wishless as their intrinsic nature. Furthermore, Subhūti, [all phenomena] have suchness as their intrinsic nature.

All phenomena have the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as their intrinsic nature; all phenomena have the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as their intrinsic nature; all phenomena [are thus]. By this method also, Subhūti, it should be understood that all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature.
If, Blessed One, all phenomena have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, then by what skill in means is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has first produced the thought of awakening endowed?

Practicing the perfection of generosity, he purifies the Buddha-field and brings sentient beings to maturity. Likewise, practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, he purifies the Buddha-field and brings sentient beings to maturity. Thus it is with the first dhyāna.
Practicing as far as the fourth dhyāna, from loving-kindness up to equanimity;
from the attainment of the sphere of infinite space up to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
In the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the noble eightfold path;
in the concentration of emptiness, the concentration of signlessness, and the concentration of wishlessness;

in the meditative absorptions, the immeasurables, up to the nine successive attainments; in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Practicing in great loving-kindness, great compassion, and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects, he purifies the buddha-field and brings sentient beings to maturity. The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, this very thing should be understood as the skill in means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."

When he cultivates familiarity with phenomena that have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, he purifies a buddha-field and brings sentient beings to maturity; yet he knows that both that buddha-field and those sentient beings have non-existence as their intrinsic nature. Furthermore, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, in the perfection of generosity—
Practicing on the path to awakening, he cultivates familiarity with it.

Practicing in the perfection of ethical discipline, he cultivates familiarity with the path to awakening. Practicing in the perfection of patience, he cultivates familiarity with the path to awakening. Practicing in the perfection of vigor, he cultivates familiarity with the path to awakening.

Practicing the perfection of meditation, he cultivates familiarity with the path to enlightenment. Practicing the perfection of wisdom, he cultivates familiarity with the path to enlightenment. Up to practicing the knowledge of all aspects, he cultivates familiarity with the path to enlightenment, and he knows that very path to enlightenment as having the nature of non-existence. Furthermore, Subhūti, that bodhisattva mahāsattva...

Practicing in the six perfections, he cultivates familiarity on that path of awakening until he is endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata; until he is endowed with the four grounds of self-confidence;
until he is endowed with the four analytical knowledges; and until he is endowed with the unique qualities of a Buddha and great loving-kindness.

And he becomes endowed with great compassion. Subhūti, this is that path of awakening; abiding on this path, one fulfills the perfections. Having fulfilled the perfections, one will attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) through wisdom associated with a single moment. In that state, one will abandon all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanānusandhi*) by means of non-arising abandonment.

Surveying the trichiliocosm with the Buddha-eye, he will not perceive even "non-existence," let alone "existence. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom regarding all phenomena whose intrinsic nature is non-existence. This indeed, Subhūti, is [the way].
The skill in means (*upāyakauśala*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is that he does not perceive even non-existence (*abhāva*), let alone existence (*bhāva*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, when that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he gives a gift; while giving that gift, he does not conceptualize it.

He does not take it as a sign, nor does he attend to it as either existent or non-existent. He does not conceptualize the recipient, does not take them as a sign, nor does he attend to them as either existent or non-existent. He does not conceptualize the giver, does not take them as a sign, nor does he attend to them as either existent or non-existent. That very mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*)...

He does not apprehend it; he does not take it as a sign, nor does he take it as an object. He does not perceive it... up to... he does not conceptualize the perfection of wisdom, nor does he take it as a sign.
One does not attend to it as either existent or non-existent. Even that perfection of wisdom which one cultivates, one does not perceive it, nor does one take it as a sign;
one does not attend to it as either existent or non-existent.
Furthermore, for the sake of those beings he cultivates that perfection of wisdom, yet he does not conceptualize it, nor does he take it as a sign;
he attends to it neither as an existence nor as a non-existence. Why is that?

Because if all those dharmas are indeed non-existent, they were not made by the Buddhas, nor by the Śrāvakas, nor by the Pratyekabuddhas. For all dharmas are without an agent, being devoid of an agent.
"But, Blessed One, are phenomena indeed devoid of phenomena?
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Phenomena are indeed devoid of phenomena. He said:
If, Blessed One, phenomena are indeed devoid of phenomena, then how can a phenomenon that is devoid [of itself] perceive a phenomenon that is devoid [of itself],
as either "existence" or "non-existence"? For, Blessed One, a phenomenon that is non-existent does not know a phenomenon that is non-existent.
An existent phenomenon does not know a non-existent phenomenon; a non-existent phenomenon does not know a non-existent phenomenon;

an existent phenomenon does not know an existent phenomenon. Since there is thus no such cognition regarding all phenomena, how could there arise for a bodhisattva mahāsattva the notion that something is "existent" or "non-existent"?
The Blessed One said: "Relying upon worldly convention, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, designates it as either 'existence' or 'non-existence.'"
But not from the perspective of ultimate truth. He asked:
"But, Blessed One, is conventional reality one thing and ultimate truth another?
The Blessed One replied:
Subhūti, the worldly convention is not one thing and the ultimate truth another. That which is the suchness of the worldly convention is itself the suchness of the ultimate truth.

Yet those beings, being perverted, do not know and do not see this suchness. For their sake, the bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches by way of worldly convention, speaking of "existence" or "non-existence. Furthermore, Subhūti, those beings who perceive existence within the five aggregates do not know non-existence. It is for their sake that he thus [teaches].
"Based on the non-differentiation of phenomena,
how could they know them as non-existent? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom."
Chapter 65. Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"The 'bodhisattva practice,' the 'bodhisattva practice'—it is so called."
"What is the designation for what is called 'the conduct of a bodhisattva'?
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, it is called 'the conduct of a bodhisattva,' 'the conduct of a bodhisattva,' because this is the conduct for the sake of awakening; therefore it is called 'the conduct of a bodhisattva. Subhūti said:
"Where, Blessed One, does the course of the bodhisattva mahāsattva proceed?
The Blessed One said:

"He courses with the thought that 'form is empty. He courses with the thought that 'feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty. Thus, with respect to internal and external [phenomena]..."
By means of the sense bases, he practices the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor,

the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. He practices in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, and the emptiness of the ultimate truth.

He courses in the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of all phenomena;
he courses in the emptiness of specific characteristics. He courses in the emptiness of non-apprehension and the emptiness of non-existence.
He courses in the emptiness of self-nature and the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.

He courses in the first dhyāna; he courses in the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; he courses in loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). He courses in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). He courses in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

He courses in the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. He courses in the concentration of emptiness, he courses in the concentration of signlessness, and he courses in the concentration of wishlessness. He courses in the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments. [He courses] in the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

He practices. He practices in the four grounds of self-confidence, in the four analytical knowledges, in great loving-kindness, in great compassion, and in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He practices for the sake of purifying the buddha-field; he practices for the sake of maturing sentient beings. He practices in eloquence, he practices in the production of syllables, he practices in the entry into syllables, and in the entry into the syllable-less.

He courses [in them]. He courses in the dhāraṇīs; he courses in the conditioned realm; he courses in the unconditioned realm. Furthermore, he courses in such a way that the intellect does not become dualistic. It is in this manner, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, courses in awakening. Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, it is said, 'Buddha, Buddha. Of what is this a designation, 'Buddha'?
The Blessed One said:
"The realized reality (*bhūtārtha*) is called 'Buddha. Moreover, Subhūti, by him the true Dharma has been fully awakened to."

Therefore he is called "Buddha. Because the true reality has been realized by him, therefore he is called "Buddha. Furthermore, Subhūti, because all dharmas have been understood by him as they truly are, therefore he is called "Buddha. Subhūti said: "O Blessed One, 'enlightenment, enlightenment' is what is spoken of."
"Blessed One, of what is this a designation: 'awakening'?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, 'awakening' is a designation for emptiness."
This is a designation for suchness, this is a designation for the limit of reality,
this is a designation for the realm of phenomena. Furthermore, Subhūti, "awakening" is suchness, it is non-falsity.
It is the suchness that is not other, the state of being not otherwise;

therefore it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*). Furthermore, Subhūti, this which is called "awakening" is merely a name and a sign; therefore it is called "awakening. Furthermore, Subhūti, the meaning of awakening is the meaning of non-differentiation. Furthermore, Subhūti, this is the awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Therefore, it is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*). Moreover, Subhūti, this has been perfectly awakened to by the Blessed Buddhas;
therefore, it is called "enlightenment. He said:
"Blessed One, as for that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses here toward enlightenment..."
Does he practice by means of the six perfections, up to dwelling in the knowledge of all aspects?
O Blessed One, for which of these roots of virtue is there accumulation or diminution, decrease or increase, arising or cessation, defilement or purification?
The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, for that bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses here in this awakening, who courses in the six perfections, and so on up to coursing in the knowledge of all aspects— for him there is no accumulation or diminution of any dharma whatsoever, nor decrease or increase, nor arising or cessation, nor defilement or purification. Why is that?

For indeed, Subhūti, the awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not appear through the application of an objective referent (*ālambana*) to any dharma—whether for its accumulation or diminution, its decrease or increase, its arising or cessation, or its defilement or purification. Subhūti said:

"If, Blessed One, the awakening of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not appear through the application of an objective referent to any dharma, then how [is it so]?"

Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva embrace the perfection of generosity? How does he embrace the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom?
How does he practice in internal emptiness; how does he practice in external emptiness, in internal-and-external emptiness, and so on up to the emptiness of specific characteristics?

How does he practice in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and so on up to the successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*)?

He practices. How does he practice in the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness? How does he practice in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, in the four grounds of self-confidence, in the four analytical knowledges, in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and in great loving-kindness and great compassion? How does he practice in the ten bodhisattva stages, [and transcend] the stage of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
He transcends [the world] and enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva.

The Blessed One said: "Indeed not, Subhūti; the intellect of a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not operate in duality. Indeed not, Subhūti; a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the perfection of giving through duality. Not through duality..."

He practices the perfection of ethical discipline without duality; he practices the perfection of patience without duality; he practices the perfection of vigor without duality; he practices the perfection of meditative concentration without duality. Without duality...

He courses in the perfection of wisdom. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva takes hold of the perfection of giving, up to taking hold of the perfection of wisdom, until he attains the knowledge of all aspects. He said:
"If, Blessed One, one does not course in the perfection of giving by means of duality,"

He does not course in the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom by means of duality.
How then, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva increase his roots of goodness from the first production of the thought of awakening until the final production of the thought of awakening?
The Blessed One said:
Subhūti, those who course in duality do not increase in their roots of virtue. Why is that?
Subhūti, it is because all foolish common people rely upon duality.
They do not increase in their roots of virtue. A bodhisattva mahāsattva, however, courses in non-duality;

from the first production of the thought of awakening, he increases in roots of virtue, and so on until his final production of the thought of awakening, he increases in roots of virtue. Therefore, he cannot be overcome by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
If he were crushed by those unwholesome roots such that he would fall to the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha,
or if he were overcome by other unwholesome dharmas—
being so overcome, he would not increase in wholesome roots while practicing the perfection of generosity.

As long as one practicing for the sake of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) does not increase through roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Subhūti asked: "But, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of roots of goodness? The Blessed One replied:
Indeed it is not so, Subhūti;
a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of wholesome roots,
nor does he practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of unwholesome roots.

And it is not possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to attain all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) without having attended upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, without having fulfilled the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), and without being sustained by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). He asked:

"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having attended upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, being sustained by the roots of virtue, and being sustained by spiritual friends, attain all-aspect omniscience?"

The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, from the first production of the thought of awakening, attends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and [hears] whatever those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, speak."

He masters all of it—the discourses (*sūtra*), songs (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), inspired utterances (*udāna*), introductory narratives (*nidāna*), legends (*ityuktaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), expanded teachings (*vaipulya*), marvelous qualities (*adbhutadharma*), and accounts of past deeds (*apadāna*); having mastered them, he makes them thoroughly familiar through speech, reflects upon them with the mind, and penetrates them well through insight, thereby attaining the *dhāraṇī*. Through the attainment of this *dhāraṇī*, he [attains] the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

He generates them. Once these analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) have been generated, even when he has passed through various births, those qualities never perish until he attains the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, being sustained by those roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) toward the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, he is never reborn in the miserable states or in the unfavorable conditions (*akṣaṇa*). And by means of those roots of virtue, he grasps the purification of the basis (*āśrayapariśuddhi*).
By means of those bases through which he purifies the buddha-field and brings sentient beings to maturity,
and being embraced by those roots of virtue, he is never separated from spiritual friends,
nor from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and the śrāvakas who belong to the Buddha-vehicle.

They speak in various ways. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should attend upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, plant roots of merit, and cultivate spiritual friends. ((65)) [f. 258b]
(AdSPG I 173) Chapter 66.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
Furthermore, Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attend upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; does not fulfill the roots of virtue; and is not sustained by spiritual friends;
"Could it be that a bodhisattva mahāsattva would attain all-aspect omniscience?

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva who, without having attended upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, without having fulfilled the roots of virtue, and without being sustained by spiritual friends, could attain all-aspect omniscience."
For what reason?

Even after having attended upon the Buddhas, planted roots of merit, and served spiritual friends, one is still unable to attain all-aspect omniscience; how much less so without having attended upon the Buddha Bhagavāns?

It is impossible that one could attain the knowledge of all aspects without having fulfilled the roots of virtue and without having attended upon spiritual friends. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to reach the culmination of awakening,
and who wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, should attend upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, plant roots of virtue, and attend upon spiritual friends.

"For what reason, Blessed One, does the Blessed One say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having attended upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having planted roots of merit, and having served spiritual friends, does not [attain] omniscience?
Because of being devoid of skill in means."
Thus, he has not heard this skillful means from those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
nor has he planted those roots of virtue; nor has he attended upon those spiritual friends who teach him this skillful means. He said:
“Blessed One, what is that skill in means endowed with which a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the knowledge of all aspects?
The Blessed One said:

“In this regard, Subhūti, from the first production of the thought of awakening onwards, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of generosity, gives gifts with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects.”
[He gives] to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; to the Pratyekabuddhas; to the Śrāvakas; to those who have become human beings; and to those who have not become human beings.

Endowed with those mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects, he does not form the notion of a gift regarding his giving, nor does he form the notion of a recipient regarding the recipient.
There is no perception of a donor in the donor. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, he knows all phenomena to be empty of their own specific characteristics; he sees all phenomena as non-existent, unproduced, unaccomplished, and unarisen. And he penetrates the characteristic of phenomena as being incapable of performing any function whatsoever.
He enters into all phenomena by way of their characteristic of being unconditioned. Endowed with this skill in means, he increases in roots of goodness;
increasing in roots of goodness, he practices the perfection of generosity.
While practicing the perfection of generosity, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-field. Not...

And he does not hope for the fruit of giving—that fruit of giving which one might enjoy within saṃsāra—except for the sake of protecting sentient beings and for the sake of liberating sentient beings; thus he practices the perfection of giving. This is the chapter on the Instruction in Skillful Means. ((66)) (AdSPG I 175)
Reversal 67.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), from the first production of the thought of awakening (prathamacittotpāda) onward, maintains ethical discipline with mental attentions (manasikāra) associated with the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). For him, there is no passion at all.
It does not obscure the mind— neither affliction nor delusion, neither latent tendencies nor outbursts, nor any other unwholesome states that act as obstacles to awakening,
such as stinginess, immorality, a disturbed mind, a lazy mind, or inferiority.
Whether it be a mind of vigor, a distracted mind, a mind of faulty wisdom, pride, contempt, overweening pride, the pride of "I am," or the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Why is that?
Because he knows all phenomena to be empty of their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-śūnya).

He perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unarisen, unperfected, and unproduced. He penetrates the true nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), realizing that all phenomena are incapable of performing any function; thus he penetrates them by way of their unconditioned characteristic (*asaṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
Endowed with this skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), he increases in roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*). As he increases in roots of virtue, he...

He practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). While practicing the perfection of ethical discipline, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-field. Yet he does not long for the fruit of ethical discipline—that fruit of ethical discipline which might be enjoyed within cyclic existence—except for the sake of protecting sentient beings and bringing them to maturity; it is for this purpose that he practices the perfection of ethical discipline.
(AdSPG I 176) Chapter 68.
In this same way, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation are to be practiced. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva...

When a Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, from the first production of the thought of awakening onward, he cultivates wisdom through mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects. His mind is not obscured by passion, nor by hatred, and so on, up to the mind of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha. Why is that?

For in this way, Subhūti, he knows all phenomena to be empty of their own specific characteristics; he perceives all phenomena as non-existent, unproduced, unperfected, and unarisen. He penetrates the characteristic of phenomena, realizing that "all phenomena are nothing and lack any efficacy," thus penetrating them by way of the characteristic of the unconditioned. Endowed with this skill in means, he [proceeds].
He increases by means of the roots of goodness; increasing by means of the roots of goodness, he courses in the perfection of wisdom.

Coursing in the perfection of wisdom, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the Buddha-field. Yet he does not desire the fruit of wisdom—that fruit of wisdom which one might enjoy within saṃsāra—except for the sake of protecting sentient beings and for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
He practices the perfection of wisdom.
((68)) Chapter 69.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the first dhyāna, up to entering the fourth dhyāna;
he enters loving-kindness, up to equanimity;

he enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite space, up to entering the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. And yet, he does not grasp at the maturation [of these results]. Why is that?

For he is endowed with skill in means, by which skill in means he knows those meditative concentrations, immeasurables, and formless attainments to be empty of their own characteristics, and so on, up to knowing them to be unproduced. Furthermore, Subhūti,
from the first production of the thought of awakening, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, endowed with skill in means, courses in the path that is to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
And he does not attain the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor does he attain arhatship. Why is that?

Because he knows all phenomena to be empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnya*), up to knowing them as unproduced (*anabhinirvṛtta*). And while practicing within those factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣika-dharma*), he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. This, Subhūti, is...

This is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), he enters the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) and enters the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), yet he does not realize the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), nor does he realize anything up to arhatship. That...
For what reason?

Because he knows all phenomena to be empty of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnya*), up to knowing all phenomena to be unproduced (*anabhinirvṛtta*). Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates familiarity with the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

He cultivates familiarity with the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, and great compassion. Yet he does not attain the knowledge of all aspects until his buddha-field has been purified and sentient beings have been brought to maturity. Thus it is, Subhūti.
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom. He said:
"O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is indeed possessed of supreme intelligence who practices in such profound dharmas and yet does not grasp at their maturation. The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in such profound dharmas is possessed of supreme intelligence, and yet he does not grasp at their maturation. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not deviate from intrinsic nature. Subhūti said:
"From what does it not deviate by way of its own-being?
The Blessed One said:
"It does not deviate from non-existence. Furthermore, as for what Subhūti has said:
From what does it not deviate from its intrinsic nature?
It does not deviate from the intrinsic nature of form;
it does not deviate from the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
He does not deviate from the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity; he does not deviate from the intrinsic nature of the perfection of ethical discipline;
he does not deviate from the intrinsic nature of the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.

He does not waver from the intrinsic nature of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); he does not waver from the intrinsic nature of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); he does not waver from the intrinsic nature of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). He does not waver from the intrinsic nature of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), up to and including the intrinsic nature of the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

[He does not waver] from the intrinsic nature of the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the concentration on the signless (*ānimitta-samādhi*), and the concentration on the wishless (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).

It does not waver from the intrinsic nature of the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments; it does not waver from the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to and including the intrinsic nature of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. It does not waver from the intrinsic nature of great loving-kindness and great compassion. For what reason?

For it is thus, Subhūti: that which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these phenomena is non-existence (*abhāva*). Indeed, Subhūti, it is not possible for non-existence to be fully awakened to by means of non-existence. He asked:
"But, Blessed One, is it possible for existence to be fully awakened to by means of existence?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He asked:
"Is it possible to fully awaken to existence by means of non-existence?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He asked:
"Is it possible to fully awaken to non-existence by means of non-existence?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He asked:
"Is it possible to fully awaken to non-existence by means of existence?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti. He said:
"In that case, Blessed One, would there be neither attainment nor realization?

If there is no realization of non-existence by means of non-existence, no realization of existence by means of existence, no realization of existence by means of non-existence, and no realization of non-existence by means of existence? The Blessed One [replied]:
"There is realization, but not by means of this fourfold production. He asked:
"In what way, then, O Blessed One, is there realization?"

The Blessed One said: "That which is neither existence nor non-existence is such a realization (*abhisamaya*) wherein these conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) do not exist; it is a realization that is non-proliferated and free from proliferation. He asked:
"But what, Blessed One, is the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied:
"To think that form (*rūpa*) is permanent or impermanent is the conceptual proliferation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. [The same applies to] feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

"Permanent" or "impermanent"—this is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). "Form is pleasure" or "form is suffering"—this is conceptual proliferation. "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pleasure" or "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering"—this is conceptual proliferation. "Form is self" or "form is not-self"—this is conceptual proliferation. "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are self" or "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not-self"—this is conceptual proliferation.

Or, "form is peaceful" or "it is not peaceful" is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). "Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are peaceful" or "they are not peaceful" is conceptual proliferation. "Form is to be fully understood" or "it is not to be fully understood" is conceptual proliferation.
[The same applies to] feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

To say "it is to be fully understood" or "it is not to be fully understood" is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). To say "the noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood" is conceptual proliferation;
to say "the origin is to be abandoned" is conceptual proliferation; to say "cessation is to be realized" is conceptual proliferation.
"The path is to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation. "The four dhyānas are to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation.

"The four immeasurables are to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation. "The four formless attainments are to be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation. "I shall cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts" is conceptual proliferation.

"The four bases of psychic power are to be cultivated"—this is conceptual proliferation. Likewise, "the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path are to be cultivated"—this is conceptual proliferation. "The gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness are to be cultivated"—this is conceptual proliferation. [So too are] the eight liberations and the nine successive attainments.
"To be cultivated" is conceptual proliferation;
"I shall transcend the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship" is conceptual proliferation;
"I shall transcend the stage of a pratyekabuddha" is conceptual proliferation; "I shall fulfill the ten bodhisattva stages" is conceptual proliferation.
Thus, "I shall enter the bodhisattva's certainty" is conceptual proliferation; "I shall purify the buddha-field" is conceptual proliferation;
"I shall bring sentient beings to maturity" is conceptual proliferation; "I shall produce the ten powers of a Tathāgata" is conceptual proliferation.

"To produce the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha" is conceptual proliferation. "I shall attain the knowledge of all aspects" is conceptual proliferation. "I shall abandon the afflictions along with all their habitual tendencies and residual impressions" is conceptual proliferation. Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom...
Not proliferating [the concepts] "form is permanent" or "form is impermanent," he does not proliferate;

not proliferating [the concepts] "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent" or "they are impermanent," he does not proliferate... not proliferating [the concepts] "it is permanent" or "it is impermanent," he does not proliferate, until he shall attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Thus, not proliferating conceptual elaborations (*prapañca*), he does not engage in proliferation. Thinking, "I shall abandon all afflictions along with their underlying tendencies and habitual traces," he does not engage in proliferation. Why is that?

For intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not proliferate intrinsic nature. Non-existence (*abhāva*) does not proliferate non-existence. Furthermore, apart from intrinsic nature and non-existence, no other phenomenon (*dharma*) is perceived.

That which would proliferate, that by which one would proliferate, or that wherein one would proliferate—therefore, Subhūti, form is free from proliferation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are free from proliferation; even up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is free from proliferation. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should train] in the perfection of wisdom, which is free from proliferation.

One must practice in this way. Furthermore, Subhūti, there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form; there is no intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; indeed, there is no intrinsic nature of anything up to and including the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
That which has no intrinsic nature is beyond conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). For this reason, Subhūti, it is beyond conceptual proliferation.

Form is free from conceptual proliferation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are free from conceptual proliferation. Up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is free from conceptual proliferation. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva. He said:
“Blessed One, if no intrinsic nature of any dharma is apprehended, by which path does a bodhisattva mahāsattva enter the bodhisattva’s determination (nyāma)—
by the path of the śrāvaka, or the path of the pratyekabuddha, or the path of the Buddha? The Blessed One replied:

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not enter the bodhisattva’s fixed course by way of the path of the śrāvaka, nor by way of the path of the pratyekabuddha, nor by way of the path of the Buddha. Rather, Subhūti, it is after training in all paths that a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the bodhisattva’s fixed course. It is just as, for example, the person on the eighth stage [the *aṣṭamaka*] [enters the stream] by way of all paths.
Having trained, he enters the certainty of rightness (*samyaktvanyāma*). Yet, he does not attain the fruit as long as he has not produced the path to that fruit;

in the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having produced all paths, enters the certainty of a bodhisattva. And he does not attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as long as the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) has not been attained.
It occurs. Through the attainment of that samādhi, by means of wisdom conjoined with a single moment, he attains the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). He said:

"If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must enter the bodhisattva-determination after having fulfilled all paths, then, Blessed One, is not the path of the eighth-rank practitioner (*aṣṭamaka*) one thing, that of the stream-enterer (*srotaāpanna*) another, and that for the sake of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) yet another?"

The path of one who has entered the first stage is different from that of a once-returner; the path of one who has entered the stage of non-returning is different from that of a non-returner; the path of one who has entered the stage of arhatship is different from that of an arhat; the path of a pratyekabuddha is different from that of a tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly awakened buddha. If, Blessed One, the paths of these are distinct, [how can they all be called the "one vehicle" (ekayāna)?]
How then should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fulfilled all paths, enter the bodhisattva-niyāma? If, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must fulfill all paths,
then, Blessed One, let it not be that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having produced the path of the eighth person, becomes an eighth person.
Having generated the path of seeing, one would become a stream-enterer;

having generated the path of cultivation, one would become a candidate for the fruit of once-returning. One would become a once-returner, a candidate for the fruit of non-returning, a non-returner, and a candidate for the fruit of arhatship.

He might become an Arhat after generating the path of a Pratyekabuddha, or he might become a Pratyekabuddha; yet, Blessed One, it is impossible and out of the question that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having become one of the eighth stage, would enter the fixed course of a Bodhisattva.
It is impossible that one who has not entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva could attain all-knowledge;

such a thing is impossible. Likewise, it is impossible [that one could attain all-knowledge] after having attained the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, without first entering the fixed course of a bodhisattva.

It is impossible that one who has not entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva should attain all-aspect omniscience; such a thing cannot exist. Therefore, Blessed One, how should we understand it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fulfilled all paths, enters the fixed course of a bodhisattva?
"Having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, one attains the knowledge of all aspects and abandons even the continuity of all habitual tendencies.
The Blessed One said, "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. It is impossible, Subhūti, it is out of the question that a bodhisattva mahāsattva..."

It is impossible that one who has become a srotāpanna, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, and having likewise attained up to arhatship, and having attained pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, should enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva—this cannot happen. It is impossible that one who has not entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva should attain the knowledge of all aspects—this cannot happen. However, Subhūti, [it is otherwise].

From the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing in the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), transcends eight stages (*bhūmi*) by means of knowledge and vision. What are the eight?

They are: the stage of bright insight (*śuklavidarśanabhūmi*), the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the stage of the eighth person (*aṣṭamakabhūmi*), the stage of vision (*darśanabhūmi*), the stage of refinement (*tanubhūmi*), and the stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāgabhūmi*).

The stage of one who has accomplished what was to be done (*kṛtāvībhūmi*) is the stage of the Pratyekabuddha. Having thus transcended these eight stages by means of knowledge and vision, he enters the Bodhisattva’s determination (*nyāma*) through the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).

Having entered the Bodhisattva’s determination, by means of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*), [he abandons] all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies (*sarvavāsanānusandhikleśa*).
He abandons them. In this regard, Subhūti, that which is the knowledge of the eighth-rank practitioner is the patience of the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
that which is both the knowledge and the abandonment of the stream-enterer is the patience of the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
that which is both the knowledge and the abandonment of the once-returner is the patience of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. That which...
The knowledge and abandonment of a non-returner is the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; the knowledge and abandonment of an arhat is the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
the knowledge and abandonment of a pratyekabuddha is the patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Thus, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fulfilled the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enters the bodhisattva’s certainty by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatājñāna*). Having entered the bodhisattva’s certainty, he abandons all afflictions along with their residual impressions and latencies (*sarvavāsanānusandhikleśa*) by means of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatājñāna*). In this way, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fulfilled all paths, [attains] the unsurpassed...
Having fully awakened to perfect enlightenment, one becomes the source of sustenance for the fruits of all sentient beings. He said:
"Blessed One, as for these paths—the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha—"
"In that regard, Blessed One, what is the path of the knowledge of the aspects of the path?
The Blessed One said:

"In this case, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must generate the purification of the knowledge of the aspects of the path. In this regard, Subhūti, this is the purification of the knowledge of the aspects of the path:"
By whatever aspects, by whatever marks, and by whatever signs the path is indicated— therein those aspects, those marks,
and those signs must be fully awakened to by the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
having fully awakened to them, they must be declared to others, taught, and revealed.
They are to be made known and established so that another may understand for the sake of training them;
therein, by the bodhisattva mahāsattva, all sounds, conventions, and vocal expressions [are to be employed].

They must be proclaimed and maintained, so that by means of them—just as an echo is understood through the sense of being a mere cognition—one may make known the entire trichiliocosm. Therefore, Subhūti, by this method also, a bodhisattva mahāsattva must fulfill all paths; having fulfilled the knowledge of the aspects of the path, he must understand the dispositions of sentient beings.
The path of beings in the hells must be known, their cause must be known, and their fruit must be known;

and then those in the hells must be turned away from the path, turned away from the cause, and turned away from the fruit; those in the animal realm must be turned away from the path, turned away from the cause, and turned away from the fruit.
Those belonging to the realm of Yama must be turned away from the path, turned away from the cause, and turned away from the fruit.

The path of the *kiṃnaras*, *mahoragas*, *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, and humans must be known; their cause must be known; their fruit must be known. The path of the gods must be known; their cause must be known; their fruit must be known. [The path] of the *brahmans*...

The path must be known, the cause must be known, and the fruit must be known. The path of the Ābhāsvara gods must be known, their cause must be known, and their fruit must be known. The path of the Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha gods must be known, as well as their cause.

The fruit must be known. The path of the gods of the sphere of infinite space must be known; its cause must be known; its fruit must be known. This continues up to the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: their path must be known; their cause must be known;
their fruit must be known. The four foundations of mindfulness must be known; the four right efforts [must be known].

The four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment are to be known; likewise, the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are to be known; and the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four [assurances] are to be known.

The grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*) are to be known; the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are to be known; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are to be known;

great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) is to be known; and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is to be known. Furthermore, by whichever paths those beings who are to be established in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpatti-phala*) are to be established, he establishes them in the fruit of stream-entry; likewise for all up to those who are to be established in arhatship (*arhattva*).

He establishes them in arhatship. Those who are to be established in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, he establishes them in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment. Those who are to be established in [unsurpassed] enlightenment, he establishes them in enlightenment. This, Subhūti, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge of the aspects of the path, in which the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained, [attains his goal].

He penetrates the dispositions of sentient beings. Having penetrated the dispositions of sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma accordingly. And that teaching of the Dharma by him becomes neither deficient nor in vain. Why is that?
Because in this way his faculties have been manifested for others. He [knows] the going and the coming of sentient beings...

And he understands both passing away and rebirth. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course in the perfection of wisdom. Within this perfection of wisdom, all paths are included—whatever factors conducive to awakening there are, in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva should course, or in which śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas should course. He said:

If, Blessed One, both the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣika-dharma*) and awakening itself—all these phenomena—are neither conjoined nor disjoined, formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being characterless; how then, Blessed One, do the factors conducive to awakening bring about awakening? For indeed, Blessed One, that which is neither conjoined nor disjoined [cannot be a cause].
Formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and having a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being characterless—a dharma does not bring about or take away any other dharma.

Just as, Blessed One, space does not bring about or take away any dharma, even so, Blessed One, a dharma that is empty of its own characteristic does not bring about or take away any other dharma. The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. Subhūti, a phenomenon that is empty of its own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa-śūnya) is neither a bringer nor a taker of any phenomenon whatsoever. However, Subhūti, for the sake of those beings who do not know that phenomena are empty of their own specific characteristics, it is taught thus: 'These factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣika-dharma) lead toward awakening.'"

Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is form, and that which is feeling, and that which is perception, and those which are mental formations, and that which is consciousness; and that which is the perfection of generosity, and that which is the perfection of ethical discipline,

and that which is the perfection of patience, and that which is the perfection of vigor, and that which is the perfection of meditative concentration, and that which is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is internal emptiness— [all these are non-dual].

And external emptiness, up to and including self-characteristic emptiness; and the first dhyāna, up to and including the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and the four foundations of mindfulness, up to and including the noble eightfold path; and the three gateways to liberation, up to and including the eight liberations, and up to and including the nine successive meditative attainments.

Furthermore, whatever there is— from the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, up to great loving-kindness, great compassion, and even omniscience—
all these dharmas in this noble Dharma and Vinaya are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, and non-obstructive.

They have a single characteristic, namely, the characteristicless. Furthermore, Subhūti, these have been spoken by the Tathāgata merely for the sake of introducing sentient beings [to the truth] through worldly convention, and not according to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train everywhere in both knowledge and vision.

Having trained in knowledge and vision, some phenomena are to be penetrated, while other phenomena are not to be penetrated. Which are the phenomena that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in knowledge and vision, should penetrate?
And which are the phenomena that, having trained in knowledge and vision, should not be penetrated?
Having trained in the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one should not penetrate them through [limited] knowledge and vision;

rather, all dharmas in all their aspects should be penetrated by means of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatājñāna). It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom within the noble Dharma and Vinaya. He said:
“Noble Dharma and Vinaya, noble Dharma and Vinaya,” it is said, O Blessed One. To what extent, O Blessed One, is it called “noble Dharma and Vinaya”?
The Blessed One said:
“In this regard, Subhūti, the disciples, the pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, and the Tathāgatas, Arhats...”

The perfectly awakened ones are neither conjoined nor disjoined with passion; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with hatred; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with delusion; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the view of a self-identity; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with doubt; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the adherence to rites and rituals; [they are neither conjoined nor disjoined] with sensual desire and ill will.
They are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with attachment to the realm of form or the formless realm; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with ignorance;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with mental restlessness; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the first dhyāna, up to the fourth dhyāna; [and] with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

They are neither conjoined nor disjoined with compassion; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with sympathetic joy; they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with equanimity; up to: they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the four foundations of mindfulness.
Insofar as they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with great loving-kindness and great compassion;

neither conjoined nor disjoined with the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), nor conjoined nor disjoined with the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*); for that reason they are called "Noble Ones" (*ārya*). And this is their Dharma and their Vinaya.
Therefore, it is called the Noble Dharma and Vinaya. Why is that?

Because all those phenomena are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics. Being formless, they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with what is formless;
being invisible, they are neither conjoined nor disjoined with what is invisible.
Non-resistant things are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the non-resistant;

signless things are neither conjoined nor disjoined with the signless. Subhūti, this is the perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas—formless, invisible, non-resistant, characterized by a single characteristic, and signless—in which...
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way, such that having trained therein, he does not perceive the characteristic of any dharma whatsoever. Subhūti said:
"Furthermore, Blessed One, one should not train in the characteristic of form."

One should not train in the characteristic of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. One should not train in the characteristic of the eye, nor indeed up to the characteristic of the mind;
one should not train in the characteristics of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena;
nor should one train in the characteristics of the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, or the consciousness element.
One should not train in the characteristic of the perfection of generosity;

one should not train in the characteristic of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom; one should not train in the characteristic of internal emptiness, up to and including the characteristic of the emptiness of self-characteristic.
One should not train in the characteristic of the first dhyāna, nor should one train in the characteristics up to the fourth dhyāna;

one should not train in the characteristic of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), nor should one train in the characteristics up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);
one should not train in the characteristic of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), nor should one train in the characteristics up to the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
One should train;
one should not train in the characteristic of the concentration of emptiness, nor of the concentration of signlessness, nor of the concentration of wishlessness;
one should not train in the characteristic of the liberations, nor of the successive attainments.
One should not train in the characteristics of the ten powers, nor of the four fearlessnesses, nor of the four analytical knowledges, nor of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

one should not train in the characteristic of great loving-kindness, nor of great compassion; one should not train in the characteristic of the noble truth of suffering, nor train in the characteristic of its origin, nor train in the characteristic of its cessation, nor train in the characteristic of the path, nor train in the characteristic of the noble ones, nor in the characteristic of dependent origination in its forward and reverse order.

"One should not train in the characteristic of the conditioned realm, nor should one train in the characteristic of the unconditioned realm. If, Blessed One, one should not even train in these characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), how, Blessed One, can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, without having trained, transcend the stage of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas regarding the characteristics of all phenomena and the characteristics of conditioned formations? Without transcending the stage of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas..."
How will he enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva?
Without entering the fixed course of a bodhisattva, how will he attain the knowledge of all aspects?
Without attaining the knowledge of all aspects, how will he turn the wheel of Dharma?
Without having set the wheel of Dharma in motion, how will he liberate sentient beings from saṃsāra—
whether by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna?
The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, if there were a characteristic of any dharma, then a bodhisattva mahāsattva would have to train in those characteristics. However, Subhūti, since all dharmas are without characteristics, formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic— namely, the absence of characteristics— therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not [train] in characteristics at all.
One should not train in the absence of marks. For what reason?
Because it is not the case that things were previously without marks and later came to possess marks; for this reason...

Subhūti, these dharmas were without characteristics in the past and they are without characteristics now; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train neither in the characteristic nor in the absence of a characteristic. Why is that?
Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this realm of the absence of characteristics remains ever established. Subhūti said:
If, Blessed One, all dharmas are without characteristics and not of different characteristics,
how then will there be the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
For, Blessed One, without having cultivated the perfection of wisdom, it is not possible for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to transcend the level of the śrāvaka or the level of the pratyekabuddha.
Without transcending the level of the śrāvaka and the level of the pratyekabuddha, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable to enter the bodhisattva’s fixed course;
without entering the bodhisattva’s fixed course, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable to produce the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena;
and without producing the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, one is unable to produce the superknowledges.
A bodhisattva cannot purify a buddha-field or bring sentient beings to maturity without the higher knowledges (*abhijñā*).
Without purifying the buddha-field and bringing sentient beings to maturity, one cannot attain the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Without attaining the knowledge of all aspects, one cannot turn the wheel of Dharma.

Without setting the wheel of Dharma in motion, it is not possible to establish sentient beings in the fruit of stream-entry, nor in the fruit of once-returning, nor in the fruit of non-returning, nor in arhatship, nor in pratyekabuddha-enlightenment;

nor is it possible to establish sentient beings in the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, nor to establish them in the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline or that consisting of cultivation. The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. All dharmas, Subhūti, are without marks (*alakṣaṇa*); they are not of different marks. Subhūti asked: "How then does the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-bhāvanā*) occur with respect to dharmas that are without marks? The Blessed One said:
