"Subhūti, the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither of different marks nor of a single mark. Subhūti, the cultivation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the cultivation of the absence of marks (*alakṣaṇa-bhāvanā*)."
The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. He asked:
"In what way does the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom become signless?
The Blessed One said:
The cultivation of the non-conceptualization of all phenomena is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. He asked:
"In what way, Blessed One, is there the non-conceptualization of all phenomena?
The Blessed One replied:

The cultivation of the dissolution of form is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the dissolution of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the dissolution of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation of the dissolution of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the dissolution of accumulation is [the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom].

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the elimination and non-conceptualization [of phenomena]. The cultivation of the elimination and non-conceptualization of the first dhyāna is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the elimination and non-conceptualization of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the elimination and non-conceptualization of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. [Likewise is] the cultivation of the elimination and non-conceptualization of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-contemplation of the sphere of infinite space. The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-contemplation of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-contemplation of the recollection of the Buddha.

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-contemplation of the recollection of the Dharma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of ethical discipline, the recollection of renunciation, the recollection of the deities, the recollection of disenchantment, the recollection of mindfulness of breathing, the recollection of death, and the recollection directed toward the body.

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the thorough elimination of the perception of permanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of self, and the perception of purity.

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the thorough elimination of dependent origination. The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the thorough elimination of the perception of a self, the perception of a sentient being, the perception of a living soul, the perception of a person, the perception of a human, and the perception of a man.

The cultivation of the non-cultivation of the notion of a nourisher (*poṣa*), the notion of a person (*pudgala*), the notion of an agent (*kāraka*), and the notion of an instigator (*kārapaka*) is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The cultivation of the non-cultivation of the notion of permanence, the notion of pleasure, the notion of purity, and the notion of self is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.

The cultivation of the analytical meditation on the foundations of mindfulness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the analytical meditation on the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the analytical meditation on the concentration of emptiness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the analytical meditation on the concentration of signlessness and the concentration of wishlessness is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the analytical meditation on the eight liberations is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the analytical meditation on the nine successive attainments...

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the analytical discernment of the concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; it is the cultivation of the analytical discernment of the concentration with no applied thought and only sustained thought; it is the cultivation of the analytical discernment of the concentration with neither applied nor sustained thought. It is the cultivation of the analytical discernment of the noble truth of suffering; it is the cultivation of the analytical discernment of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-conceptualization of the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-conceptualization of the knowledge of exhaustion. It is the cultivation of the non-conceptualization of the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, analytical knowledge, and knowledge of things as they truly are.

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-cultivation of the perfection of generosity. The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-cultivation of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, and the emptiness of the ultimate truth.

The cultivation of the non-cultivation of conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, emptiness without beginning or end, emptiness of non-dispersal, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of existence, emptiness of self-nature, and emptiness of the self-nature of existence is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the non-cultivation of the ten powers of a Tathāgata is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. The cultivation of the non-cultivation of the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha [is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom].

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-cultivation of great loving-kindness and great compassion. The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-cultivation of the fruit of stream-entry. The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-cultivation of the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, and individual enlightenment.

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-cultivation of the knowledge of all aspects. The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is the cultivation of the non-cultivation of the abandonment of all latencies and their continuations.

The cultivation of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: "But how, Blessed One, is the cultivation of the non-cultivation of form the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom? ... up to ... how is the cultivation of the non-cultivation of the abandonment of all latencies and their connections the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:

In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not cultivate the thought that form is an entity, nor does he cultivate the thought that up to consciousness is an entity. He does not cultivate the thought that up to all-aspect omniscience is an entity, nor does he cultivate the thought that the abandonment of all latencies and their connections is an entity. Why is that?
Subhūti, for one who perceives entities, there is no cultivation of the perfection of generosity;

there is no cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, or the perfection of meditative concentration. Subhūti, for one who perceives entities, there is no cultivation of the perfection of wisdom.
For one who perceives entities, there is no cultivation of the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, for one who is attached to entities, there is this attachment to giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom. For one who is thus attached, there is no liberation. Subhūti, for one who perceives entities, there is no cultivation of the applications of mindfulness.
There is no cultivation of the right efforts, no cultivation of the bases of psychic power, no cultivation of the faculties, no cultivation of the powers;

no cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, no cultivation of the path, no cultivation of emptiness, no cultivation of the signless, no cultivation of the wishless; indeed, there is no cultivation of the knowledge of all aspects. Why is that?
For in this way, Subhūti, he is attached to existence. When this was said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"What, O Blessed One, is existence?
And what is non-existence?"
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, duality is existence;
non-duality is non-existence. Subhūti asked:
"What, Blessed One, is duality?
The Blessed One said: "The perception of form, Subhūti, is duality."
The notion of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is duality;
the notion of the eye up to the notion of the mind is duality;
the notion of form up to the notion of phenomena, up to the notion of the Buddha, the notion of awakening, and the notion of the conditioned realm [are duality].
Subhūti, the notion of the unconditioned realm, up to all notions and even non-notion—all this is duality.
As long as there is duality, so long is there existence;
as long as there is existence, so long is there the conditioned.
"As long as there are formative forces (*saṃskāra*), so long are sentient beings not fully liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.
Therefore, Subhūti, by this very method it should be understood:
for one who possesses dualistic perception, there is no giving, no ethical discipline, no patience, no diligence, no meditative concentration, and no wisdom."
There is no path, there is no attainment, and there is no realization;
there is not even the conformable patience,
so how much less could there be the full comprehension of form, up to the full comprehension of consciousness?
What is the full comprehension of all-aspect omniscience?
For one who lacks the cultivation of the path,
how could there be the fruit of stream-entry, how could there be anything up to arhatship, and how could there be pratyekabuddhahood?
From where up to the abandonment of all latencies and their continuations? (69) Chapter 70. (AdSPG I 197)
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

“If, Blessed One, those who perceive entities do not possess even the patient acceptance that accords with reality (*anulomikī kṣānti*), how much less could there be attainment, and how much less realization?”
Furthermore, for one who perceives non-existence, would there not be the patient acceptance that accords with truth (*anulomikī kṣānti*),

or the stage of bright insight (*śuklavidarśanabhūmi*), or the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), or the stage of the eighth person (*aṣṭamakabhūmi*), or the stage of seeing (*darśanabhūmi*), or the stage of refinement (*tanubhūmi*),
or the stage of freedom from passion (*vītarāgabhūmi*), or the stage of one who has completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvībhūmi*), or the stage of a pratyekabuddha, or the stage of a bodhisattva?

Or the stage of a Buddha; or the cultivation of the path— that cultivation of the path by relying upon which one does not abandon the afflictions associated with Śrāvakas or those associated with Pratyekabuddhas,
and by which afflictions being obscured, one would not enter the Bodhisattva’s determination (nyāma).
Without entering the fixed course of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattvanyāma*), one would not attain all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*);
and without attaining all-aspect omniscience, one would not abandon the afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies (*sarvavāsanānusandhikleśa*).
If, Blessed One, there is no arising of any dharma that is arising, and it is impossible to attain all-aspect omniscience without having produced these dharmas?
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, Subhūti, so it is. For one who perceives non-existence, there is no conformable patience, up to and including the abandonment of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.
Subhūti asked: "But, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom have the perception of existence or the perception of non-existence?"
Whether it be the perception of form up to the perception of consciousness,
or even the perception of the knowledge of all aspects,
or the perception of passion or the perception of the abandonment of passion.
Whether it be the perception of hatred or the perception of the abandonment of hatred;
the perception of delusion or the perception of the abandonment of delusion; the perception of ignorance or the perception of the abandonment of ignorance.

Whether it be the perception of volitional formations or the perception of the abandonment of volitional formations; whether it be the perception of consciousness or the perception of the abandonment of consciousness; whether it be the perception of name-and-form or the perception of the abandonment of name-and-form.
Either the perception of the six sense bases, or the perception of the abandonment of the six sense bases;
either the perception of contact, or the perception of the abandonment of contact;
or the perception of feeling, or the perception of the abandonment of feeling.
Whether it be the perception of craving or the perception of the abandonment of craving;
the perception of grasping or the perception of the abandonment of grasping;
the perception of existence or the perception of the abandonment of existence;
Either the perception of birth or the perception of the abandonment of birth;
either the perception of aging-and-death or the perception of the abandonment of aging-and-death;
or the perception of sorrow and lamentation or the perception of the abandonment of sorrow and lamentation.
Either the perception of suffering or the perception of the abandonment of suffering;
either the perception of origination or the perception of the abandonment of origination;
either the perception of cessation or the perception of the abandonment of cessation.
Is it the perception of the path, or the perception of the abandonment of the path,
up to the perception of the knowledge of all aspects, or the perception of the abandonment that abandons all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies?
The Blessed One said:

"Not so, Subhūti. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, he does not form a perception of existence or a perception of non-existence regarding any dharma whatsoever. This very state, wherein there is neither a perception of existence nor a perception of non-existence, is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s conformable patience; this alone is his cultivation of the path."

Where there is neither the perception of existence nor the perception of non-existence—this itself is its fruit, where there is neither the perception of existence nor the perception of non-existence. Furthermore, Subhūti, non-existence is indeed the path of the bodhisattva mahāsattva;
non-existence itself is the realization. Therefore, Subhūti, by this method also, it should be understood in this way:
"All dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature. He asked:

"If, Blessed One, all dharmas have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, then how, Blessed One, have all dharmas that have non-existence as their intrinsic nature been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata?"
"For the sake of whose perfect awakening has mastery over the domain of all phenomena been attained? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"In this regard, Subhūti, while I was formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva,"
Practicing in the six perfections,

secluded indeed from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, I attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna— which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with joy and bliss— and so on up to the fourth dhyāna. Thus, I...
Not grasping at the signs of those meditations and the factors of meditation,
I do not conceive through those meditations,
nor do I relish the meditations.
I do not apprehend the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Thus, I enter those meditative absorptions which are purified in their aspects;

having brought those meditative absorptions to fruition, I direct my mind toward the realization of various types of knowledge, up to the realization of the knowledge of the divine ear, the realization of the knowledge of the thoughts of others, and the realization of the knowledge of recollecting former abodes.

I direct my mind toward the realization of the knowledge of the divine eye. In the realization of those [knowledges], not grasping at signs, I do not conceive pride through those superknowledges, I do not relish them, and I do not apprehend them. Thus, I view those five superknowledges as equal to space and I enter into them. Subhūti, with wisdom endowed with the single characteristic, I [attain] the unsurpassed...
Having fully awakened to perfect enlightenment, [he realized]: "This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering;
this is the cessation of suffering."

"I have understood, as it truly is, that 'this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges,
great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, I [lead] sentient beings..."
"I give a prediction regarding three categories.
He asked: "How, Blessed One, were the four dhyānas, which have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, produced by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha?
How were the six superknowledges, which have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, produced?"
"How are beings and non-beings designated within the three groups?
The Blessed One said:
"If, Subhūti, there were an intrinsic nature of sensual desires, or of evil, unwholesome states, or of conditioned entities, or if there were a self-nature or an other-nature [in them],"

Subhūti, when I was formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, it was not by perceiving sensual pleasures as having the nature of non-existence, nor by perceiving evil, unwholesome states as having the nature of non-existence, that I attained and dwelt in the four dhyānas. This is because, Subhūti, there is no intrinsic nature in sensual pleasures or in evil, unwholesome states, neither their own-being nor another-being.
It is solely because its intrinsic nature is non-existence;

therefore, formerly, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

In this way, I attained and dwelt in the fourth dhyāna. Subhūti, if there were any existence, intrinsic nature, or extrinsic nature in the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), then, Subhūti, having realized that all superknowledges are without intrinsic nature (*abhāvasvabhāva*), I would not have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*). But since, Subhūti, there is no existence, no [intrinsic nature], nor [extrinsic nature] in any of the superknowledges...
There is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*),
except for the very nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva*);

therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having realized that all supernormal knowledges (*sarvābhijñā*) have the nature of non-existence, has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*).
